💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ocean Power Technologies announced on November 23, 2026 that Nauticus Robotics had signed a non-binding letter of intent to acquire its WAM-V unmanned surface vessel business for $8 million in Nauticus Series C convertible preferred stock at closing, plus up to $2 million in additional cash.
  • According to recent reports, nauticus’s announcement specifies that the proposed asset purchase includes associated software and intellectual property.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ocean Power Technologies announced on November 23, 2026 that Nauticus Robotics had signed a non-binding letter of intent to acquire its WAM-V unmanned surface vessel business for $8 million in Nauticus Series C convertible preferred stock at closing, plus up to $2 million in additional cash.

According to recent reports, nauticus’s announcement specifies that the proposed asset purchase includes associated software and intellectual property. The unmanned surface vessels, or USVs, would extend Nauticus’s subsea robotics portfolio into surface operations, with ToolKITT integration intended to enable coordinated operations between WAM-V vessels and Aquanaut autonomous subsea robots.

The contingent cash would comprise 20% of proceeds from Nauticus at-the-market share sales through December 31, 2026, and a 5% royalty on WAM-V revenue. Nauticus president and CEO John Gibson remarked the preferred-stock structure would expand the company’s autonomous robotics capabilities “without impacting current cash reserves.”.

Nauticus describes ToolKITT as modular, vehicle-agnostic software that can work alongside existing vehicle-control software when a vehicle’s software interfaces permit. It is designed for Nauticus and third-party underwater vehicles as well as surface vessels. Current functions center on pilot assistance, software-assisted control and repeatable workflows; obstacle avoidance remains in development, and the product page tells customers to begin integration now and blueprint for delivery in early 2027.

Industry observers note that nauticus describes Aquanaut 2.1 as an all-electric, untethered vehicle with ToolKITT-native autonomy for transit, survey and inspection, and lists customer configurations up to a 3,000-meter design rating. The underlying Mk2 platform has demonstrated an operating depth of 2,300 meters, while autonomous manipulation and collision and obstacle avoidance remain future capabilities. The integration goal therefore goes beyond those single-vehicle functions: coordinated WAM-V–Aquanaut operations are an objective of the proposed acquisition.

OPT describes WAM-V as a modular, wave-adaptive platform for coastal, littoral, harbor and inland operations and reports more than 80 platforms delivered globally. Its patented articulating suspension and twin-hull configuration support sensor, communications and mission payloads, while modular interfaces allow propulsion and equipment to be configured for mapping, monitoring, inspection, surveillance and data collection.

The parties are targeting signing and closing within 45 days, subject to a definitive agreement, approval by both boards, due diligence, required regulatory approvals, and consents from Nauticus’s lender and preferred stockholders. Nauticus cautioned that neither a definitive agreement nor completion of the transaction is assured.

It has been revealed that OPT indicates it has reduced ongoing operating expenses by 65% as part of its strategic review. Following the WAM-V transaction, it would focus on its U.S. PowerBuoy business, which serves U.S. government customers including the Department of Homeland Security, and on its MERROWS and MDAS software. A separate consulting agreement with Stratum Holdings provides up to $3 million in annual retainer payments to OPT in exchange for U.S. exclusivity while the companies evaluate PowerBuoy technology for powering and connecting offshore data centers.

Recent findings suggest that the proposal would give Nauticus a surface-vessel business on which to pursue shared autonomy, while OPT would retain a narrower business centered on PowerBuoy and software. The next substantive test is whether the parties can secure the required approvals and turn ToolKITT’s cross-vehicle architecture into the coordinated surface-and-subsea operations Nauticus envisions.

Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reiver

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software.
  • Every numbered statement below is false.
  • Sources indicate that these are not made up for effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names” — a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true, but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software. That article started a whole genre of Falsehoods Programmers Believe articles. This article ("Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto") is one of my contributions to that genre.

Every numbered statement below is false. Each one is followed by what is actually true — and where to read more.

Sources indicate that these are not made up for effect. Each one is backed by the specification, or by a live request to real ATProto servers (made in November 2026).

According to recent reports, handles can change. The account's DID is what is permanent — the accounts specification calls it (DIDs) “unique and immutable”.

My handle changed! My handle was first reiver.bsky.social, then became reiver.myatproto.social, and then later became reiver.blacksky.team. You can see that if you dig through the data at plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit. (did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz is my DID-PLC DID.).

So, a handle is a good database key for a user.

Use the DID. Store the handle only for display (cosmetic) purposes — and re-check what each DID's handle is from time to time.

Industry observers note that but, you need to normalize the DID before using it. DIDs are URIs, and URI schemes are case-insensitive (RFC 3986) — so DID:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz and did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz are the same DID. ATProto requires the normalized (lowercase) form: normalize DIDs when they come from user input, store and compare only the normalized form, and reject non-normalized DIDs that arrive in protocol data.

When a user changes their handle, the first part stays the same — such as reiver.bsky.social → reiver.myatproto.social → reiver.blacksky.team.

A fresh handle does not have to have anything in common with the old one. joeblow.bsky.social → me.example.com → bbqlover.net → ilikeicecream.com would be fine. Changing a handle just means pointing the account at a different domain — com.atproto.identity.updateHandle takes any valid handle, and only “Verifies handle validity”.

In a recent development, for example, Bluesky's own account (did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur) started out as bluesky-team.bsky.social, and then became bsky.app. You can see that in its audit log at plc.directory/did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur/log/audit. (Another reason to key people by DID, and not by any part of their handle.).

You can trust a handle you saw five minutes ago.

According to recent reports, A handle can change at any moment. The user can switch to a new handle. The domain's owner can point it at a different DID — or the domain can expire, and be registered by someone else. Or, its DNS record or /.well-known/atproto-did file can just disappear, and the handle stops resolving. The handle specification notes “If the handle for a known DID is confirmed to no longer resolve, it should be marked as invalid.”.

Sources indicate that so, a handle → DID mapping is only as good as when you last checked it. The specification recommends caching handle resolution “up to some lifetime”, and re-resolving “periodically”. Watch the firehose for #identity events, which announce handle changes. And, never use a cached handle to decide who someone is (for example, for permissions) — use the DID.

According to recent reports, an account might have no handle in its DID document (no at:// entry in alsoKnownAs), or a handle that no longer resolves back to it. The DID specification claims “an account whose DID document does not contain a valid and confirmed handle can still participate in the atproto ecosystem. Software should be careful to either not display any handle for such account, or obviously indicate that any handle associated with it is invalid.”.

In API responses, such an account's handle may show up as the special value handle.invalid — which “can not be used in most situations (search queries, API requests, etc).” And, the handle field on the firehose's #identity event is optional. So, your code needs a “no handle” case.

Every handle ends in .bsky.social.

Any Internet domain can be a handle. And, other PDSes hand out their own — the blacksky.app PDS, for example, offers .blacksky.app, .myatproto.social, .cryptoanarchy.network, and others.

Even if a user's handle is not a .bsky.social handle now, their first handle was.

A user's first handle is whatever they got when their account was created — on whichever PDS they signed up with. com.atproto.server.createAccount just takes a “Requested handle for the account”, and each PDS offers its own domains. So, someone who signed up on blacksky.app might start out as alice.myatproto.social — and never have had a .bsky.social handle at all.

You can see this in a DID's audit log on plc.directory (https://plc.directory//log/audit) — the very first operation (the one that created the DID) highlights the first handle, and the first PDS. For example, the audit log for did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w (plc.directory/did:plc:ub2k2k5zahuegnkkvxjk5y2w/log/audit) has just 1 operation — the one that created it, on November 13th, 2026. Its first handle was shadowoftruth.myatproto.social, and its first PDS was blacksky.app. It has never had a .bsky.social handle.

A handle is a third-level domain — like alice.bsky.social, alice.blacksky.app, or alice.myatproto.social.

Sources indicate that A handle can have any number of segments, as long as there are at least 2. example.com is a valid handle — and so is apple.banana.cherry.example.com. The handle specification only says “there must be at least two segments” (so a bare top-level domain like com is not allowed), each segment can be 1 to 63 characters, and the whole handle can be at most 253 characters. Its own examples include a.co, 8.cn, and XX.LCS.MIT.EDU; and the official test vectors include john.test.bsky.app, and a valid handle with 10 segments.

According to recent reports, with DNS (a TXT record at _atproto.) or HTTPS (/.well-known/atproto-did). You need to support both.

If a DID document lists a handle, the account owns that handle.

Anyone can put any handle in their own DID document. The handle has to resolve back to the same DID — both directions must agree. Otherwise, show handle.invalid.

com.atproto.identity.resolveHandle checks both directions for you.

Its own lexicon indicates it “Does not necessarily bi-directionally verify against the the DID document.” (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.).

Handles are case-sensitive — so keep the capitalization the user typed.

Handles are not case-sensitive. The handle specification says “Only normalized (lowercase) handles should be stored in records or used in outbound API calls. Applications should not preserve user-provided case information and attempt to display handles in anything other than lower-case.” Its example: “the handle input string BlueskyWeb.xyz should be normalized, stored, and displayed as blueskyweb.xyz.”.

It is just decoration, for display. The handle specification says “Handles may be prefixed with the "at" symbol (like @user.example.com) in user interfaces, but this is not a valid syntax for a handle in records, APIs, and other back-end contexts.” So, strip it from user input before resolving.

On example.com's own site, it is fine to show @alice.example.com as just @alice.

The handle specification says “Handles should generally not be truncated to local context. For example, the handle @alice.example.com should not be displayed as @alice, even in the local context of an example.com service.” (It also warns that very long handles “can result in similar complications when truncated at the start or end” — for example, a handle that starts with paypal.com being shown as paypal.com….).

It has been revealed that did:web is supported too. Your code needs to handle both.

In ATProto, “did:web is restricted in atproto to only full domains, not paths or port specification” (from the record key specification).

Whatever plc.directory returns for a DID is that DID's document.

Recent findings suggest that check that the document's id matches the DID you asked for. (See: How-To Resolve a DID to a PDS.).

A did:plc is case-insensitive — so DID:PLC:… or did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR is fine.

Sources indicate that the did: and the method name (plc) must be lowercase — “The URI starts with lowercase did:”, and “The method segment is one or more lowercase letters”. And, a did:plc identifier is lowercase too: “the entire identifier is lower-case (and should be normalized to lower-case)” (from the did:plc specification). The ATProto specification says “protocol implementations should reject DIDs with invalid casing.” (plc.directory answered did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR, did:PLC:…, and DID:PLC:… with 400 “Resolution of non-PLC DIDs not supported”.).

(This is about DIDs in protocol data — records, tokens, API responses. As a URI, the did: scheme is case-insensitive, so DID: means the same thing — but ATProto requires the normalized, lowercase form there. DIDs typed in by a user may be normalized; see item 2. And, even under the general DID syntax, the method name must be lowercase, so did:PLC:… is invalid on its own.).

DIDs are case-sensitive — so did:plc:abc… and did:plc:ABC… are 2 different accounts.

In a recent development, for did:plc, the uppercase one is not a different DID — it is not a valid did:plc at all, since its identifier is lowercase-only base32. The ATProto specification states “the currently-supported methods are not case sensitive, and could be safely lowercased”, and that “It is permissible to attempt case normalization when receiving user-controlled input, such as when parsing public URL path components, or text input fields.” So: reject bad casing in protocol data; lowercasing what a user typed is fine.

If a DID parser accepts it, it is a valid DID.

According to recent reports, A generic DID parser only checks the generic syntax — which allows uppercase in the identifier (the test vectors list did:method:VAL as valid). The indigo library's syntax.ParseDID accepts did:plc:Z72I7HDYNMK6R22Z27H6TVUR — but plc.directory rejects it. Generic syntax is not the same as a valid did:plc.

A did:plc's DID document never changes.

The DID never changes — but its DID document can. Each change is a signed operation, and the handle (alsoKnownAs), the PDS (the #atproto_pds service), the signing key (#atproto), and the rotation keys can all be changed.

For example, my DID's audit log (plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit) has 4 operations:.

Sources indicate that and, the did:plc specification has 2 more surprises. A “tombstone” operation “clears all of the data fields and permanently deactivates the DID”. And, there is a 72-hour window during which a higher-authority rotation key can “"rewrite" history”. So, do not cache a DID document forever — re-resolve it from time to time, and watch the firehose for #identity events.

“Personal” Data Server means one server per person.

Sources indicate that “Many PDSes will host multiple owners” (the glossary). Most host many.

Bluesky users' data is on bsky.social.

The server a user logs in at is the server that has their data.

It has been revealed that it might be an entryway — a separate OAuth server for many PDSes. puffball.us-east.host.bsky.network's /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource lists https://bsky.social as its authorization server. (blacksky.app, on the other hand, lists itself.).

Accounts can migrate to another PDS — that is a core design goal. Always look up the current PDS from the DID document (and do not cache it forever).

A user's PDS can show them everyone's posts.

A PDS only has its own accounts' data. For timelines, threads, and counts, it forwards the request to an AppView. (See: ATProto PDS.).

A user's PDS builds (or renders) their timeline.

The timeline (app.bsky.feed.getTimeline) is built by an AppView. The PDS just forwards the app's request to it. And, no server renders it — the AppView returns JSON, and the app (on the user's phone or computer) renders that.

According to recent reports, (This one used to be closer to true. Bluesky's feed generator starter kit still notes “In the future, the PDS will hydrate the feed with the help of an App View, but for now, the PDS handles hydration itself.” Today, the AppView does it. See: ATProto Feed Generator.).

Bluesky's PDS software is the only PDS software.

Any server that implements the right end-points is a PDS. (For example, the Blacksky team's rsky project, written in Rust, includes rsky-pds.).

Self-hosting a PDS means you have to index the entire network.

A PDS only stores its own accounts' data. Indexing the network is the job of relays and AppViews — a self-hosted PDS uses someone else's. (In Bluesky's PDS software, PDS_CRAWLERS defaults to https://bsky.network, and PDS_BSKY_APP_VIEW_URL defaults to https://api.bsky.app.).

Sources indicate that that is why the hardware is small. The official PDS instructions recommend 1 GB of memory, 1 CPU core, and a 20 GB SSD — for 1 to 20 customers. (See: ATProto PDS.).

Every record on the network is a Bluesky post.

Industry observers note that A repository can hold records of any type — any lexicon, from any app — all mixed together in the same user's repository. Calendar events, bookmarks, blog posts, game state, workout logs, or a custom app's own schema: each is just another collection. (And, by default, a PDS accepts records whose lexicon it does not know — “optimistic validation”.).

For example, my repository (reiver.blacksky.team) has these collections, according to com.atproto.repo.describeRepo:.

Only one of those 14 collections is Bluesky posts (app.bsky.feed.post). Even among Bluesky's own record types, most are not posts — likes, reposts, follows, lists, a profile. And, actor.rpg.* and equipment.rpg.item are from a different app altogether. (See: ATProto Record.).

Everything a user does on ATProto is public.

Everything in a user's repository is public — posts, likes, follows, and even blocks (see the next item). But, not everything a user does is stored as a record in their repository. For example, in Bluesky:.

Note that this data is private from the public — not encrypted. The PDS (or chat service) that holds it can read it. And, these are features of particular apps and services (app.bsky.*, chat.bsky.*), not a privacy guarantee of the protocol itself.

(The spaces proposal would add something new: records that only some people may read — see the Spaces section, below.).

Blocks are private, like mutes.

In Bluesky, a mute is private — but a block is a public record. A block is an app.bsky.graph.block record in the blocker's repository, and its lexicon says so plainly: “Record declaring a 'block' relationship against another account. NOTE: blocks are public in Bluesky; see blog posts for details.”.

According to recent reports, so, anyone can list an account's blocks — for example, with com.atproto.repo.listRecords, or from the firehose — and see who blocked whom. If you build features on blocks, treat them as public information.

The author is the repository the record is in. (See: ATProto Record.).

A record key is unique within a repository.

“The tuple of (did, rkey) is not unique; the tuple (did, collection, rkey) is unique.”.

According to recent reports, TIDs (like 3n2opitxdyc2j) are the most common, but each record type's lexicon notes which kind of record key it uses. The record key specification defines 4 kinds:.

Some other things about record keys:.

A tid record key tells you when the record was created.

“Record keys are "user-controlled data" and may be arbitrarily selected by hostile accounts.” Do not trust them as timestamps.

A record's createdAt is when it was created.

It is whatever the client put there. The app.bsky.feed.post lexicon describes it as a “Client-declared timestamp”. A client can set it to any time — past or future.

When a record was actually seen is tracked separately, by the services that see it:.

Industry observers note that for example, for one of @bsky.app's posts, public.api.bsky.app reported createdAt as 2026-11-19T18:33:36.813Z, and indexedAt as 2026-11-19T18:33:38.543Z — close, here, but nothing requires them to be. (Even these are each one service's view — a different AppView may have indexed it at a different time.).

ATProto JSON is just regular JSON.

According to recent reports, it is JSON with extra rules, from the ATProto data model — the same data model that is also written as DRISL-CBOR (the successor to DAG-CBOR) for storing, signing, and hashing. The differences from regular JSON:.

It is not DAG-JSON either — the data model specification claims ATProto uses $link “as the key name instead of /”. And, there are practical limits too — for example, Bluesky's data validation guide suggests at most 32 levels of nesting, and 1 MiB per record (as CBOR). (See: ATProto Record.).

Records can contain floating-point numbers.

Floats are not allowed in the data model — they do not round-trip reliably, and the bytes must be exact for hashing.

You can compute a record's CID by hashing its JSON.

The CID is a hash of its DRISL-CBOR encoding. JSON is not byte-exact.

A missing field and a null field mean the same thing.

They are different — and both are different from false, 0, or an empty array.

Every record in a repository is valid against its lexicon.

In a recent development, by default, a PDS only checks records whose lexicon it knows (“optimistic validation”, or “fail-open”). Validate what you read.

A record with fields its lexicon does not mention is invalid.

Recent findings suggest that unexpected fields should be ignored — “at worst as warnings”. (Validating a post with an extra mood field against app.bsky.feed.post passes. See: ATProto Lexicon.).

A deleted record leaves a tombstone.

“Record deletion is supported without leaving a trace or "tombstone" of previous contents.”.

Deleting a record removes it from the Internet.

Deleting a record removes it from the user's repository. But, by then, copies may already be elsewhere — the creation went out on the PDS's firehose, and relays, AppViews, feed generators, search indexes, backups, and anyone else watching may have kept it.

The deletion goes out on the firehose too, and the specifications expect other services to follow it. The accounts specification indicates “When accounts remove records from their public repositories, hosting services should remove public access to that content.” And, the sync specification says mirrors should “respect repository updates (eg, record deletion) … in a timely manner (within seconds or minutes)”. But, “should” is not a guarantee — nothing forces every service to comply, and a copy someone else kept (or a screenshot) is out of the user's control.

According to recent reports, (And, since the data was signed, such a copy can still be shown to be genuine. Treat anything written to a public repository as published.).

An NSID is an address you can fetch.

Sources indicate that it is a name — a reversed Internet domain plus a name. (See: ATProto NSID.).

It is safe to lowercase an NSID.

Industry observers note that the Internet domain part is not case-sensitive, but the name is — getRecord is not getrecord. “Implementations should not force-lowercase NSIDs.”.

Implementations reject an NSID whose Internet domain part is longer than 253 characters.

The specification says 253 — but the official test vectors list a 283-character one as valid, and Bluesky's TypeScript and Go code only check the 317-character total.

If _lexicon.feed.bsky.app does not exist, try _lexicon.bsky.app.

According to recent reports, lexicon resolution is not hierarchical. If the exact record does not exist, resolution simply fails. (See: How-To Resolve a Lexicon.).

The app.bsky.* lexicons are in the bluesky-social/atproto repository on GitHub.

It has been revealed that not anymore — its main branch has no lexicons/app/bsky/ directory. Resolve them from the network instead (they are published by did:plc:4v4y5r3lwsbtmsxhile2ljac).

A union in a lexicon lists every type you will ever see there.

Unions are open by default — newly introduced types can be added. (The live app.bsky.feed.post lexicon's embed union includes app.bsky.embed.gallery, which older code will not know about.).

It can change — in compatible ways (new optional fields, more union types, etc).

You need a special library to talk ATProto.

XRPC is plain HTTP and JSON. curl works. (See: ATProto XRPC.).

A server returns the error names listed in the end-point's lexicon.

In a recent development, not always. resolveHandle's lexicon lists HandleNotFound, but public.api.bsky.app answered an unknown handle with InvalidRequest.

The specification itself warns that “many services will return generic load-balancer or reverse-proxy HTML error pages.”.

An end-point a server does not have returns 404.

A Bluesky PDS answered a made-up end-point with 401 AuthMissing.

A cursor means something you can use.

In a recent development, treat it as opaque. (One server's listRecords cursor happens to be the last record key — do not depend on that.).

Every PDS has its own firehose, and there are several relays — for example, Bluesky's bsky.network and the Blacksky team's atproto.africa. (See: ATProto Relay.).

A user's PDS knows who follows them.

It has been revealed that A follow is an app.bsky.graph.follow record — stored in the follower's repository, with the followed account's DID as its subject. So, a user's PDS knows exactly who the user follows, but not who follows them — those records are spread across everyone else's repositories, on every PDS. (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

Likes and replies live on the author's post.

They live in the repositories of the people who liked or replied. A like is an app.bsky.feed.like record in the liker's repository, whose subject is a strong reference (uri and cid) to the post. A reply is an app.bsky.feed.post record in the replier's repository, with a reply field pointing at the thread's root and the parent post. (Reposts work the same way.) The author's post record itself has no list of likes or replies, and no counts.

So, like and reply counts — and threads — are put together by services that index the network, like an AppView or a backlink index. For example, for one of @bsky.app's posts (app.bsky.feed.post/3n2opitxdyc2j), on November 22nd, 2026, public.api.bsky.app noted 1951 likes and 774 replies — and so did the Constellation backlink index. (For a recent post, they agree. For older ones, they may not — see the follower counts, below.).

It is one service's opinion. For the same account (reiver.blacksky.team), at the same time (November 22nd, 2026), public.api.bsky.app (Bluesky's AppView) noted 292 followers, api.blacksky.community (the Blacksky team's AppView) said 196, and the Constellation backlink index said 134. (See: ATProto AppView and How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

With enough work, a follower count can be computed exactly.

You would have to check every repository on every PDS — and you can never be sure you found them all, since a relay only knows the hosts it crawls. By the time you finished, the answer would have changed. And, what counts as a follower is a choice — for example, the app.bsky.graph.follow lexicon indicates “Duplicate follows will be ignored by the AppView.” (See: How-To Count an ATProto Account's Followers.).

A feed generator sends you posts.

It sends a skeleton — a list of post URIs. The AppView fills in the posts. (See: ATProto Feed Generator.).

A label is a signed annotation. What to do with it (hide, blur, warn, nothing) is up to each app and user. (See: ATProto Labeler.).

Account status (active, deactivated, etc) can be verified cryptographically.

“Unlike other aspects of atproto, account status is not self-certifying”. It is passed along hop by hop — so different services may disagree. When in doubt, ask the account's own PDS (com.atproto.sync.getRepoStatus).

Recent findings suggest that bluesky is one app built on it. Others use their own lexicons — for example, site.standard.document, community.lexicon.calendar.event, and actor.rpg.sprite.

ATProto is a microblogging protocol.

Microblogging (short posts, like Bluesky's) is just one thing built on it. The overview describes ATProto as “a decentralized protocol for large-scale social web applications”. Nothing in the core protocol is about posts — records, repositories, XRPC, and sync work the same for any record type. What a record is comes from its lexicon, and anyone with a domain can define fresh ones.

For example: long-form documents (site.standard.document), calendar events (community.lexicon.calendar.event), game sprites (actor.rpg.sprite), custom feeds (app.bsky.feed.generator), and, in the spaces proposal, bookmarks, private forums, and group chats. Even the protocol's own lexicons are published as records (com.atproto.lexicon.schema).

(Falsehoods that come from comparing ATProto with ActivityPub, the Fediverse, and Mastodon.).

Unlike ActivityPub (and the Fediverse, and Mastodon), ATProto does not use JSON-LD.

It has been revealed that DID documents are JSON-LD. plc.directory serves them with the content type application/did+ld+json, and each one starts with an @context:.

(That is from plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz. A did:web document has one too — for example, api.bsky.app/.well-known/did.json.).

What is true is that ATProto's own data — records, lexicons, XRPC — is not JSON-LD. And, ATProto software usually reads DID documents as plain JSON — the ATProto DID specification says which fields to read, and does not call for JSON-LD processing.

Like on Mastodon, an ATProto handle includes the user's server — @user@server.

On Mastodon, a user's full address is a user name and a server — Mastodon's documentation says it is “in the form @username@domain”, and that “@user@example.com is not the same as @user@example.org.”.

Industry observers note that an ATProto handle is just one domain name — like reiver.blacksky.team — and it claims nothing about the user's server. The server (PDS) is found separately, from the DID document. (A handle shown as @reiver.blacksky.team has just one @, as a decoration.).

ATProto has nothing like a Fediverse “instance”.

The difference is that it is more hidden. It is not part of the user's identity or handle — reiver.blacksky.team does not say which PDS hosts it. It is not what decides what a user sees — that is mostly the AppView. And, a user can move to another PDS while keeping the same DID, handle, posts, and followers.

Like Mastodon, ATProto looks up handles with WebFinger.

Mastodon uses WebFinger (/.well-known/webfinger) — its documentation claims “WebFinger is required for fully interoperating with Mastodon.”.

ATProto does not. A handle is resolved with a DNS TXT record at _atproto., or with https:///.well-known/atproto-did. (See: How-To Resolve a Handle to a DID.).

Like on Mastodon, when a user moves to a new server, their posts stay behind, and their followers have to be moved over.

On Mastodon, moving an account moves followers — but Mastodon's documentation indicates “Your posts will not be moved, due to technical limitations”, and that “Mastodon at the moment does not support importing posts or media”. Moving also has to “force everyone to unfollow your current account and follow your fresh account”.

According to recent reports, on ATProto, moving to a fresh PDS includes “migrating data from the old PDS to the new PDS” (from the accounts specification) — the whole repository, posts and all. And, the account keeps the same DID. Since follow records point at the DID, followers do not have to be moved at all. (See: ATProto PDS.).

Like ActivityPub servers, ATProto servers send posts to each other's inboxes.

In ActivityPub, a server pushes each activity to its recipients — the ActivityPub specification describes it being “inserted into the actor's inbox (delivery)”, by HTTP POST.

Like in ActivityPub, to trust a copy of a post, you have to check it against the server it came from.

It has been revealed that the ActivityPub specification states servers should do “something at least as robust as checking that the object appears as received at its origin”, and that “No particular mechanism for verification is authoritatively specified”. (Mastodon uses HTTP Signatures, to check who sent an activity.).

Industry observers note that ATProto data checks itself. Repository commits are signed with the account's key, and records are identified by their hash (CID) — so a copy can be checked no matter who it came from. The data model specification notes this “makes it possible to redistribute content and trust copies even if coming from an untrusted party.” (See: ATProto Record.).

ATProto and the Fediverse cannot talk to each other.

Industry observers note that they are different protocols — but there are bridges. For example, Bridgy Fed describes itself as “a decentralized social network bridge. It connects the fediverse, the web, and the Atmosphere (Bluesky).” With it, people on one network can follow, reply to, like, and repost people on the other.

(These are about the spaces proposal, which is not yet part of the specification.).

According to recent reports, “Atproto spaces provide access control, not confidentiality. They are not end-to-end encrypted.”.

A space is stored on one server.

Industry observers note that each member's records stay on that member's own PDS. “The space does not colocate records on a single network host.”.

A copy of space data proves who wrote it.

Space data is authenticated with MACs, not signatures — on purpose, so that it “should not carry proof of authorship that survives a leak outside its access boundary.”.

Most of these come from the same idea: ATProto separates things that are usually tied together.

So, the safe defaults are: key everything by DID; resolve, do not assume; validate what you read; ignore what you do not understand; and expect other servers to disagree with yours.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.

It has been revealed that dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds. In the Bistro night scene, standard three.js under WebGL leaves the cobblestones cool and flat, with a blown-out white hotspot around the round shop sign. Even with WebGPU and SSGI turned on, the lamp glare stays harsh and the pavement loses multi-bounce warmth. Slide the divider across to ThreeRT, and warm golden light spills from the shop window across the facade while overhead string lights tint the street in their own colors.

Industry observers note that the Zero-Day sci-fi corridor shows an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline. On the three.js side, ceiling pipes and glossy floors pick up heavy speckle noise, and unlit industrial housings sink into dark blue shadows. ThreeRT keeps those white and grey panels legible through soft indirect bounce light from tiny amber emitters. It doesn't rely on light probes or baked maps, so moving the camera at 60 fps never breaks the reflections of off-screen geometry.

In a recent development, that matters for the future of ray tracing in the browser. Today, ThreeRT runs its Rust and wgpu path tracer inside a native client while exposing a familiar three.js-style TypeScript API. The same scene code still runs as plain three.js in any browser or WebView, which gives developers one codebase across both worlds. As WebGPU hardware ray tracing matures on the web, that gap is closing fast.

You can see the range in the project gallery, from the OpenStrikeRT foundry hall where a furnace lights the surrounding concrete, to smaller studies like Jeweller's Window, Daylight Home, and Boutique Showroom. Each surface reacts to real emitters instead of faked ambient fill. See the full project on ThreeRTâs website.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • British retailer Next has become the latest high street name to find itself caught up in a cyberattack, although it insists the data accessed by hackers is "benign" and its customers have nothing to worry about.
  • According to recent reports, the clothing and homeware giant told investors on Monday that a third-party supplier had suffered a security breach, allowing an unauthorized party to access information relating to Next.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Retailer insists customer details are safe and the data accessed is 'benign,' but won't say exactly what hackers got their hands on.

British retailer Next has become the latest high street name to find itself caught up in a cyberattack, although it insists the data accessed by hackers is "benign" and its customers have nothing to worry about.

According to recent reports, the clothing and homeware giant told investors on Monday that a third-party supplier had suffered a security breach, allowing an unauthorized party to access information relating to Next. The retailer notes its own systems remain untouched and that, so far, there's no evidence that customer personal data has fallen into the wrong hands.

"We have been informed that one of our third-party online suppliers has experienced a cyber incident which has resulted in unauthorized access to certain benign data relating to NEXT," the company stated in its statement, which it shared with The Register. "We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier.".

The breached supplier provides technology services to Next, and the "benign" information accessed is understood to be low-level data. Sensitive customer details, including addresses, passwords, and banking information, are believed to be unaffected.

Recent findings suggest that next hasn't identified the supplier, explained exactly what the hackers managed to get their hands on, or revealed how much information was accessed, and declined to say when asked by The Register. However, the retailer has seemingly decided that the stolen data won’t be of much use to the criminals responsible.

"Our investigations are ongoing; however, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised," Next stated. "The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or NEXT.".

Next also stressed that its own IT infrastructure had escaped unscathed, saying it was "confident that NEXT’s own systems have not been compromised and that this remains an incident affecting the supplier's environment.".

Despite repeatedly describing the compromised information as harmless, Next indicates it is treating the incident "with the utmost seriousness" and is working with the affected supplier, law enforcement, and relevant regulators.

The incident comes just weeks after fellow British fashion retailer Asos suffered a breach of its own, with hackers gaining access to customer information through third-party platforms.

According to recent reports, that attack, which came to light on October 6 when customers received an unauthorized push notification through the Asos app announcing that the firm had been hacked, was traced to a social engineering scam. An attacker impersonated a trusted contact to trick an Asos employee into handing over login credentials, which were then used to access external platforms.

Asos later admitted that the intruders had accessed customer names, contact details, and some account information, but passwords and payment card details were apparently off limits.

Next reckons its customers have been luckier, but there’s a lot it isn’t telling us. The company has gone to some lengths to assure customers that the stolen data is harmless, but without knowing what was taken or who was supposed to be looking after it, we're largely left taking its word for it. ®.

Tech Report: Aligning to What? Rethinking Agent Generalization in MiniMax M2

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it's been fantastic to see the community dive into our newly introduced MiniMax M2, with many highlighting its impressive skills in complex agentic tasks.
  • According to recent reports, if you've worked with LLM Agents, you've felt this pain: the same model can feel brilliant in one framework and useless in another.
  • It has been revealed that when we designed M2, we knew we had to tackle this problem head-on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it's been fantastic to see the community dive into our newly introduced MiniMax M2, with many highlighting its impressive skills in complex agentic tasks. This is particularly exciting for me, as my work was centered on the agent alignment part of its post-training. In this post, I'd like to share some of the key insights and lessons we learned during that process.

According to recent reports, if you've worked with LLM Agents, you've felt this pain: the same model can feel brilliant in one framework and useless in another. An agent might crush a tool-use leaderboard but fail spectacularly at a simple, real-world task. This gap between benchmark performance and practical usability is one of the biggest challenges in the field.

It has been revealed that when we designed M2, we knew we had to tackle this problem head-on. This led us to two core, and sometimes conflicting, objectives:.

So, who do we align with? The answer is both. We align with benchmarks to build skill, but we must ultimately align with the user by ensuring those skills work everywhere.

While the methods for acing benchmarks are a deep topic for another day, I want to focus on that second, trickier objective: How do we train an agent for the wild?

Industry observers note that early in the project, we hit a frustrating wall. Agent performance was inconsistent, and we struggled to diagnose why. After many discussions, especially with Professor @Junxian He and @Wenhu Chen, we arrived at our first major conclusion: Agents require Interleaved Thinking.

This means that an agent's internal monologue—its "thinking"—can and should happen at any point during a task, not just once at the beginning like a standard reasoning model. This design is critical for two reasons:.

This principle became a cornerstone of M2's effectiveness.

Pro Tip for M2 Consumers: Because M2 relies on Interleaved Thinking, its context is its memory. For best performance, you must retain the full session history, including the thinking steps. We've noticed that much of the community feedback about performance gaps stems from accidentally discarding this vital context, which is a common practice with simpler reasoning models.

Our initial theory was simple: tool scaling is agent generalization.

We started with a minimal set of tools (a Python interpreter, search engine, a browser) to build a baseline of tool-calling capability. The roadmap was clear: scale up the number and variety of tools, and the agent's ability to generalize to unseen tools would naturally follow.

Sources indicate that at first, this worked. Our benchmark scores climbed to respectable levels. But as we dug deeper, we realized we were solving the wrong problem. The model aced the tests, but if we changed the environment even slightly—like swapping to a different scaffolding framework—its performance would plummet. We were still far from our goal of a "practically useful" model.

This led to our second, more profound realization: Agent generalization is not just about adapting to upcoming tools; it's about adapting to perturbations across the model's entire operational space.

According to recent reports, this sounds abstract, so let's break it down. Think about everything that can change in a single agent task:.

Recent findings suggest that our work on M2 taught us an immense amount about agents, generalization, and data, but it has opened up more questions than it answered. Many of our ideas are still on the whiteboard. In the coming months, we will be exploring these frontiers even more deeply, and we can't wait to bring you the next generation of powerful and genuinely useful models.

Is this the reason I observe output degradation in subsequent rounds in Chatbox+M2 API? Questions answered correctly in the first turn sometimes become incorrect.

The Danger of Old News, If It’s Also Fake News

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although the sheer scale of the Internet Archive makes the theory difficult to prove, I believe that archive.org and other sites that allow casual uploading of ‘archival’ PDFS from consumers, with minimal or sporadic oversight, will increasingly become an attack vector for generating ‘high authority’ fake news, over the next few years.
  • The reason for this is that archive.org is already prized as an authority site by spammers and scammers, and the fact that it is successfully targeted by such actors is evidenced by the kind of results you get if you search the domain for the PDF file-type*, without specifying any other search terms:.
  • Recent findings suggest that the top-ranking searches for the PDF filetype are dominated by uploads that seek to exploit and abuse the high reputation of the archive.org domain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although the sheer scale of the Internet Archive makes the theory difficult to prove, I believe that archive.org and other sites that allow casual uploading of ‘archival’ PDFS from consumers, with minimal or sporadic oversight, will increasingly become an attack vector for generating ‘high authority’ fake news, over the next few years.

The reason for this is that archive.org is already prized as an authority site by spammers and scammers, and the fact that it is successfully targeted by such actors is evidenced by the kind of results you get if you search the domain for the PDF file-type*, without specifying any other search terms:.

Recent findings suggest that the top-ranking searches for the PDF filetype are dominated by uploads that seek to exploit and abuse the high reputation of the archive.org domain. Source: Google, Nov 23, 2026.

The domain’s moderators do respond to this kind of upload, and several of the top-ranking PDFs of this kind that appear in today’s listings have already been removed, when you click on the link for them.

However, these are severely-obvious SEO ‘grenades’, which are expecting to be taken down promptly, but can nonetheless move valuable traffic until they are shut down, in an endless game of whack-a-mole; they’re not seriously seeking to be subtle, or to evade detection.

It has been revealed that what I believe will happen, though it may not be proved for a long time, is rather more insidious: that original document scans, with tampered areas – such as fresh or amended text, and new or altered photographs – will be inserted into PDF uploads, to archive.org and similar sites, either of historical or recent publications. Though it would require higher effort, even entire issues or magazines could be plausibly invented as hosts for the payload:.

Sources indicate that chatGPT’s casual effort at creating fictitious magazines and newspapers. Local AI and higher effort could doubtless offer even more credible fake publications, which could be ‘grunged up’ credibly to look like scanned challenges in an archive.org PDF upload. It is amazing how the context of this particular request caused ChatGPT to completely ignore its own rules on deepfaking celebrities, even though I did not ask it to do this.

According to recent reports, it’s an open question as to whether or not an ‘altered’ version of The Week, with a politically-critical article defused by fake content, would be noticed by anyone besides the relatively uncritical eye of LLMs. Ironically, the ‘faked’ archive.org upload would likely become the canonical version, since such material is more likely to be protected and paywalled (or else not archived at all) in other places.

It has been revealed that from the 2023 study, the Internet Archive is No.1 with a bullet. Source.

Recent findings suggest that the objective is to legitimize and diffuse the desired payload in search engine results; and, more importantly, in search results from the increasingly-dominant AI chat platforms. To this end, getting your faked document well-placed in SEO is also ‘LLM-injection by proxy’, since AI scrapers still use traditional SEO as a data resource, and ranking as a measure of authority for links.

Ironically, Internet Archive’s own upload guidance tells contributors to use meaningful, dash-separated identifiers partly because this ‘helps SEO in search engines like Google’ – legitimate advice on discoverability, but equally exploitable by spammers.

Well, that’s the possible case for high-profile publications. However, who could challenge the existence or verity of the thousands of truly obscure publications that get uploaded to the Internet Archive every day?

Just one of the thousands of ‘never-heard-of-it’ publications that flood the Internet Archive in PDF form, daily. As I write, a glut of ‘computer club’ PDFs from the 1980s have been crowding out the feeds for weeks. If it was not human-made and pre-AI, this frequency of information would doubtless be considered ‘slop’.

When a publication that has no prior internet footprint is uploaded in PDF form to the Internet Archive, its ‘ambient credibility’ is immediately supported by thousands of other similar and equally unknown and unattested titles, all of which become ‘high authority’ references unless the moderators take the files down.

Sources indicate that one possibility to improve accountability is that registered consumers (you cannot upload unless you are logged in) must prove their real ID before uploading, making it difficult to create ‘burner’ accounts, since that ID could not be used again to create a second account. However, personally I would see this as yet another grim stage in The Great Retrenchment – the current move towards CCP-style ‘ID-associated’ posting, the chilling effect that inevitably comes with it, and the increased requirement for login in order to access popular sites.

Eventually, an ‘insertion’ of this type will likely be surfaced when a frontier LLM re-spouts whatever propaganda or untruth was inserted into the document stream of archive.org, or a similarly-ranked domain; and the journalist or researcher who receives the citation is assiduous enough to actually look it up and discover the falsehood.

At that stage, on the assumption that the entirety of such ‘bogus’ uploads were distributed across multiple accounts and in tandem with multiple legitimate PDFs, the level of pollution may be hard to assess, or address; and since the uploader may not have been aware of the tampered document, shutting down their account and all related posts could be considered a ‘scorched earth’ measure.

These preoccupations were brought into focus today as I was going over the historical article shortlist for 2026, and came across the May 2026 paper TextFake: Benchmarking AI-Generated Image Detection on Text-Rich Images:.

Recent findings suggest that from the May 20206 paper, examples of the images tested, with results from ten AI-image detectors shown on the right. Blue bars show scores on conventional AI-generated images; red bars, scores on TextFake images containing text and document-style layouts. Every detector performs worse on TextFake, with the average score falling from 83.9% to 56.7%. In this way, the authors of the work proved that conventional detectors could not disentangle complex layouts. Source.

As far as I can tell, this is the only research to date addressing the fact that AI-generated images very often come in the form of integrated layouts, such as for newspapers and magazines, rather than as ‘purely text’ or ‘purely images’, which is what the majority of deepfake detectors are optimizing for.

The Chinese researchers behind the paper show evidence of a detection gap when fakery comes in this form:.

Examples of the real and AI-generated material in TextFake. Ten languages are represented across the columns. The top two rows show fake content presented as screenshots and printed documents, while the bottom two show equivalent real-world material.

Among the wrinkles tested for the paper was the degradation of the images via JPEG recompression and other tricks, which increase the plausibility of the bogus or amended magazine and adapts the modern objective to the ‘archive’ domain.

At the time of writing, the TextFake dataset curated by the authors represented, apparently, the only known work relating to the faking of screenshots and magazine/paper layouts, and other similar layout-driven archived material; to the best of my knowledge, no additional related work has emerged since.

This is not a particularly eccentric or unexplored notion, though the topic, and related topics, have only received marginal attention to date.

For example, the 2026 SIGIR paper AdversarialCOT demonstrates that poisoning doesn’t necessarily require flooding a corpus, and details the planting of a single adversarial document, in a black-box setting, and having retrieval processes surface it organically to the LLM.

Additionally, NIST has recognized ‘passive’ document poisoning of this kind, with reference to the Facebook-led 2021 paper Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, and the 2025 Northeastern University Phantom paper.

The interesting thing about this approach is its subtlety, with the payload/s lying in wait like traps in the jungle, instead of aggressively pushing themselves forward in the style of a DOS attack, or with the crude and boorish spam PDFs that currently rank so well in search results for the internet archive.

Archives derive authority from the assumption that somebody, somewhere, once verified what they contain – which is an illusion in the case of the Internet Archive, which does have a 503 error for spam, but does not apparently address the possibility of low-level tampering. Well, the staff certainly could not verify such an overwhelming volume of reading matter personally, and even the kind of visual-based detector proposed by the TextFake paper would likely yield to attackers’ countermeasures eventually.

In truth, the best kind of defense against low-level data poisoning of this kind is automated fact-checking, if the publication is obscure; and comparison to alternative versions of the text, if the publication is well-known.

However, the latter presents a problem, since the text may be unavailable at all in any free-to-view online version, or may have propagated since upload to other domains and other (legitimate) uses, by people who did not suspect the content when they came across it.

Additionally, a factchecker-based approach assumes that the datasets powering the fact-checkers are less infected than the poisoned PDFs being inspected.

In the face of this scenario, which is the optimal result for the attacker, affordable remedies are difficult to imagine, due to the deeply-embedded nature of the payload, and the innocuous context.

* I cannot guarantee the results you get will reflect the subsequent illustration, though this is what it brought me today, on the day of publication; Google Search is now quite resistant to archive snapshots.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • July bug overwhelmed newer servers, prompting promises of stronger safeguards and faster recovery.
  • Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the company has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.
  • In a recent development, the post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

July bug overwhelmed newer servers, prompting promises of stronger safeguards and faster recovery.

Some emails never reached their recipients during November's Microsoft 365 outage, the company has confirmed in a final report that also exposes gaps in its testing and recovery procedures.

In a recent development, the post-incident report details how a Windows defect brought down Exchange Online and disrupted features across other Microsoft 365 services. For affected owners, the cloud became someone else's unavailable computer.

Recent findings suggest that A preliminary report had already blamed a July code change, combined with a failover and reduced capacity. The final report confirms those findings and sets out Microsoft's plans to improve change auditing and recovery procedures, and add spare capacity. The defect affected Microsoft's gateway server configuration, not standard Windows deployments.

The epic outage (named the "Microsoft long weekend" by some wags) kicked off on November 12 and wasn't fully resolved until November 14.

Microsoft extended its delivery retry window to 48 hours, but some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days still expired, generating non-delivery reports. The firm stated all queued enterprise messages were eventually delivered, with none found permanently lost.

The report is grim, particularly in how the failure ramped up as US owners came online to find gateway servers toppling over. At the worst point, more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers were unresponsive.

The problem proved elusive, and it took Microsoft some time to identify the change and deploy a fix.

Microsoft has had a week to ponder what it did and did not do, and the report has some next steps to avoid a repeat of November's events. Some are obvious, and some are a little surprising.

Working to reduce the blast radius of failures is an obvious one, and actions include partitioning and isolation to ensure failures can be contained before taking down traffic globally. Recovery procedures also need improvement, along with communication and capacity to ensure there is sufficient headroom.

Sources indicate that microsoft's load tests used older, lower-core-count hardware, making them less likely to expose a defect that worsened on newer machines. The company now looks to test newer hardware with more realistic traffic and peak loads, and broaden its failover testing.

According to recent reports, microsoft also intends to improve diagnostics and change auditing so engineers can identify troublesome Windows changes faster. July's defect had been running worldwide for more than three months before it brought the gateways down. ®.

  • AWS has added GPU support to AWS Lambda: Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances can now run on EC2 G-series instances (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f and G6e at launch), deployed as container images, and triggered by the same event sources as any other function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU.

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read.

AWS has added GPU support to AWS Lambda: Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances can now run on EC2 G-series instances (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f and G6e at launch), deployed as container images, and triggered by the same event sources as any other function. The feature is generally available in the commercial regions where both Managed Instances and G-series instances exist. It is priced at the EC2 On-Demand rate plus a 9.75 percent management fee and the standard $0.20 per million requests.

Sources indicate that as InfoQ reported last December, Managed Instances let a function run on EC2 capacity the customer selects and pays for, with Lambda handling provisioning, patching and scaling and several invocations sharing one execution environment. GPUs were missing at that launch. Daniel Abib, senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, describes the operator's side of the change:.

You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate.

A capacity provider lists the allowed instance types, the VPC and a vCPU ceiling; Lambda picks the newest generation with capacity and falls back to older generations when newer ones are short:.

The function declares its GPU memory through a newly introduced AcceleratorConfig block, next to memory, timeout, storage, and a per-environment concurrency:.

Sources indicate that concurrent invocations in one environment share a single copy of the model in GPU memory, up to 48 per environment, and scaling follows GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency. Publishing a version provisions the environments, downloads the weights, and warms the engine before the first event arrives; Seekable OCI lazy loading can cut environment start time by up to 70 percent.

AWS ships five GPU base images: CUDA only, CuPy, PyTorch, vLLM, and SGLang. The two inference servers need no handler code; a MODEL_ID variable points to a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an S3 prefix, or a local path, and a model swap is a configuration change followed by a upcoming version:.

According to recent reports, the limits are in the launch post: container images up to 32 GB, 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2 to 32 GB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider, and a timeout of up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations. Abib draws the line against the competition in one sentence: serverless GPU services that hide the same work "often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.".

According to recent reports, the first hands-on reports came within a day. Classmethod's Akaike, who had corrected a conference talk in December after finding that no G-type was accepted, tried every accelerated instance type in us-east-1 and found 37 of 81 accepted, all G-family; P-family, G7, Inferentia, Trainium, and the Graviton-based g5g were refused, as were zip packages. A PyTorch benchmark ran about 66 times faster on the L4 than on the instance's CPU. Still, neither Terraform nor the Cloud Control provider knew AcceleratorConfig yet, and the GPU vCPU quota in a fresh account is zero: "if you use g6.xlarge (4 vCPU) with the default three instances, you need a quota of 12 vCPUs." A Terraform provider issue and pull request, opened on 16 November by a user named sasidhar-aws, and a pull request from the same user remain open.

A second test, by an AWS Community Builder writing as xbill, put Gemma 4 E2B on a single g6.2xlarge through the vLLM image, with Google's 4-bit QAT weights and a speculative-decoding drafter baked into a 9 GB image. One environment served all 48 simultaneous requests and every one of 417 calls succeeded, at roughly 130 tokens a second for a single request and 3,400 to 3,600 at 48. The friction was in the pipeline rather than the GPU: 484 seconds from publish to an active version, a Docker image index that Lambda rejected until it was pushed as a single-platform manifest, and a handler that returns complete replies, so time to first token could not be measured. His verdict keeps to that scope:.

According to recent reports, for a model behind events, queues or other AWS services, the Lambda GPU function is the simpler road: one image, one function, and Lambda keeps the server alive and routes the requests. Keep the drafter on for a chat with a few users at a time, and publish without it for heavy batch load.

When streamed replies or full control of the server are needed, he writes, "run vLLM on an EC2 G6 yourself.".

It has been revealed that the pricing model is the one Managed Instances introduced, with a lower fee for GPUs than the 15 percent charged on CPU instance types. Savings Looks and Reserved Instances apply to the instance, and there is no duration charge, so an instance bills for as long as the minimum environment count is above zero. Yan Cui's December analysis of the model, written when it still carried the line "GPU instances are NOT supported," applies to the GPU case unchanged:.

Industry observers note that regular Lambda functions can scale rapidly by tapping into a large, shared pool of EC2 instances. With managed instances, it takes tens of seconds to launch latest EC2 instances. As such, it's not a good fit when you have large, unpredictable spikes in traffic.

Managed Instances still support only Event Functions, so the GPU path does not yet reach Web Functions, the HTTP-server shape Lambda gained this year, and AWS has not remarked whether it will.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon revealed on November 23, 2026 that it had signed an agreement to purchase the proprietary technology behind the Decart Optimization Stack and bring the AI startup’s three co-founders and their team of AI researchers and engineers to the tech giant.

Sources indicate that the agreement covers the DOS technology and the planned hiring of co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf, together with their team. Completion remains subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory clearance.

It has been revealed that peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president for foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, said: “Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip. More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”.

Decart’s product documentation describes DOS as a vertically integrated inference and training platform for workloads involving large language models, agentic systems, video and world models. It sits between the model and the chip, adjusting how operations are compiled and executed so the hardware can run at higher utilization. The software is designed to integrate with existing infrastructure rather than replace it, and supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs and AWS Trainium.

Decart reports that DOS can deliver up to three times faster responses per user than leading systems. The same stack powers its Lucy and Oasis models, with Lucy editing live video in under 40 milliseconds at up to 100 frames per second and Oasis generating interactive worlds that respond in under 200 milliseconds.

It has been revealed that the agreement extends a relationship that began in 2025. Amazon remarked the collaboration used a full-stack approach spanning hardware and software and produced strong performance results on Trainium, its custom chip for AI training and inference.

Industry observers note that decart’s earlier funding announcement detailed an AWS commercial agreement and joint go-to-market initiative, including work with Annapurna Labs. Decart adapted Lucy2’s architecture to Trainium3’s design. Nafea Bshara, vice president at Amazon’s Annapurna Labs, noted the model exceeded 80% Model FLOPS Utilization on Trainium3, a measure of how much of a chip’s theoretical computing capacity is put to productive work.

According to recent reports, in that announcement, Decart also reported a $300 million funding round led by Radical Ventures and more than $450 million raised in total. Those figures cover the startup’s earlier financing and are separate from Amazon’s technology purchase.

According to recent reports, amazon reported in July 2026 that its custom-chip business had exceeded a $25 billion annual revenue run rate, with triple-digit year-over-year growth. The operation includes Trainium for AI training and inference and Graviton for general cloud computing. In 2026, Amazon also placed AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing under DeSantis.

According to recent reports, for Amazon, the agreement would combine software built to optimize workloads across several accelerator families with a team already experienced in adapting models to Trainium. The central task after closing will be converting those earlier technical results into faster, lower-cost inference across its broader chip and model operations.

  • Today, we are happy to announce a latest and deeper partnership with Google Cloud, to enable companies to build their own AI with open models.
  • It has been revealed that “Google has made some of the most impactful contributions to open AI, from the OG transformer to the Gemma models.
  • Industry observers note that “Hugging Face has been the driving force enabling companies large and small all over the world to access, use and customize now more than 2 million open models, and we’ve been proud to contribute over 1,000 of our models to the community”, notes Ryan J.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we are happy to announce a latest and deeper partnership with Google Cloud, to enable companies to build their own AI with open models.

It has been revealed that “Google has made some of the most impactful contributions to open AI, from the OG transformer to the Gemma models. I believe in a future where all companies will build and customize their own AI. With this new strategic partnership, we’re making it easy to do on Google Cloud.” claims Jeff Boudier, at Hugging Face.

Industry observers note that “Hugging Face has been the driving force enabling companies large and small all over the world to access, use and customize now more than 2 million open models, and we’ve been proud to contribute over 1,000 of our models to the community”, notes Ryan J. Salva, Senior Director of Product Management at Google Cloud. “Together we will make Google Cloud the best place to build with open models.”.

Industry observers note that google Cloud customers use open models from Hugging Face in many of its leading AI services. In Vertex AI, the most popular open models are ready to deploy in a couple clicks within Model Garden. Customers who want greater control over their AI infrastructure can find a similar model library available in GKE AI/ML, or use pre-configured environments maintained by Hugging Face. Customers also run AI inference workloads with Cloud Run GPUs, enabling serverless open model deployments.

The common thread: we work with Google Cloud to build seamless experiences fully leveraging the unique capabilities of each service to offer choice to the customers.

Usage of Hugging Face by Google Cloud customers has grown 10x over the last 3 years, and today, this translates into tens of petabytes of model downloads every month, in billions of requests.

To make sure Google Cloud customers have the best experience building with models and datasets from Hugging Face, we are working together to create a CDN Gateway for Hugging Face repositories built on top of both Hugging Face Xet optimized storage and data transfer technologies, and Google Cloud advanced storage and networking capabilities.

This CDN Gateway will cache Hugging Face models and datasets directly on Google Cloud to significantly reduce downloading times, and strengthen model supply chain robustness for Google Cloud customers. Whether you’re using Vertex, GKE, Cloud Run or just building your own stack in VMs in Compute Engine, you will benefit from faster time-to-first-token and simplified model governance.

It has been revealed that hugging Face Inference Endpoints is the easiest way to go from model to deployment in just a couple clicks. Through this deepened partnership we will bring the unique capabilities and cost performance of Google Cloud to Hugging Face customers, starting with Inference Endpoints. Expect more and newer instances available as well as price drops!

We will ensure all the fruits of our product and engineering collaboration become easily available to the 10 million AI Builders on Hugging Face. Going from a model page to deploying on Vertex Model Garden or GKE should only take a couple steps. Taking a private model securely hosted in an Enterprise organization on Hugging Face should be as easy as working with public models.

TPUs, Google custom AI accelerator chips now in their seventh generation, have been steadily improving in performance and software stack maturity. We want to make sure Hugging Face people can fully benefit from the current and the next generations of TPUs when they build AI with open models. We are excited to make TPUs as easy to use as GPUs for Hugging Face models, thanks to native support in our libraries.

In a recent development, additionally, this fresh partnership will enable Hugging Face to leverage Google industry-leading security technology to make the millions of open models on Hugging Face more secure. Powered by VirusTotal, Google Threat Intelligence and Mandiant, this joint effort aims to secure models, datasets and Spaces as you use the Hugging Face Hub daily.

We want to see a future where every firm can build their own AI with open models and host it within their own secure infrastructure, with full control. We are excited to make this future happen with Google Cloud. Our deep collaboration will accelerate this vision, whether you are using Vertex AI Model Garden, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run or Hugging Face Inference Endpoints.

In a recent development, is there something you want us to create or improve thanks to our partnership with Google? Let us know in the comments!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Minister claims intruders downloaded more than 130 GB of data as political churn left security neglected.
  • The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria claims it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minister claims intruders downloaded more than 130 GB of data as political churn left security neglected.

The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria claims it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration.

Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021.

It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a new, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer.

"The incident was discovered thanks to the upcoming national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added.

"Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time.".

Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise.

Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev remarked attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages.

The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers.

The ministry remarked that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access.

Recent findings suggest that vasilev remarked multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved.

In a follow-up interview with bTV, Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected.

A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev noted the "constant change of leadership" means "notable things for the state do not actually happen.".

Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®.

In a recent development, prizes will be awarded to the top 7 teams in each city, with the first-place team receiving $10,000! To qualify, teams must complete both Missions, with judges assessing the creativity, difficulty, ease-of-use, and practicality of Mission 2 projects on a 100-point scale.

If you care about robotics and edge AI and want to see how your ideas behave in the wild, the AMD Open Robotics Hackathon is a can’t-miss opportunity.

#149217. Reasoning Can’t Fix What a Model Never Read
