💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments.
  • When fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics.
  • RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments. TRL users can now discover, install, and run RapidFire AI as the fastest way to compare multiple fine-tuning/post-training configurations to customize LLMs without major code changes and without bloating GPU requirements.

When fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics. RapidFire AI lets you launch multiple TRL configs concurrently--even on a single GPU--and compare them in near real time via a upcoming adaptive, chunk-based scheduling and execution scheme. In internal benchmarks referenced in the TRL page, this delivers ~16–24× higher experimentation throughput than sequentially comparing configs one after another, enabling you to reach much better metrics much faster.

RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.

Drop-in TRL wrappers — Use RFSFTConfig, RFDPOConfig, and RFGRPOConfig as near-zero-code replacements for TRL's SFT/DPO/GRPO configs.

Adaptive chunk-based concurrent training — RapidFire AI shards the dataset into a given number of chunks and cycles configs at chunk boundaries to enable earlier apples-to-apples comparisons and also maximize GPU utilization.

Interactive Control Ops (IC Ops) — From the dashboard itself, you can Stop, Resume, Delete, and Clone-Modify, possibly with Warm-Start, any runs in flight to avoid wasting resources on underperforming configs and double-down on better performing configs--no job restarts, no juggling separate GPUs or clusters, no resource bloat.

Clone promising configurations with modified hyperparameters, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights, all from the live dashboard.

Sources indicate that multi-GPU orchestration — The RapidFire AI scheduler automatically places and orchestrates configs across available GPUs on chunks of data via effcient shared-memory mechanisms. You focus on your models and eval metrics, not plumbing.

MLflow-based dashboard — Real-time metrics, logs, and IC Ops in one place as soon as you start your experiment. Support for more dashboards such as Trackio, W&B, and TensorBoard coming soon.

Sources indicate that rapidFire AI splits your dataset randomly into "chunks" and cycles LLM configurations through the GPUs at chunk boundaries. You get incremental signal on eval metrics across all configs much more rapidly. The automatic checkpointing via an efficient shared-memory-based adapter/model spilling/loading mechanism keeps training smooth, stable, and consistent. Use IC Ops to adapt mid-flight to stop low-performers earlier and clone promising ones with tweaked config knobs, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights.

Industry observers note that sequential vs. Task Parallel vs. RapidFire AI: The adaptive scheduler maximizes GPU utilization across multiple configs and GPUs. The bottom row shows IC Ops in action—stopping, cloning, and modifying runs mid-flight.

The dashboard launches at http://localhost:3000 where you can monitor and control all your experiments.

These are designed as drop-in replacements so that you can keep your TRL mental model while gaining far more concurrency and control for your fine-tuning/post-training applications.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, maxon has introduced Maxon Plus, a set of AI-assisted 3D tools that can generate a base model from a prompt or a reference image, create texture variations, and give collaborators a way to review interactive 3D assets from a browser.
  • For a 3D artist, getting a plausible image isn’t the same as getting an object that can go into a scene.
  • It has been revealed that model Generator makes an editable 3D base model from text or an image.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, maxon has introduced Maxon Plus, a set of AI-assisted 3D tools that can generate a base model from a prompt or a reference image, create texture variations, and give collaborators a way to review interactive 3D assets from a browser. The services run on the web, with select features built into Cinema 4D and ZBrush. Maxon Plus is sold separately from Cinema 4D, ZBrush and Maxon One.

For a 3D artist, getting a plausible image isn’t the same as getting an object that can go into a scene. The geometry still has to hold up when viewed from another angle, and the asset may need changes to its silhouette, surface or detail. Maxon’s approach is to supply an editable starting point and let artists do that work in the software they already use.

It has been revealed that model Generator makes an editable 3D base model from text or an image. Artists can steer the result at the preview stage. When they run the generator inside Cinema 4D, the application remeshes the output, rebuilding its polygon structure so artists can work on it further. The tool is aimed at jobs such as roughing out a prop or filling in background objects rather than delivering a finished asset without review.

Texture Generator starts with geometry the artist already has. The tool accepts prompts or reference images and can use front, back and side views as guidance. It can generate a fresh UV layout, which maps a flat texture onto a 3D surface, or preserve an existing layout. Inside Cinema 4D, artists can texture individual parts of the same object, making it possible to test changes to one surface without reworking the rest.

In a recent development, clay Builder generates a simpler output: a low-polygon mesh without textures. In ZBrush for iPad, it serves as a base for hand sculpting. The tablet app already has touch-based controls and supports subdivision, which lets artists add geometry as they move from broad shapes to finer detail. Starting with a rough mesh gives artists something to shape without also committing them to an AI-generated finish.

Maxon Review, launching in public preview, is separate from generation. It handles still images and video as well as interactive 3D assets. A collaborator can rotate a model in the browser and pin a note to the exact view and area they are discussing. In Cinema 4D, the artist can return to that viewpoint with the annotations intact. In desktop ZBrush, comments appear in a floating window.

This could spare a team the familiar round of screenshots and calls just to agree on which corner, seam or surface needs a revision. It also gives producers and clients who do not need to edit the scene a way to give specific feedback without joining a live screen share.

Maxon Plus follows the organization’s September addition of a Model Context Protocol server for Cinema 4D. That earlier feature lets an assistant automate chores like organizing imported objects, with Cinema 4D applying changes on the artist’s machine and putting them in its undo history. The fresh generators work differently: Maxon states third-party providers power its cloud AI features, and that it identifies the provider for each feature and prohibits them from training generative AI models on user material. Artists can turn off AI features and Maxon Plus cloud services at the account level.

It has been revealed that generative operations, including previews, use monthly credits that do not carry over. Maxon states the tool indicates the credit cost before each operation and that Maxon Review does not use credits during its public preview. The distinction matters for artists testing a series of variants: the real cost depends on how many tries it takes to get a model or texture worth keeping.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1056 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

Focus on Your AI Agents Before Worrying About an AI Apocalypse

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A business can make progress with agentic AI and lose control of it at the same time.
  • The conversation around AI risk often gravitates towards extreme scenarios.
  • While these questions warrant serious consideration, organizations don’t need to imagine a rogue system bringing operations to a halt to understand the risks of poorly managed AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A business can make progress with agentic AI and lose control of it at the same time. Such is the concern of AI agent sprawl, or the uncontrolled spread of agentic tools throughout an organization.

The conversation around AI risk often gravitates towards extreme scenarios. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus offers some fairly alarming examples, from resisting shutdown and blackmailing human customers to “existential risks to humanity.”.

While these questions warrant serious consideration, organizations don’t need to imagine a rogue system bringing operations to a halt to understand the risks of poorly managed AI. The challenge businesses face, while more grounded, is far more immediate. It is ensuring that the agents they’re already deploying remain secure, useful, and accountable.

AI agents are becoming easier to develop and deploy by the day, and it demonstrates. By 2030, agentic AI is on track to account for two-fifths of all AI value, by which point, 42% of companies will have to grant agents autonomy, indicates BCG.

Between readily available off-the-shelf tools and increasingly accessible development platforms, it’s become easy for individual employees and teams to automate tasks without waiting for their IT department to build them a bespoke solution.

This shouldn’t be taken to undermine the value of agentic AI’s accessibility. It encourages innovation, creates the opportunity to improve entrenched processes, and enables those closest to a problem to experiment with ways of solving it.

It has been revealed that the difficulty is that these same conditions make the proliferation of AI agents almost inevitable. Agents can be created faster than an organization can establish how they should be monitored, maintained, and governed. Gartner predicts that the average Fortune 500 enterprise could have more than 150,000 AI agents by 2028, compared with fewer than 15 in 2025.

It has been revealed that A large agent inventory isn’t automatically a problem. What is an issue is whether an organization has sight of which agents exist, the data they can access, the permissions they have, and – importantly – who is responsible for the decisions those agents make.

Without that visibility, a business can expose itself to risk while believing it’s simply becoming more productive.

While some tools will prove useful and become embedded in everyday work, others might be abandoned or quietly forgotten. This creates a security risk. If organizations lose track of which agents remain active and what they can access, those tools can easily become entry points into sensitive systems and data.

A similar problem applies to information handling. An agent might process or share confidential material without sufficient human oversight of where that information goes or how it’s used. The more fragmented the environment, the harder it becomes for businesses to keep on top of these risks.

Industry observers note that accountability is another challenge. Agents make mistakes; they might apply the wrong policy or take inappropriate actions. But when things go wrong, identifying the responsible party shouldn’t depend on detective work. Businesses need to know who owns the agents, the rules they operate under, and who is expected to act when things go awry.

These aren’t problems that can be solved by asking employees to be more careful. They require a clear view of the systems operating across the organization, the permissions they have, the teams responsible for them, and the authority to manage them consistently.

Tackling agent sprawl doesn’t mean discouraging employees from building agents altogether. What businesses need is to change the environment in which their agents are created and managed. A move away from disconnected tools with their own assumptions and standards, and towards one governed environment that pulls together the shared knowledge, standards, and controls required to build fully informed agents.

According to recent reports, picture it as a sort of super-agent: in essence, one single agent with all the context it needs, from organizational expertise to organization policies and processes. It’s this agent that creates and governs all the other project-specific agents – like a Queen Bee in charge of her hive.

Recent findings suggest that this sort of governed environment ensures AI agents remain manageable, without stripping staff of the freedom to experiment and innovate. It gives businesses clear visibility of which agents exist, the purpose they serve, the information they can access, and whether they remain necessary, while ensuring they operate within the boundaries of established standards.

According to recent reports, and alongside effective oversight, businesses need to establish clear ownership. Not only should the purpose of an agent be clear, but so should the person or team accountable for it, ensuring human judgment and expertise remain embedded in each decision and process.

In a recent development, as agents move from individual experiments into business-critical workflows, the consequences of getting things wrong, while not existential, become more significant. What this means for businesses is ensuring governance doesn’t remain static. The controls around these systems need to evolve in lockstep with AI agents themselves.

Sources indicate that we are only beginning to see what agentic AI can make possible for businesses, but realising that potential will take more than deploying more agents. Shared context, consistent standards, and clear ownership will help businesses distinguish what works from what doesn’t. Businesses will be able to scale successful approaches and, critically, keep humans at the helm where judgment and experience matter most.

In a recent development, ultimately, AI maturity will be measured by how well organizations manage their AI agents. The real advantage sits with the businesses that understand what each agent does, why they do it, and who is accountable for the outcome.

Vikas Nehru is the Chief Technology Officer at Kantata, where he leads the business’s Engineering, Platform, and Support teams. He has over 20 years of experience in B2B SaaS, from successfully guiding startups to IPOs, to leading PE-owned companies through major acquisitions. Based in Las Vegas, Vikas holds degrees in Computer Science from the University of Alberta.

Industry observers note that OVHcloud AI Endpoints are a fully managed, serverless service that provides access to frontier AI models from leading research labs via simple API calls. The service offers competitive pay-per-token pricing starting at €0.04 per million tokens.

The service runs on secure infrastructure located in European data centers, ensuring data sovereignty and low latency for European owners. The platform supports advanced features including structured outputs, function calling, and multimodal capabilities for both text and image processing.

Industry observers note that built for production use, OVHcloud's inference infrastructure delivers sub-200ms response times for first tokens, making it ideal for interactive applications and agentic workflows. The service supports both text generation and embedding models. You can learn more about OVHcloud's platform and infrastructure at https://www.ovhcloud.com/en/public-cloud/ai-endpoints/catalog/.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.
  • Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code, an experimental feature in which the model writes JavaScript to drive its tools instead of requesting each Bash, Read, or Edit call separately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Claude Code Adds Experimental Code Mode to Orchestrate Tool Calls with JavaScript.

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.

Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code, an experimental feature in which the model writes JavaScript to drive its tools instead of requesting each Bash, Read, or Edit call separately. Code Mode is off by default, requires Claude Code v2.1.323 or later, and is enabled with the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 environment variable. Anthropic warns it may change or be removed in any release.

Recent findings suggest that in a normal session, Claude asks for one tool call, reads the full result, and decides the next step. In Code Mode, one script can run commands in parallel, pass one result into the next call, and return only the output the model needs. The documentation's example finds a file with rg, raises a retry limit, runs the tests, and returns just the path and test output. The conversation still demonstrates each tool call and diff, while the generated code sits in the transcript viewer. Anthropic recommends it for edits repeated across many files, searches that need filtering, and independent commands. Code that Claude waits on stops after ten minutes; sessions started in auto or bypassPermissions mode can push it to the background for up to two hours while the conversation continues.

The permission model is the part architects should read first. Each call inside a script still goes through deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks, but in auto mode the classifier reviews the script before it runs, not each call, and cannot see values computed at run time. A git push can now reach a hook as cd 'app' && git push, so hooks must check every part of a command; a hook matching the REPL tool can read the JavaScript from tool_input.code. Project settings cannot enable Code Mode, so a cloned repository cannot switch it on, and administrators can block it through managed settings.

In a recent development, code Mode runs only in interactive terminal sessions of the native build, on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or Fable 5.2, through a Claude subscription or Console account. It does not work with -p, the Agent SDK, the VS Code panel, the Desktop app, Amazon Bedrock, gateways, or zero-data-retention organizations. Agent teams need v2.1.326. Anthropic has published no token or latency figures for it.

George (@bolyki) compared Code Mode with normal mode across eight interactive Sonnet 5.5 runs and posted:.

Same results every time. Context 20-25% smaller. On the bigger task: 37% fewer tokens, 19% lower cost. But it is not faster, and on a tiny task it cost more.

Ravi Madabhushi, who builds agent auth infrastructure, pushed back on claims that the feature makes MCP obsolete:.

It doesn't materially change anything wrt authentication, authorization and audit policy layers; Your agent still makes those same MCP calls, with the same auth tokens and context and what materially changes is how much context gets into the model window and how much can be discarded.

The idea, and the name, predate Anthropic's release. Cloudflare introduced Code Mode for MCP converting MCP tools into a TypeScript API that models code against inside sandboxed Workers, where bindings keep API keys away from generated code. Anthropic's own post on code execution with MCP described one workflow dropping from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens, and the Claude API offers programmatic tool calling in a remote code execution container. Code Mode instead runs the script in the developer's local session, against Claude Code's built-in tools and permission system.

Recent findings suggest that code Mode remains opt-in and experimental, and Anthropic collects feedback through /feedback. Setup steps and troubleshooting are in the Claude Code documentation.

Quality IMAP, Part 2: Mailbox Concurrency

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deuxfleurs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation.
  • It has been revealed that aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network concerns and hardware failures.
  • This is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the second part in a series discussing why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and presenting our work on making Aerogramme's IMAP code as high-quality as we can. Today we focus on challenges that arise when considering concurrent access to a mailbox.

It has been revealed that aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network concerns and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

This is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement. In the previous post, we talked about the first class of features: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents. In this post, we talk about the second class of features that make implementing an IMAP server tricky: concurrent access to user mailboxes.

Concurrent and distributed software are famously hard to get right; concurrency bugs are known to be hard to find. In our recent work on refining Aerogramme we have tried to approach the problem from different angles. This is the topic of this post: the different ways in which we have improved the correctness of Aerogramme in concurrent settings.

This work was funded by NLNet under the "Aerogramme 1.0" grant, and could not have been possible without their support.

Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat!

A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox. For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer. Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing. In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes.

According to recent reports, why must clients be able to coordinate when accessing the same mailbox? Assume that we are an email client that sends two commands to read information from a mailbox. Since another client can modify the mailbox in between the two commands, the information we read may have been invalidated by the other client and is now inconsistent! Clients thus need to be able to detect concurrent changes made by other clients. Similarly, a client that reconnects to the server after being offline needs to fetch the changes that happened while it was disconnected. This is possible thanks to mechanisms defined by the IMAP specification and that specifically exist because concurrent access is allowed.

The overall consistency of the mailbox data must be taken seriously: an IMAP server exposing inconsistent views of a mailbox could result in a confused client deleting the wrong emails, for example.

To our best knowledge, concurrent mailbox behaviors are tackled in the following (parts of) specifications:.

The base IMAP4 specification has few explicit mentions of concurrent mailbox access, but does talk about re-synchronizing disconnected clients, which can be seen as a restricted form of concurrent access. It defines mechanisms for assigning IDs to emails (UIDNEXT/UIDVALIDITY) and associated properties which can be extrapolated to concurrent contexts. This is relevant when concurrently adding upcoming emails to a mailbox. After an email has been added to a mailbox it cannot be modified, so there are no issues with reading emails concurrently.

The improvements that we will talk about in this post are related to these aspects of the base IMAP specification.

According to recent reports, as an additional complication, IMAP defines in fact two (!) email-numbering systems. One of these has the drawback that deleting an email can invalidate email IDs used in concurrent commands. This is purely a quirk of a numbering system that can nowadays be considered legacy, but must still be supported. This issue is not acknowledged in the base IMAP specification, leaving a class of problematic behaviors completely unspecified, but is later addressed in an informational RFC which specifies what to do in such cases.

Aerogramme's latest release includes changes and bugfixes to make sure that we follow the recommendations of this informational RFC, but we won't enter into the details of these legacy quirks in this post.

It has been revealed that email flags can be modified concurrently, but the base IMAP specification does not specify a mechanism for clients to coordinate around flag changes. This is done in the later CONDSTORE specification that extends IMAP with mechanisms to coordinate flag changes across concurrent connections. Aerogramme has preliminary support for CONDSTORE, but we disabled it in the last release, as we found out it needs a redesign to be nicer to email clients1.

A later specification further extends IMAP and CONDSTORE by adding a more general mechanism (QRESYNC) for synchronizing all mailbox changes across concurrent sessions. Aerogramme does not supports QRESYNC at the moment2.

On top of the complexity carried by the IMAP specification, Aerogramme's distributed infrastructure comes with its own challenges. Not only we need to think about concurrency at the IMAP protocol level, but also internally in Aerogramme: how do we handle concurrent changes to the server internal data storage? Can we simply take a lock or a transaction over mailbox data each time we need to patch it, serializing all concurrent updates? The answer is no: things are a bit more complicated...

It has been revealed that recall that Aerogramme is a distributed IMAP server. A typical Aerogramme deployment looks like this:.

According to recent reports, in this schema, A nodes are Aerogramme instances running on separate servers. Running multiple Aerogramme nodes provides fault-tolerance: even if some of the nodes crash, the Aerogramme cluster stays operational as long as one node remains available. When an email client (a C node) connects to the "Aerogramme cluster" (the dashed potato), it can open a connection to any of the Aerogramme nodes, depending on what kind of load-balancing is implemented.

Aerogramme nodes do not talk to each other directly and do not store data themselves. Instead, they connect a shared Garage cluster (itself geo-distributed with fault-tolerance properties) which stores data for the whole Aerogramme cluster (emails, mailbox state, etc.).

This means that an Aerogramme node deals with concurrency at two levels. It must handle concurrent connections from email clients to a mailbox, as we explained before. But it must also handle concurrent changes made by other Aerogramme nodes to the data stored in Garage. These concurrent accesses must be coordinated properly so that the Aerogramme cluster exposes a consistent view of a mailbox (according to IMAP's consistency requirements), even when connecting concurrently to different nodes of the Aerogramme cluster.

A central challenge in Aerogramme's design is that Garage does not provide locks, transactions, or anything that would require distributed consensus between Garage nodes. This is by design, and it allows Garage and Aerogramme to perform well even with non-negligible latency between nodes. The consequence for Aerogramme is that its nodes cannot simply reason on their shared data as if it was updated sequentially. The approach used by Aerogramme insteadâa convergent operation logâis a central part of its design. We'll talk more below on how we adjusted the consistency properties provided by Garage when storing that operation log.

Industry observers note that A basic IMAP mechanism is assigning IDs to emails when they are added into a mailbox. Adding emails concurrently can already make it tricky to assign these IDs. Our first step was to find a way of testing this case and to fix any bugs that we would find.

For context, IMAP specifies that each email in a mailbox must be assigned a UID: a number that identifies it uniquely. UIDs are assigned in increasing order; this allows clients to check if new emails have been added by checking the value of the mailbox "next UID". On top of that, IMAP also allows the server to renumber the emails with different UIDs. When this happens, the IMAP server must increase the value of UIDVALIDITY, a global integer counter attached to the mailbox. Now, in Aerogramme, increasing UIDVALIDITY is done in some cases when emails are added concurrently in the mailbox in a way that would assign conflicting UIDs; an unavoidable consequence of its distributed architecture.

It has been revealed that from an IMAP client's perspective UIDVALIDITY must always increase monotonically. We also assume that this property must hold across all concurrent connections; although the specification does not say so explicitly, it is the most prudent assumption since a single client may open multiple connections to the same mailbox.

Industry observers note that the logical next step is to setup a test bench to ensure that it holds in practice for Aerogramme! We deployed an Aerogramme cluster with three nodes, running on a simulated network with added latency between nodes. Then:.

Running Aerogramme on this test bench found state synchronization bugs: bugs showing that Aerogrammeâs distributed state (stored in Garage) was not always properly synchronized between nodes and concurrent sessions. Amusingly, most of these bugs were not specific to the IMAP logic related to UIDVALIDITY...

It has been revealed that fixing these synchronization bugs motivated a redesign of the internal read/update mailbox interface. In Aerogramme, the IMAP "business logic" accesses mailbox state stored in distributed storage using an abstract interface exposing a small number of operations. Before, these operations were the following (in pseudo-Rust):.

The synchronization bugs found during testing revealed that this interface is in fact error-prone and tricky to reason about:.

The solution was to redesign Aerogramme's mailbox state interface to provide more control over state synchronization: reading concurrent changes from storage becomes a separate operation, laying the following interface:.

According to recent reports, this fresh interface separates local reasoning about mailbox contents from synchronization. This makes it easier to write the IMAP logic in a way that is "obviously correct". Plainly speaking, this interface provides "local" views of mailbox state, where a view (denoted as self above) is specific to a client connection. Then, get and push_op operate on the local view with sequential semantics and are both fast; and calls to sync mark explicitly the places in the code where we have to think about concurrent changes. (Note that push_op synchronously updates remote storage, so there is no risk of losing write by forgetting to run sync.).

Notice that the design of this interface reflects the high-level distributed architecture that we described in the previous section. For instance, an implementation of the interface needs to "merge" the operations pushed concurrently with push_op when they are put together in distributed storage, in a way that is consistent with local views; this is backed by the "convergent operation log" mentioned earlier and domain-specific logic3. Note that this interface offers no transactional or lock-like operations; matching Garage's lack of consistency primitives.

Most of the changes described here were part of Aerogramme 0.4, with in particular #129 implementing the refactoring of the state synchronization interface.

Talking about consistency guarantees in Aerogramme raises the question: what are the consistency guarantees provided by Garage, its storage backend?

Industry observers note that this question is most relevant for Garage K2V, a NoSQL-inspired key-value store, which is used to store mailbox state as an operation log. (Garage K2V is experimental and was added in Garage for the needs of Aerogramme.) Mailbox state describes (among other things) email numbering, and as we've seen before, we want this information to be properly synchronized between Aerogramme nodes.

Recent findings suggest that garage K2V provides read-after-write consistency4: this guarantees that as soon as a write is acknowledged by Garage, any subsequent read will see the update made by the write. In terms of Aerogramme's state synchronization interface, after running push_op(op);, this guarantees that sync(); get() returns a state that includes op on any Aerogramme node.

It has been revealed that however, it turns out that read-after-write consistency alone is not enough for Aerogramme. Let's think of the fact that UIDVALIDITY needs to increase monotonically according to the IMAP specification. This means that calling sync(); get() twice on any two Aerogramme nodes must return a state that is more recent the second time than the first. In other words, when making several reads to Garage K2V in sequence, we must not see time go backward. This means that, to ensure consistency of the UIDVALIDITY counter, Aerogramme needs Garage K2V to guarantee an additional consistency property called monotonic reads!

Recent findings suggest that as a result we have extended Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads consistency. Luckily, the design of Garage makes it possible to provide monotonic reads at only a small performance cost. For a reference, Martin Kleppmann's Designing data-intensive applications (in particular ChapterÂ 9, "Linearizability and quorums") helps understanding which scenarios lead to non-monotonic reads in a quorum-based architecture like Garage's, and what to implement to guarantee monotonic reads.

To experimentally validate our changes, we first built a test bench that triggers non-monotonic reads on stock K2V. Reproducing non-monotonic reads requires variable network delays, so we deployed a Garage cluster with 3 nodes, on a simulated network with delay between cluster nodes. This test setup allows observing non-monotonic reads, by running:.

Sources indicate that we then modified Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads by default, by implementing "synchronous read repair". We validated that we cannot observe non-monotonic reads anymore on our test bench, while they could be observed before this change: a good sanity check.

This change in Garage K2V ensures that there are no scenarios in which a precise combination of network delays in the cluster results in an IMAP client observing non-increasing values of UIDVALIDITY. One could argue that this is unlikely to happen in practice; and indeed, we could not reproduce it with our simple-minded test bench: while we could observe non-monotonic reads with Garage K2V alone, we could not observe non-monotonic UIDVALIDITY on a full Garage+Aerogramme deployment with the same testing methodology. Nevertheless, we want Aerogramme to rest on strong, correct foundations as much as possible; eliminating a rare but possible cause of bugs was fully worth the effort.

The work described here was made available as part of Garage 2.4.0; it required no specific change in Aerogramme itself.

Industry observers note that we designed Aerogramme to be part of a low-tech computing stack meant to be robust and reliable when hosted outside of data-centers, and Aerogramme's geo-distributed design is part of the answer. In the future, we hope to expand on the values and high-level ideas behind Aerogramme; this will have to be for an other blogpost...

The current implementation (now gated by a feature flag disabled by default) tends to disconnect clients more often than reasonable. This is correct with respect to the specification, but likely leads to bad UX in clients. We are working on a better strategy that does not require disconnecting clients.

The first step would be to gather data on how many clients actually support QRESYNC today...

We have not shown this "domain specific" merge logic (here, mailbox-specific) because it is a whole different topic, but it needs to be provided when instantiating the generic interface shown before with concrete state and operations.

read-after-write consistency is also the key consistency guarantee provided by Garage S3.

Breaking: Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

📅 24 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1437 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important applications of AI.
  • According to recent reports, the task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling.
  • This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important applications of AI. Research is a foundational knowledge-work task: collecting, reading, and synthesizing information underpins everything from writing and decision-making to coding itself. Yet human-driven research is constrained by memory, reading speed, and time. AI research agents, by contrast, can process vast amounts of information, synthesize insights instantly, and scale effortlessly. Because of this, research agents are emerging as a top use case for AI today and will soon become a core subcomponent of broader agentic workflows across content generation, coding, sales, and more. In this post, we share the technical and philosophical lessons we’ve learned building a state-of-the-art research agent, and where we believe the field is headed.

According to recent reports, the task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling. Building applications on top of rapidly improving models is, however, a modern engineering challenge. How can we design software today that absorbs the performance gains from future model releases?

This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.

We learned this the hard way seven months ago, when we had to abandon our first attempt at deep research and rebuild the entire system from scratch. The first architecture was complicated and sophisticated (we thought this was a good thing), but its assumptions became bottlenecks when the next generation of models arrived.

According to recent reports, over the last seven months, model capabilities have quietly but meaningfully evolved (especially in their tool-calling abilities). This single optimization focus has pushed us from workflows to agents. We believe future models will be trained to solve the current pain points of agent developers. Every model is ultimately consumed by a harness, so models should evolve in service of that harness. We hope to see models improve in high-recall summarization (for context compression), tool-calling reliability, and concision in writing.

Similarly, tools should evolve to support LLMs and widely adopted agent harnesses. The best tools should perform some context engineering on the tool side, abstracted away from the agent. They should return only the most relevant data instead of dumping large volumes of tokens into the context window. As a tool provider, we’ve invested heavily in our advanced search feature, which has context engineering baked in. This in turn lowers hallucinations and latency for the downstream agent processes.

To build agents that improve over time, we followed a few guiding principles:.

Industry observers note that long-horizon research tasks expose a fundamental challenge in current agent design: the task of maintaining a clean, optimized context window over time. If curating context is not a task the engineer pays close attention to, the agent is almost destined for failure. The following outlines our thinking around this concept within the deep research domain.

Using Tavily’s Advanced Search is the natural first step to take in overcoming this challenge, in that it abstracts away the processing of raw web content and returns only the most relevant content chunks from each source. In leveraging this functionality, we let Tavily Search do the heavy lifting and allow Tavily Research to reap the benefit, gathering the most valuable content in a latency-efficient manner.

Sources indicate that ensuring that the agent does not overfit to a single research thread is the next step towards an effective context-gathering pipeline. It is in this regard that global state persistence and source deduplication is paramount, and in our case, it helps threefold:.

At Tavily, interacting with the web is our bread and butter. Architecting a refined web-retrieval system engineered for deep research was a foundational building block for our deep research agent design as a whole.

Humans research in an inherently unstructured, iterative way. We start by defining the task: what we’re trying to accomplish and what information we need. We next gather data from our sources, extracting the key insights and holding them in short-term memory, letting these distilled thoughts guide our subsequent actions.

In a recent development, this cycle repeats: collect information, distill it, decide what to do next. Only once we’ve gathered enough understanding to produce the final deliverable do we return to the original sources, using them as references to assemble the finished product.

We believe that deep research agents should be designed in a similar manner, in that tool outputs should be distilled into reflections, and only the set of past reflections should be used as context for your tool caller. Similar to humans, it is only at the point when your agent begins to prepare the final deliverable that you must provide the raw information as context, so as to ensure there is no information loss.

This approach differs from traditional context structuring in a ReAct agent-based architecture. Typically, tool calls and outputs are propagated through the tool calling loop, with previously retrieved/generated tokens being persisted in the context window on each subsequent iteration. This pattern can be seen in LangChain’s Open Deep Research agent implementation, and from a token consumption perspective, it can be modeled by the following quadratic series, where n n n is the amount of tokens the tool calling model is invoked with on each tool calling iteration, and m m m is the number of tool calling iterations.

n+2n+3n+⋯+mn  =  n⋅m(m+1)2n + 2n + 3n + \cdots + mn \;=\; n \cdot \frac{m(m+1)}{2}n+2n+3n+⋯+mn=n⋅2m(m+1)​.

Contrarily, our proposed method of context engineering removes this token propagation (as the knowledge distillations, even when aggregated, are negligible when compared to the quantity of tokens gathered from web) and can be modeled by the following linear series.

n+n+n+⋯+n  =  nmn + n + n + \cdots + n \;=\; nmn+n+n+⋯+n=nm.

When comparing the two approaches, tokens are saved on a per-agent basis by a factor of m+12 \frac{m+1}{2} 2m+1​, and when extrapolating this over a multi-agent system and with consumption at scale, the absolute value of tokens saved becomes even more significant.

Through this methodology, we were able to reduce token consumption by 66% (when compared to Open Deep Research) while achieving SOTA on DeepResearch Bench – the intersection of quality and efficiency in full effect.

In a recent development, building production-grade agents is a balancing act. We leaned into autonomy to maximize performance and quality, while still meeting strict requirements for latency, cost, and reliability.

Industry observers note that LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, and we found that giving them guard-railed freedom to reason and iterate produces the strongest results. Autonomy, when gone wrong, can cause agent behavior to go off track. Tools can be called incorrectly, LLMs can overfit to a subtopic, and expected reasoning patterns may break. No single safeguard will catch all of these issues.

Industry observers note that A shift in engineering mindset is required: treat failure modes as core design considerations, not afterthoughts. Simple guardrails like tool-call retries or model cascades help, but proactively anticipating anomalies, reinforcing proper patterns in prompting and edge-case testing is what enables production-grade, long-running agents.

Industry observers note that from our experience, it’s better to expose a small, essential toolset to the agent rather than a large, complex one. We were tempted to over-engineer by adding many tools that seemed useful in theory, but in practice this created latest failure modes and made it harder for LLMs to consistently choose the right tool and iterate effectively.

Recent findings suggest that we used evals to steer our development process but also recognize their shortcomings. LLM-as-a-judge evals are difficult to trust: current models are non‑deterministic, uninterpretable in their reasoning, and can turn into bottlenecks, especially for long‑running agents where a single experiment can take days to complete.

Industry observers note that rather than optimizing for benchmark scores, we optimized for directional feedback. The core question was always: did this change make the agent more reliable and more useful in practice? Evals became a tool for validating that direction, not the optimization target. Intuition and careful agent‑trace monitoring consistently provided higher‑signal feedback than any single eval score. Overall, the best outcome is rarely the highest numerical score. For production systems, improvements like reduced token usage, reliability, lower latency, and fewer failures are more valuable than a one‑point bump on an eval.

In a recent development, what is r in your solution ? Is it a scratch pad that is updated in the LLM context between each round of research ?

r in the solution is the research insight from previous tool call.

A great insight on getting more by doing less.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.

In a recent development, the card is the poster here. The Purple, one of the newly introduced card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip. The same violet bleeds into a painted field behind the card, so object and world share one color. Wolff Olins spent time in Seoul before drawing anything, talking with customers and young Koreans. More than eight in ten South Koreans in their twenties still live with their parents, so people define themselves through taste and through what they choose to carry. A card notes something about who you are and who you intend to become, and that became the design problem.

Sources indicate that the system runs on a simple split. A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card. Around that core, each card gets its own world. The entry cards, M, X and Z, use a generative system of bright color and repetition, so no two faces repeat the same pattern. A type specimen sheet sets the grotesque in full, and the card specification drawing marks the 1.58 ratio every face must hold.

Scale does the talking in the applications. The wordmark stays small and bracketed while a single figure, 93 percent, fills a whole green panel, and the card faces run at poster size on street walls. The card ratio repeats across posters, totes and packaging, so the system reads as one object cut to different sizes.

In a recent development, the physical pieces carry the same discipline. Modular packaging holds the whole range together: a grey box with a debossed Hyundai Card mark and a red peel tab, each card sealed in a protective layer that peels back to reveal its character. The dotted halftone on the Purple card reads as texture before it reads as pattern. The tote bag carries the bracketed wordmark on green, with a black band at the base.

Color is the flex in the system. Violet owns the Purple card, acid green owns the commercial card and the big figures, and black and grey hold everything together. The butterfly image indicates what the generative color does when it leaves the card: the same violet, painted loose across a wing, with the pattern breaking into dots. Every card keeps the same bones and gets a different skin.

  • Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture.

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.

According to recent reports, agoda has introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries without rewriting the existing service. The approach combines component-based code organization, automated architecture checks, and incremental migration. The team reported 64% shorter median code review time and 34% shorter time to initial substantive feedback for framework-backed changes compared with legacy code.

Industry observers note that the change addresses growing maintenance challenges in BAPI, which coordinates cancellations, booking amendments, refunds, and customer communications. Agoda extracted the API from its aging core monolith in 2019 through a largely line-by-line migration. As development increased, merge requests more than quadrupled between 2022 and 2025, while some files exceeded 4,000 lines.

According to recent reports, the team characterized the migration as a tactical design trade-off, drawing on John K. Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design,.

Recent findings suggest that we had deliberately traded a strategic design approach for a tactical one to prioritize speed to market. This tactical mindset was exactly what the business needed at the time.

Rather than undertake a complete rewrite, the team introduced architectural boundaries incrementally.

Recent findings suggest that the framework, called Platform, organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking, and payments rather than technical layers. Each component encapsulates its business logic and data access behind defined interfaces, with application, service, repository, and model layers contained within the component. This package-by-component approach aims to localize changes and reduce dependencies between business domains.

Platform framework boundaries inside a domain module (Source: Agoda Blog Post).

Agoda uses the Data Mapper pattern to keep repository-specific models, including database entities and API payloads, out of business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, making it easier for developers to find where domain objects and service inputs are constructed.

Recent findings suggest that the team also uses ArchUnit to encode architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration. For example, repository-specific models can only be accessed by their respective repositories. Violations fail the build rather than relying on code reviewers to identify unauthorized dependencies manually.

The team described these constraints as architectural fitness functions, a concept discussed by Neal Ford and Mark Richards in Software Architecture: The Hard Parts. One engineer explained:.

By codifying our layer boundaries into an ArchUnit test suite, our CI pipeline serves as an automated guardrail, catching structural drift on every pull request before a human reviewer ever sees it.

Platform is now the default for latest modules, while existing functionality is migrated incrementally when feature development provides an opportunity.

Agoda compared framework-backed and legacy merge requests in Q2 2026. Median review completion time was 1.08 hours for framework-backed changes, compared with 3.02 hours for legacy changes. Time to first substantive feedback was 10.34 hours versus 15.77 hours. Between June and August, framework-backed changes also used 29% fewer AI prompts per 100 changed lines, although median prompts per merge request were similar (20 vs. 22). Agoda cautioned that the AI findings were directional due to the short observation period. A related approach is Spring Modulith, which provides module verification and dependency-cycle checks for Spring Boot applications.

Industry News: Dr. Yanpei Cao, Co-Founder and Chief Scientist of VAST – Interview Series

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yanpei Cao is Co-Founder and Chief Scientist of VAST, where he leads research and technical direction for generative 3D and interactive world models.
  • In a recent development, VAST develops 3D foundation models and world models and is the firm behind Tripo, a platform for generating and editing 3D assets from text and images.
  • Before co-founding VAST and developing Tripo, you spent years researching 3D reconstruction and computer graphics, and immersive content at organizations including Tencent, Owlii, and Tsinghua University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dr. Yanpei Cao is Co-Founder and Chief Scientist of VAST, where he leads research and technical direction for generative 3D and interactive world models. He holds a PhD from Tsinghua University and has worked across computer graphics, 3D reconstruction, and immersive content creation. Before VAST, he served as a principal researcher at Tencent and co-founded volumetric capture company Owlii, which was later acquired by Kuaishou.

In a recent development, VAST develops 3D foundation models and world models and is the firm behind Tripo, a platform for generating and editing 3D assets from text and images. Its work spans mesh geometry, topology, texturing, rigging, and animation, alongside Project Eden and real-time generative rendering through EdenLive. In this interview, Cao discusses native quad meshes, production workflows, the remaining challenges in generative 3D, and the research needed to build persistent interactive worlds.

Before co-founding VAST and developing Tripo, you spent years researching 3D reconstruction and computer graphics, and immersive content at organizations including Tencent, Owlii, and Tsinghua University. What inspired you to make the leap from research to entrepreneurship, and what was your original vision for Tripo when you founded the tech giant in 2023?

In fact, after finishing my PhD at Tsinghua University, I went on to co-found Owlii to focus on volumetric capture. I co-founded the tech giant because there weren’t any around doing that type of 3D technology research. The company was later acquired by Kuaishou.

Sources indicate that to me entrepreneurship is never about leaving research behind. Rather, it is a continuation of the research I have been doing since college years.

In 2023, we founded VAST, the manufacturer behind Tripo AI, with the vision of democratizing 3D creation and building interactive worlds.

Recent findings suggest that as the Co-founder and Chief Scientist of Tripo AI, I am deeply involved in our core research, technical direction, and key technological decisions. Building a organization allows me to take fundamental research beyond the lab, translate technological breakthroughs into real products, and make advanced generative 3D capabilities accessible to a broader audience.

Since the company’s founding, we have developed powerful 3D-native foundation models, and we are working on our world model Project Eden, which released a preview in May and EdenLive, a real-time generative rendering, earlier this month.

Recent findings suggest that three years on, I’m happy to see that our 3D-native foundation models, including the P and H series, have been widely adopted in 3D content generation in gaming, film production, education, industrial design and much more. We have effectively lowered the bar for 3D creation. More importantly, our 3D-native foundation models have freed 3D professionals from the tedious work of 3D creation and help improve productivity of the industry.

And with the release of EdenLive as part of our world model, Project Eden, we are getting ever closer to realizing our vision of building interactive worlds.

Tripo recently introduced P2.0, positioning it as a major step toward production-ready AI-generated 3D assets. What are the most significant improvements over previous generations, and how does this release address the limitations that have historically prevented AI-generated models from being used directly in professional workflows?

Sources indicate that topology has been the barrier between AI-generated 3D and real production: game and film pipelines are built on quad meshes. Previously AI got there only through slow, unstable retopology. P2.0 removes that barrier by promptly generating clean quad meshes natively, with clean part separation and the edge flow an artist would lay out manually. Quad mesh topology also makes 3D assets easier to edit and deform, making them better suited for downstream production workflows.

It has been revealed that tripo P2.0 automatically separates body, clothing, and accessories into independent pieces during generation. This matters for game pipelines where characters need separated meshes for material assignment, level of detail (LOD) management, or modular assembly.

It supports a much broader polygon range: from 500 to 50,000 triangles, or up to 25,000 quads. This allows creators to generate assets for different production budgets—from lightweight mobile content to high-fidelity game hero assets.

It supports Mesh Edit, which lets creators select and regenerate any region of a mesh without altering the rest of the asset.

In a recent development, one of P2.0’s most notable advancements is native quad topology generation, which produces structured meshes suitable for editing, rigging, and animation. Why has generating clean, usable topology been such a difficult challenge for generative AI, and what technical breakthroughs made this possible?

The fundamental difficulty lies in how 3D geometry is represented. Many earlier generative approaches relied on autoregressive methods, representing a mesh as a sequence of tokens and generating those tokens one after another. However, unlike language, a 3D mesh does not have a natural linear order. Its vertices, edges, and faces form a connected spatial structure. When that structure is converted into an artificial sequence, generation becomes increasingly difficult as geometric complexity grows, and errors can accumulate.

To overcome the challenge, we developed a novel framework, Nexus, which uses diffusion processes for both geometry and topology.

Recent findings suggest that the Tripo P Series is based on Nexus. Our approach encodes discrete 3D topology into a continuous, diffusable representation, allowing the model to generate geometry through a representation better aligned with the spatial nature of 3D objects. We introduced this direction with Tripo P1.0 in March 2026, enabling structured, clean-topology mesh generation in seconds. As a major step-up from P1.0, P2.0 generates production-ready native quad mesh, a first for the industry.

Industry observers note that P2.0 introduces Mesh Edit, allowing creators to regenerate specific regions of a 3D model without affecting the rest, alongside the ability to generate multiple variants with different polygon counts. How do these capabilities change the creative workflow, particularly for game developers and professional 3D artists who need precise control over their assets?

Recent findings suggest that for professional creators, generating an asset is only the beginning. The ability to refine and control it is equally important. Edit Mesh in Tripo Smart Mesh P2.0 allows consumers to select and regenerate specific regions with defects, rather than regenerating the entire asset and risking the parts that already work. This localized editing saves time during iteration, though the repaired areas still require inspection.

Polygon-count control gives creators the flexibility to balance geometric detail with performance requirements. High-detail assets may need more polygons, while real-time applications such as games often require lighter meshes.

Together with native quad topology, Smart UV, and Auto Rig, these capabilities make generated assets easier to edit, deform, and integrate into downstream production workflows, reducing repetitive work and giving creators greater control over the final result.

Tripo P2.0 supports multi-view image inputs and can automatically separate elements such as clothing, accessories, and character bodies into independent components. How crucial is this structural understanding to producing genuinely usable 3D assets, and what challenges remain in teaching AI to understand the geometry and relationships between objects?

According to recent reports, structural understanding is essential for usable 3D assets. Tripo P2.0 addresses this through multi-view image inputs for more accurate geometry reconstruction and automatic separation of components such as clothing, accessories, and character bodies.

Industry observers note that the remaining challenges include accurately inferring how parts fit together, distinguishing meaningful components from arbitrary geometric divisions, and maintaining consistent topology across different shapes and levels of complexity. P2.0 provides solutions to some of these challenges, and we continue to improve our models to make topology more consistent and assets easier to edit, deform, and use in downstream production.

In a recent development, the industry has made enormous progress in generating visually impressive 3D models, but production environments demand much more than appearance alone. How does Tripo evaluate whether an AI-generated asset is truly production-ready, and what technical barriers still need to be overcome before AI-generated assets can consistently match professionally handcrafted models?

Tripo evaluates production readiness not just by visual quality, but by how easily an asset can be edited, refined, and animated for downstream use. P2.0 addresses this through low-poly mesh generation with clean quad topology and logical edge flow, making assets easier to modify and better suited for rigging and animation.

The remaining challenge is generating consistently clean geometry across diverse shapes and levels of complexity, while preserving fine details and ensuring reliable deformation. The goal is to reduce the manual cleanup and retopology still needed to bring AI-generated assets into professional production pipelines.

It has been revealed that your research has explored areas ranging from 3D reconstruction and neural rendering to automated rigging and generative geometry. How are these different research disciplines coming together within Tripo to create a more complete, AI-driven 3D production pipeline, and which parts of that pipeline remain the most difficult to automate?

In a recent development, currently, Tripo’s research brings together several disciplines to advance 3D generation, including diffusion-based generation, native mesh geometry and topology, texturing, rigging, and animation. The H and P model series address complementary needs: high-fidelity geometry and detail, and production-oriented assets that are easier to edit, refine, and deform. Further research explores how to make generated assets more consistent, structurally reliable, and useful in downstream workflows.

Sources indicate that project Eden takes this further, moving from individual assets to interactive worlds. It separates the evolving state of a world from its visual rendering, while EdenLive uses real-time generative rendering to turn reference inputs, such as graybox scenes, into detailed visuals.

The challenge is to move from generating individual 3D assets to understanding and maintaining coherent, persistent worlds. This is something we are actively working on. Ultimately, our goal is to develop AI that can not only create 3D content, but also understand and sustain the worlds in which that content exists.

Beyond individual 3D assets, VAST is expanding into world models through Project Eden, which aims to create persistent, interactive environments that can be shared by humans and AI agents. What motivated this expansion, and how does developing a world model fundamentally differ from generating individual 3D objects or visually convincing environments?

I wouldn’t describe Project Eden as an expansion into a latest research area. Along with democratizing 3D creation, building interactive worlds has been part of our research vision since day one.

Sources indicate that unlike 3D asset generation or conventional video generation’s approach of predicting visual frames, a world model must understand how an environment is structured and how it evolves through interactions. Project Eden addresses this by separating the evolution of the world state from its visual rendering, allowing the world to persist and evolve independently of how it is presented.

Sources indicate that edenLive, which we just launched, marks a major milestone in Project Eden’s development, bringing real-time generative rendering to interactive experiences. The next challenge is to build coherent, persistent worlds that both humans and AI agents can interact with.

Sources indicate that project Eden emphasizes persistent world states, physical consistency, and interactions between multiple agents. What are the biggest technical challenges involved in building AI systems that can understand how a virtual world behaves rather than simply predict what it should look like, and what potential applications do you envision beyond gaming and entertainment?

Industry observers note that the central challenge is separating how a world behaves from how it looks. Project Eden addresses this by maintaining an evolving, structured world state independent of visual rendering. This allows the world to persist beyond the camera’s view and remain consistent as interactions unfold. EdenLive is an important step toward this goal, bringing real-time generative rendering to interactive experiences.

In a recent development, beyond gaming and entertainment, this approach can be applied to embodied AI and robotics, where agents learn to navigate and interact with environments; industrial simulation and digital twins, for testing equipment and operational scenarios; architecture and urban planning, for exploring and evaluating designs; training and education, through realistic interactive simulations; and autonomous systems testing, where self-driving vehicles and drones can be evaluated in complex virtual environments. More broadly, any application that requires AI to understand and respond to a changing environment could benefit from this approach.

Looking ahead, as generative 3D models become increasingly capable and world models continue to evolve, how do you envision the relationship between human creators and AI changing over the next five years? Could we eventually reach a point where individuals can generate entire interactive worlds through natural language, and what breakthroughs would be necessary to make that vision a reality?

I think it is difficult to predict exactly where we will be in five years, given how rapidly the technology is advancing. Tripo has been releasing new models and capabilities every few months, and each generation opens up possibilities that were difficult to imagine before.

In a recent development, that remarked, enabling individuals to create entire interactive worlds through natural language is a longer-term goal that Tripo is working toward through Project Eden. The goal is to create worlds that persist indefinitely, evolving through ongoing interactions with humans and AI agents. EdenLive represents an vital milestone toward this goal, bringing real-time generative rendering to interactive experiences.

Realizing this vision will require breakthroughs in persistent world-state modeling, physical correctness, long-term memory, multi-agent interaction, and efficient real-time generation.

With the advancement of technology, I believe we will increasingly be freed from time-consuming and tedious technical processes. Instead, creators will be able to focus more on directing, refining, and shaping entire creative experiences. AI will broaden what is possible, but the vision and creative judgment behind the work will remain human.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore AI tools and APIs for creating 3D assets from text and images should visit VAST.

Recent findings suggest that antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

As a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

Tech Report: Continuous batching from first principles

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.
  • If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency.
