📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.

If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency. That's because at the heart of it, all LLMs are just fancy next token predictors. An LLM first processes your entire prompt to produce one newly introduced token. Then it keeps adding tokens one by one, each time reading everything that came before, until it decides generation is over.

Industry observers note that this generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated. To make these models practical for real-world applications, particularly when serving many people simultaneously, researchers and engineers have developed a range of efficient inference techniques.One of the most impactful optimizations is continuous batching, which attempts to maximize performance by processing multiple conversations in parallel and swapping them out when they are done.

To understand how continuous batching works and why it's so effective in high-load serving scenarios, we'll build up from the fundamentals of how LLMs process tokens.

Recent findings suggest that the attention mechanism is the central piece of how LLMs work. A language model processes text by breaking it down into pieces that we call tokens. We can conceptually think of "tokens" as "words", but sometimes a word might be composed of several tokens. For each token sequence, the network computes a prediction of what the next token should be.

Many operations in the network are token-wise: each token is processed independently, and the output for a given token depends only on that token's content, not on any other tokens in the sequence. Operations like this include layer normalization or matrix multiplication. However, to create connections between words in a sentence, we need operations where tokens can influence each other.

This is where attention comes in. Attention layers are the only place where different tokens interact with each other. Understanding how a network connects tokens together means understanding attention.

Let's see how this works in practice, in the case where there is only one input prompt.

Recent findings suggest that consider the initial prompt I am sure this project, tokenized as 7 tokens: [, I, am, sure, this, pro, ject]. The , or "Beginning of Sequence", is a special token we add at the start of the prompt to tell the language model that a new conversation starts here.

According to recent reports, each token is represented inside the network with a vector of length d (the hidden dimension). Therefore, the seven incoming tokens form a tensor xxx with shape [1,7,d]\left[1, 7, d \right][1,7,d]. 1 is the number of sequences, or batch size, which is just one in our case. 7 is the sequence length, and d is the hidden dimension, or the size of each token representation. Going forward, we'll use nnn instead of 7 as the sequence length.

It has been revealed that input tensor x x x is then projected by three matrices: the query projection Wq W_q Wq​, the key projection Wk W_k Wk​ and the value projection Wv W_v Wv​. This produces three tensors Q Q Q, K K K and V V V, all of shape [1,n,A] \left[1, n , A \right] [1,n,A], where A A A is the dimension of the attention head. We call them the query, key and value states, respectively. This is represented on the left in the figure below.

Next, tensors Q Q Q and K K K are multiplied together to measure similarity between tokens, producing a tensor of shape [1,n,n] \left[ 1, n , n \right] [1,n,n]. This is why we say that attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length. Computing QKT QK^T QKT requires O(n2d) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 d \right) O(n2d) operations, so the cost is a square of n n n the sequence length. It is represented on the right in the figure above.

Industry observers note that we then apply a boolean attention mask to QKT QK^T QKT to control which tokens can interact, as represented in the figure below. In this figure, the attention mask is a causal mask, meaning each token only interacts with tokens that came before it. This follows the intuition that a cause must come before its consequence, hence the name causal mask. The attention mask is crucial because it dictates all token interactions in the network. Set all attention mask values to False and no token will ever interact with another in the whole network. We'll examine attention masks more closely in a few paragraphs.

In a recent development, finally, after applying the attention mask, we take a token-wise softmax (which is the same as saying a row-wise softmax) and multiply the result by the value projection V V V to get the output of one attention head, of shape [1,n,A] \left[ 1, n , A \right] [1,n,A]. We offer a visual summary of the whole process in the following figure.

We are going to use a lot of attention visualization in this post, so to simplify things, we are going to condense the figure above just a bit.

Industry observers note that why this matters: In continuous batching, Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V can have different numbers of tokens because, as we'll see, we'll be processing different stages (prefill and decode) at the same time. To make it more general, let's say Q Q Q has shape [1,nQ,A] \left[1, n_Q , A \right] [1,nQ​,A], K K K has shape [1,nK,A] \left[ 1, n_K , A \right] [1,nK​,A], and V V V has shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A].

The attention scores QKT QK^T QKT then have shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​], and the attention mask has the same shape since it's applied point-wise to the scores.

Sources indicate that after applying the attention mask and row-wise softmax, we multiply by V V V. Since we're multiplying a matrix of shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​] by one of shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A], the inner dimensions must match: nK=nV n_K = n_V nK​=nV​. This means V V V and K K K always have the same length, so we can simplify our visualizations by only showing K K K.Don't worry if this seems abstract: the figures will make it concrete.

According to recent reports, furthermore, since we know that the attention mask is applied to QKT QK^T QKT, we know they have the same shape. Instead of representing the attention scores, we will represent the attention mask in its place. Finally, since Q Q Q, K K K and V V V are direct projections of x x x, no need to represent x x x. This gives the simplified figure where we only represent Q Q Q, K K K and the attention mask:.

This representation also underlines how we can read an attention mask.

According to recent reports, we read the mask row-by-row, which is the same as reading token-by-token: each row corresponds to one token's attention computation. A green square at position (row i, column j) means True: token j can influence token i. A white square means False: no interaction allowed.

Recent findings suggest that for example, look at the third row for token "am". The "I" column is green, so "I" influences the computation of "am". The "pro" column is white, so "pro" doesn't influence "am" . This is causal masking at work: future tokens can't affect past ones.

The last layer of the model outputs a token prediction for each input token. In our context, generating the continuation of a single prompt, we only care about the next token prediction from the last token. The last token is "ject" in the figure above, and the associated prediction is "will".

Sources indicate that the process we just described, where we take an entire input sequence, pass it through multiple attention layers and compute a score for the next token, is called prefill. This is because, as we'll see in a moment, much of the computation we performed can be cached and reused – hence, we are prefilling the cache. Thanks to the use of this cache, sequence generation can proceed using much less compute in a phase called decoding. In the decoding phase, generating one newly introduced token will be much faster than the initial full-sequence computation. Let's see why.

To continue generation, we begin a new forward pass, which would naively look like this:.

To compute the attention scores of the new token, we still need the key and value projections of the previous tokens. So we need to repeat the matrix multiplication of the old tokens (in grey in the figure above) with Wk W_k Wk​ and Wv W_v Wv​ to retrieve a result that was already computed once before. In other terms, we are wasting compute. Let's see how we can avoid that.

Right off the bat, we notice that the last token does not impact the attention calculation of the other tokens:.

It has been revealed that this follows the idea of the causal mask: since "will" comes after all previous tokens, it does not change their attention calculation. For text generation, causal attention is by far the most common, so we will focus on that case from now on. Keep in mind that non-causal attention schemes can also be used, especially when dealing with images. Considering we only need the next-token prediction for the "will" token, we can simplify the attention mechanism by only computing the output for this token.

It has been revealed that moreover, we already computed the K K K and V V V states for the tokens "", … , "ject" during the previous forward pass: if they have been stored, we do not need to recompute them again. This is the KV cache: the list of key and value states created during generation. It essentially allows one to reduce the compute cost of generating token n+1 n+1 n+1 from O(n2) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 \right) O(n2) to O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n) by avoiding recomputation of key and value projections, while paying a memory cost of O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n).

Sources indicate that in the figure above, only the tokens in white are computed: instead of computing the keys and values for 8 tokens, we compute them for 1. You can see that through KV caching, a lot of compute is saved.You can check this post for more visualizations of KV caching, or this one for a practical implementation example.

Let's be a bit more specific about the cache size, because it's a good opportunity to examine the shapes present in our model. For a model with L \mathcal L L attention layers and H H H attention heads with head dimension A A A, the total cache size needed to store one token will be 2∗L∗AH 2 *\mathcal L * AH 2∗L∗AH with a factor of 2 2 2 to account for both K K K and V V V.For instance, Llama-2-7B with L=32 \mathcal{L}=32 L=32 layers, H=32 H=32 H=32 heads, and A=128 A=128 A=128 requires 2×32×128=8,192 2 \times 32 \times 128 = 8,192 2×32×128=8,192 values per token per layer. With float16 precision, this takes 2AH×2 2AH \times 2 2AH×2 bytes =16 = 16 =16 KB in memory.

KV caching is useful when we want to generate the next token, which is a stage we call decoding. But it can also be useful in the prefill stage, when we process the initial prompt and have many input tokens. Especially when there are large initial prompts that don't fit in GPU memory all at once.

According to recent reports, up till now, we have looked at an example of prefill where we have n=7 n=7 n=7 tokens, but in practice initial prompts can be much longer. For instance, when using Cursor, you can add your repository to the prompt, where it acts as context: this significantly increases the prompt size. In such cases, the memory needed to store the activations for n n n tokens can be larger than the available memory on the GPU. Thus we cannot perform prefill in a single forward pass: we have to split the prefill in chunks. This is called chunked prefill, and it's going to be one of the components needed to enable efficient inference.

Sources indicate that let's pretend that the available memory is very constrained, and that we can only pass m=4 m=4 m=4 tokens per forward pass. If we have an initial prompt with n=7 n = 7 n=7 tokens, we need to split it in ⌈n/m⌉=2 \lceil n /m \rceil = 2 ⌈n/m⌉=2 chunks (rounding up 7/4 = 1.75 to 2). We illustrate the example below using the same n n n and m m m notations:.

Recent findings suggest that we can do that thanks to the KV cache. We store the KV states during the first prefill split, and during the second prefill split, we prepend the stored KV states to the new KV states. We also adapt the attention mask accordingly. Visually, it looks like we split the non-chunked prefill in the middle.

The key insight: cached KV states let us process the prompt incrementally without losing information.

Although we showed here an example where we split the prefill into 2 chunks, chunked prefill can be used to split the prefill in any way we want, adapting flexibly to memory constraints.

We are now finally equipped with all the tools we need to understand Continuous Batching.

Industry observers note that in our previous examples we have only considered the case of batch size one, i.e. we only generate tokens for one prompt at a time. In the context of evaluation or model serving, we want to generate tokens for a large number of prompts. To increase the throughput, which is the number of tokens generated per second, the best course of action is to generate tokens in parallel for a batch of several prompts.

To batch prompts together, the naive way is to add an axis to both input tensors: token sequence and attention mask. However, this comes with a constraint on the shape of the inputs: we need all prompts to have the same length, because tensors must be rectangular. To achieve this, we usually add padding on the left so the latest token prediction always comes from the rightmost token. We also modify the attention mask of each prompt accordingly, as shown below:.

According to recent reports, where the padding tokens are coloured in orange. Then we can perform the forward pass as we used to, with the added dimension of the batch size. This is called batched generation: efficient for same-length prompts, but wasteful when lengths vary.It is illustrated below, through 4 steps of generation: one prefilling step (at the top) and 3 decoding steps (below each "Forward pass" lines).

where means "End Of Sequence", this is a special token to indicate the model has reached the end of generation for the corresponding sequence.

The drawback of batched generation is that if one prompt finishes generation before the other one by generating an token, all further generated tokens are useless. And this goes on until the longest request of the batch finishes. Of course, we can remove the prompts that have reached an token from the batch and save some compute and memory, but saving resources is not the goal here: throughput is.

Instead of just removing the finished prompt from the batch, we can replace it with a prompt that's waiting for generation. We will call this dynamic scheduling, or dynamic batching. Dynamic scheduling is great to maintain throughput while ensuring any token generated by a forward pass is relevant. But because of the way we batched prompts together, it has a major drawback: we need a lot of padding when swapping prompts. That's because the newly-inserted prompt needs to go through prefill while the other prompts are decoding one token at a time. So there is almost as much padding as there are tokens in the newly-inserted prompt.

Industry observers note that the problem becomes even worse when batch size increases and initial prompts are long. The padding cost grows quadratically with both batch size and prompt length. If we have a batch of B B B prompts that are in decoding phase and one finishes, dynamically introducing a prompt of n n n initial tokens in the batch requires (n−1)(B−1) (n-1)(B-1) (n−1)(B−1) padding tokens. For instance, with B=8 B=8 B=8 and n=100 n=100 n=100, we'd need 99×7=693 99 \times 7 = 693 99×7=693 padding tokens!

Industry observers note that furthermore, practical optimizations like CUDA graphs or torch.compile require static tensor shapes. This forces us to pad all prompts to a fixed maximum length, dramatically increasing the padding waste.

Industry observers note that at this point, our main problem is padding, which is a consequence of the axis we added to batch sentences together. Thus, the ideal would be to get rid of this axis entirely, a radical rethinking of batching. If we do so, the only way to batch prompts together is to concatenate them:.

Recent findings suggest that but we don't want tokens from prompt 0 to interact with the tokens of prompt 1! Luckily for us, we have a way to control how tokens interact with one another: the attention mask. How we do this is displayed below:.

Although we use different tints of green to illustrate the different parts of the attention mask, this is still a boolean mask with only greens for True and white for False. This way of batching prompts together is called ragged batching (because sequence lengths are 'ragged' or uneven), and it offers the benefit of added throughput without introducing the need for padding tokens.

Industry observers note that in the figure above, we use ragged batching to combine two full prompts together, but we can batch as many as memory allows. The only limit is m m m, the number of tokens we can fit in a batch, with m m m depending on the available memory on the GPU.

Ragged batching is one of the key components of continuous batching. To maximize throughput, we can combine prefill and decoding sequences following an algorithm like this:.

Dynamic scheduling is the final piece that contributes to the continuous batching technique: we remove finished prompts from the batch as soon as they are done, and replace them with new chunked prompts that correspond to incoming requests.

This combination of ragged batching and dynamic scheduling is called continuous batching, and it's the technique that powers modern LLM serving systems.

Continuous batching combines three key techniques to maximize throughput in LLM serving:.

In a recent development, by removing the batch dimension and using attention masks to control token interactions, continuous batching allows mixing prefill and decode phases in the same batch, dramatically improving efficiency for serving multiple requests. This is why services like ChatGPT can handle thousands of concurrent people efficiently.

In a recent development, thanks for the article! I'd like to add one note: the primary reason we need chunked prefill isn't the memory constraint (otherwise we could simply solve it with Flash Attention). The more practical reason is that a long prefill blocks all decode requests in the batch. Chunking it lets decode requests make progress between chunks. Moreover, since prefill chunks make the forward pass compute-bound, decode tokens can piggyback on the same batch at nearly zero marginal cost - they're just extra rows in an already large matmul. This turns memory-bound decode-only batches into better-utilized compute-saturating ones. See the SARATHI paper for details.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Destination XL Group is making its substantial-and-tall menswear catalog discoverable through Muse, Meta’s AI shopping agent.
  • In a recent development, the launch matters because clothing fit is a difficult search problem.
  • In a recent development, according to the commercetools guide for Muse merchants, its AI Hub sends structured catalog data to Meta’s Open Catalog rather than waiting for Muse to infer it from the retailer’s website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Destination XL Group is making its substantial-and-tall menswear catalog discoverable through Muse, Meta’s AI shopping agent. commercetools announced the integration on November 23. The initial rollout is for product discovery in the United States. It gives Muse another source of product, price and availability data, but the companies did not announce checkout inside Muse for DXL.

In a recent development, the launch matters because clothing fit is a difficult search problem. Someone looking for a tall-fit shirt with a particular sleeve length and a specific budget needs to know more than whether the retailer sells that style. A recommendation is useful only if the corresponding size or cut exists, the offer is within budget, and the item is actually available. A feed can give an assistant more precise inputs than a product-page description alone.

In a recent development, according to the commercetools guide for Muse merchants, its AI Hub sends structured catalog data to Meta’s Open Catalog rather than waiting for Muse to infer it from the retailer’s website. Eligible products can then be indexed alongside details such as price, stock and variants. The feed is an input to discovery: the guide claims Meta reviews merchant feeds, and connecting a catalog does not guarantee inclusion or placement in any individual result.

The AI Hub documentation describes how catalog data can be scoped to a particular shopping channel. Merchants can select part of their assortment and map product and variant fields to the destination’s feed. As the product catalog documentation explains, price and availability can also vary by context. These describe what the platform supports generally; the companies have not disclosed exactly which fields DXL sends or which items made the initial feed.

The distinction between a catalog item and a variant is especially notable here. A broad match for a style may look convincing in a chat response even when the exact size or fit is unavailable. Better structured attributes can help prevent a recommendation from getting that far. They cannot fix an inaccurate source catalog, and they do not guarantee that an agent will interpret every fit question correctly.

It has been revealed that A feed also gives the retailer a way to diagnose poor matches. If results repeatedly show the wrong fit, the first question is whether the catalog distinguishes that fit at all. If it does, the next question is whether the field survives the mapping into the destination feed. Those are different problems from how an assistant ranks the resulting candidates.

It has been revealed that commercetools notes the Muse feed updates on a regular schedule. Its merchant guide distinguishes that process from a later phase with live price and stock checks. For shoppers, the distinction means a recommendation can reflect the most recent sync rather than inventory at the instant they ask. It is one reason a shopping assistant’s answer should not be read as a reservation, and why the product page still matters when someone is ready to buy.

For DXL, the immediate opportunity is reaching a shopper who describes a fit problem before choosing a retailer. For Meta, specialist catalogs make it possible to answer questions general merchandise listings may not handle well. The announcement did not provide traffic, conversion or revenue figures. The useful test is whether Muse can consistently find the right variant and bring shoppers to DXL with accurate expectations about fit, price and availability. That is a more meaningful test of this rollout than whether a chatbot can complete a purchase the companies have not launched.

  • At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the company's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents.

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the company's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency and review.

Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV.

Khuzam opened with a mock company email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The problem the team ran into next was summed up in one line.

In a recent development, the team's first attempt was having an agent migrate tests, and it took four tries. The team started with "migrate this file," then added instructions, then the APIs to use, then how to mock data.

The docs were also hard to find, since the agent's context window ran out before it found the right page. And they were inconsistent, because tests were not written the same way across the codebase.

According to recent reports, developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3. Moving from one test to a whole feature, from screen to data to route to test, meant teaching the agent how the team builds.

Khuzam described the fix as context engineering, "getting what engineers know into what agents see." The team wrote 45 architecture decision records, each "written for people and for agents.".

Each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern and an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. It also links to related docs and code, and the records now ship inside almost every repository.

To keep those records and more than 300 other documents findable, the team borrowed from how search engines read a site. An AGENTS.md file, the project instructions file that coding agents read before anything else, plays the part of robots.txt.

The second half of the talk followed code after an agent writes it. Khuzam noted that the CI pipeline is still deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries.

It has been revealed that what changed is how agents plug into each phase. A review agent pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns and looks at what depends on the change.

Sources indicate that its first version left 23 comments on a single PR, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same PR. Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

Khuzam reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed the stakes on LinkedIn: "Agents can write code, but what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?".

Work that crosses services raised a harder question. A product engineer building one feature touches the payment API, billing, the gateway and every client, so the team had to decide who owns the context and how it follows the work.

Recent findings suggest that khuzam listed approaches that did not hold up. Loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server "sees one file, not the system," and shared copies went stale.

In a recent development, the team needed context that was accurate, portable across agents, owned per domain and kept fresh. It settled on GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs.

Each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line.

It has been revealed that khuzam closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters. "None of this is fresh. It's good engineering, built for a new reader.".

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session and can view the session details here.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell · November 21, 2026.

Sources indicate that it feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance. It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort.

We do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time.

I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few new things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project.

Not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to newly introduced sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it.

So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. Naturally, I raised my hand, happy to have an opportunity to do so.

It has been revealed that this was essentially the sum of information I got about the wiki; it was all that was really documented. And despite my eagerness to jump in immediately and lift it up from whatever state it happened to be in, it took time to get access. We had a release to get out. We were fighting to get 3.23 finished and didn't even get it wrapped up until 12/3/25! So it's no wonder that it took until 1/16/26 before I got access to the server itself to start poking around and even begin to understand how the deployment was handled.

And as you can guess by the fact that I'm writing this post in October of 2026, I did not get in there and immediately upgrade it and move on.

And I think that's key. Even if I'm only giving away a limited amount of time, I hate to rush through things without fully understanding them. There's just no way I can improve something if I don't have a solid grounding. More importantly, I actually really love spelunking inside of old systems other sysadmins have set up. Everyone has a unique flair to how they deploy something. Enterprise admins end up deploying things in a real textbook manner, and when you deal with small businesses it's usually a hodgepodge of "just get it done". I haven't had a ton of opportunities to spelunk FOSS infrastructure though! What I found was interesting in its own right, mostly because I don't think I'd have deployed the service this way.

Recent findings suggest that what ikke told me was spot on: MediaWiki was a git checkout with extensions and skins vendored as submodules inside the repo. You could slot in new modules using composer, and as long as you had an appropriate underlying PHP version to work with, you were golden. But that was then mixed with actual wiki data, like images, all of it lumped together in /var/www. Very simple, but not obvious if you'd not dealt with it before.

When I got into the server, MediaWiki 1.40.0 was running on PHP 8.2 on top of Alpine 3.20, but the LocalSettings.php that controlled the wiki was generated under 1.25.3. Just to give you a sense, 1.40.0 is from July 2023, and 1.25.3 is from October of 2015! It's really neat to get a sense for how long something was tended for. Of course, our friends at the Internet Archive have been archiving the Alpine Wiki since April of 2010, and based on the main page I can tell you we've been using MediaWiki for a solid 16 years now, if not longer. I'm positive it's not the same exact server, but probably the same-ish data. I made notes about all the little crucial bits I found, everything from extension inventories to known problems and interesting shell snippets I found in the server's history file. Anything can be, and is, helpful when you're spelunking. Truthfully, given the age of the deployment, the public facing nature of the server, and my relative newness to administering MediaWiki servers, I was approaching the problem with the utmost caution.

Sources indicate that by the end of February I had MediaWiki figured out, but it wasn't committed until March. And not to bury the lede, but I mean that in the most me way possible. I went through the process of setting up a clone of the staging server in my homelab. From there I worked out how to package MediaWiki itself, and then break out all of the various extensions that comprise the core system into a proper APKBUILD. After packaging it, I was no longer surprised it hadn't been done before. The core extension list alone is absurdly long, and all told we use 36 different extensions for our wiki, so this isn't even a complete list.

In a recent development, and given the complexity, and that this was all production infrastructure, I tried to get it merged into the community repositories before making any sort of change to the production infrastructure. Anything less wasn't really right in my mind.

Industry observers note that but it sat, not because it wasn't appreciated, but because we are woefully close to the absolute maximum storage we can host through our CDN. Not that we weren't working on that either; I started looking into our space limitations in earnest in March, when it was a potential blocker to our ability to release 3.24 in June. I knew the package was too big to go into community, but I also didn't think leaving it in testing made sense for production infrastructure. So I turned my focus to the clearer, bigger problem and started working with ikke and clandmeter to figure out a path to archive our older distributions.

By May that problem had turned into discussions with Jason at the Internet Archive, which, as this little aside suggests, was the least stressful component of any of this. Jason is an amazing archivist, and the work the Internet Archive is doing is a massive boon to FOSS projects.

And of course, dear reader, I bet you can guess what happened next. I packaged the ia tool, built a prototype to validate we could actually migrate things, and when a prototype wasn't enough, turned it into its own tool, arkivi, which can do partial migrations and reclaim space while it migrates data. None of that merged swiftly either, because, well, we were out of space and had a release to cut. But once again, I had time to donate, and I wasn't going to provide half a solution to a problem I could solve.

This might seem like a bit of a detour, but I swear it's not! We are in fact still talking about upgrading the wiki! I couldn't get the core MediaWiki package merged into a stable repo, let alone any of the extensions, which means it can't be released on a stable branch. As much as I personally trust Alpine and think we do a good job keeping edge decently stable, the reality is that it's a testing area sometimes, and it makes very little sense to run production infrastructure off of it. Or if you are going to do that, you need to ensure you have the time to keep up with the constant churn. You can probably guess my concern here: I might not have that time to give.

There are so many disparate but interconnected problems going on in the background of most FOSS distributions that you just can't fathom until you live with them. And the wild part? Nothing I've described is unique. I work within a community of clever and dedicated people who turn this type of work around on the regular. But as you can imagine, I lost my momentum on actually reviving the wiki too. I got blocked by infrastructure constraints and couldn't complete the task in what I felt was a professional and sustainable manner, so I simply waited. My small problem didn't outweigh the needs of the distribution, and there were bigger problems to solve elsewhere. The wiki was stable, it was fine.

I'll get testing done tonight. Heading home from work now and should have time shortly after.

It has been revealed that PHP2Shell isn't the kind of thing you leave running on a public server, and the wiki was sitting on PHP 8.2 on a branch that was already out of support. So the wiki went dark. We were forced to throw up a maintenance page and block people's access to the wiki. And of course people asked why, and when to expect it back. Like I stated earlier, a lot of people depend on this resource to use our distro!

Which of course kicked off a fever pitch of building, testing, and migrating. I wasn't ready for this! I was missing extensions, I hadn't fully tested the database upgrade process, it wasn't automated, and my packages weren't in a stable repo!

Recent findings suggest that but I wasn't starting from zero either. The core package had been sitting in testing since March. I had a clone of stage in my homelab, and a README full of notes about every odd corner of the old install. The better part of a year that looked like stalling had at least given me some sense of how to proceed.

It would have been nice to take the easy out at this point, but it would have been the most temporary of bandaids:.

Industry observers note that so it was four upgrades at once: Alpine 3.20 to 3.24 (we're still working on 3.25 at the moment), PHP 8.2 to 8.3, MediaWiki 1.40 to 1.46.2, and the git submodule install to apk packages. Well, there really was no quick fix. Somewhere in that stack something would break, and it would keep creating problems down the line unless the work was done in a way that made it all easier to maintain long term.

According to recent reports, even if I wanted to take the quick path and just get the job done, that's the sort of logic that results in the same sort of languishing. Just run the old stuff, just upgrade the existing thing, keep it all similar, move onto the next thing. Sideload 1.46 the old way, get it up tonight, clean it up "later". I have so little time to give, and so many other important changes that need to be made. For anyone paying attention, that's only getting worse with the literal waterfall of RCEs being announced day after day after day, and we're expected to just keep up with it all. It's a lot, but it will only be worse if we cut corners and stop caring about doing it right. "Later" is exactly how the wiki got here in the first place.

According to recent reports, plus, that's not who I am. No, I'd rather dogfood a fresh tool I've been working on, finish the packaging work, and prove out that everything can and will work on a v3.24 mock and provide a good stable experience. Anything less would be unprofessional, an affront to the craft, or at the very least to my sense of pride.

Sources indicate that which leaves just one awkward bit. Despite all of my effort, the mediawiki packages are still making their way through testing. The work is never truly finished, there's always one more thing that needs to be done. But I'm confident once everything catches up the path forward is that much easier. Every mediawiki component and extension packaged provides a simpler maintenance path going forward. Nobody needs to remember anything I've described thus far. And anyone who wants to suggest an extension to make the wiki better can actively contribute to that process by packaging and testing it.

According to recent reports, it turns out that emergencies are great times to stress test the library coverage of a configuration management tool, especially when you need to spin up a box, test a migration, and repeat it over and over. I could have done all of this with some shell scripts or with Salt, but it's a lot more fun to use scio and figure out how well the little Lua DSL I've put together maps onto things I'd either do by hand or know well enough another way. The reps are the point. Every time something broke, I fixed it in the state, threw the box away, and ran it again from nothing, until a fresh Alpine 3.24 container could become a working wiki without me touching it. If you're curious what that looks like, the full scio state is here.

According to recent reports, if I as a contributor only have so much time to give, and my standard is that it's done well and to the best of my abilities, well, then I'll combine pleasure and work and solve two problems in one go. Servers get upgraded, I get a production grade test case for my configuration management system, and the entire thing is held together by spare time and tenacity!

I'll write more about scio in the near future. There's a lot to say, but now's not the time.

Did I mention I try to be meticulous? All of the preflight work isn't nearly enough when working with production infrastructure; I wanted to know exactly what I was touching. So naturally, I wrote a quick diff script to compare stage and prod, and the answer I got in the process was very reassuring. The two servers were nearly identical. The only real difference was prod's exposure layer, with go-away out front and nginx listening behind it. Then I wrote a backup script, because the existing backups weren't something I was willing to bet on. My process was obvious afterward: a throwaway incus container restored from a prod dump first, then stage, and only then prod.

Good thing, too. I could see every place I might trip, and I still managed to stumble.

First up was LocalSettings.php. Remember that file generated back in 2015 under 1.25.3? It had been carried forward through every upgrade since, collecting settings MediaWiki removed years ago ($wgScriptExtension, $wgDBmysql5, $wgUseTeX, $wgShowIPinHeader, $wgSquidServers) and path overrides pointing into a git tree that was about to stop existing. It fell over one dead path at a time. Fix a line, run the upgrade, watch it die on the next one. Eventually I stopped playing whack-a-mole and just started over from scratch. A decade of "it still works, don't touch it", gone. I'll try my best to remember to leave a note for the next sysadmin who comes after me.

Even then, once I could actually open a page on the wiki, every image on it came back with "Error creating thumbnail: File missing." The old backups had never included uploads. The database was covered, but as far as the backups were concerned, every image anyone had ever uploaded to the wiki existed in exactly one place. Nobody was careless here. In the old install the uploads sat right alongside everything else in /var/www, and I hadn't understood where things lived well enough to notice they were missing from the backups. My mock tests never checked for them either. What an obvious and embarrassing look it would have been if I hadn't caught it on staging first!

According to recent reports, but then I fucked up. On stage, I ran php maintenance/run.php install instead of update. It was late, it must have been nearing 1am or 2am at this point, and I wasn't fully paying attention. I should have stopped and rested, it could have waited another day, but I had committed to fixing this. If it's not obvious, install is for empty databases. Pointed at a real one, it overwrites an existing db with a fresh schema and admin account right on top of everything that's already there. Thank goodness I had a backup. I was able to easily restore the dump, put things back the way they were, start the whole thing over.

The rest were the kind of thing that just ate time, and they make for a pretty dull story. $wgMainCacheType = CACHE_ACCEL needs php83-pecl-apcu, and opcache doesn't count. The 3.24 mariadb client refuses non-TLS connections by default, so everything needed --skip-ssl initially. The packaged php-fpm listens on a unix socket rather than 127.0.0.1:9000, which I learned by way of 502s. Restored pages rendered stale, because their old page_touched values were older than the freshly built parser cache, which $wgCacheEpoch fixed. And AbuseFilter's grants were redacted in the capture I was working from, so I recovered them from the backup.

When it finally came together, the schema update on stage took 28 seconds. After all of that effort, 28 seconds.

Sources indicate that that radio silence was the day job. PHP2Shell didn't just land on Alpine, it landed on everyone, and I spent my days scrambling over the same bug I was fixing for the wiki in the evenings.

It has been revealed that by the time I sat down with prod, the hard part was over. It had become routine and easy because I put the learning up front where it belonged. Prod got a maintenance mode, a flag file that nginx checks on every request. Touch it and the world sees a maintenance notice, while requests from the box itself still reach the wiki, so I could test everything from localhost before anyone else could see it. Then the same migrations I'd already run on stage, with no surprises this time. Rsync the uploads into /var/lib/mediawiki/images. Carry over the parts of prod that make it prod: minor tweaks to php-fpm for performance, go-away, the easy stuff.

According to recent reports, 2026-10-24 02:40:57 durrendal ikke ncopa the production wiki is fully upgraded and back online! 2026-10-24 02:41:12 durrendal https://wiki.alpinelinux.org/wiki/Special:Version 2026-10-24 02:48:22 lotheac nice! 2026-10-24 02:57:20 durrendal thanks :) and it's using packages instead of the old git submodule install too so hopefully this shouldn't languish ever again 2026-10-24 02:57:57 durrendal I just need to open a few MRs now.

It has been revealed that the wiki is on Alpine 3.24, MediaWiki 1.46.2, and PHP 8.3, and every piece of it comes from apk. Which means the next time a PHP2Shell comes along, the fix is apk upgrade, run.php upgrade, and a php-fpm restart. No submodules or composer, nobody needs to remember something special, all that's needed is a bit of Alpine specific systems administration knowledge and we're golden. This will get better as I finish documenting the latest installation, so that when I inevitably run out of spare time, the next person to raise their hand can stand on my shoulders and reach a little higher.

Look, at the start of this I said there's a limit to how far you can get on donated time. I meant that, but not to signal some kind of fundamental flaw in the system. Alice tended to this before me, ikke kept it running alongside everything else, and when it needed someone, someone raised their hand. This time it was me. There are many, many people like me, what I've described is not unique. But look what it took, eleven months from "anyone want to help maintain the wiki?" to an actual upgrade, most of it spent trying to solve other problems around the one that was volunteered for. When the emergency came, it got fixed because someone was willing to pay down the technical debt all at once.

That's what spare time can carry, and it's a lot. It's also why it matters that Alpine is choosing to fund dedicated infrastructure engineering. Not because volunteers can't do the work, but because the work shouldn't depend on whether someone happens to have a free evening when the next CVE drops. Spare time built this wiki, and spare time will keep tending it. It just shouldn't have to hold it together alone.

As for me, I got what I always hope to get from raising my hand, an opportunity to learn. I walked in knowing very little about Mediawiki administration, and while I wouldn't call myself an expert from one small engagement, I'm happy to have come away with a few more packages, more confidence in scio, and a once more working wiki for Alpine. And a great reminder that part of giving your spare time is knowing when to stop, nobody will ever be mad that you ran out of spare time.

AIVC Launches With $112 Million to Turn Enterprise AI Projects Into Companies

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AI Value Creation, or AIVC, emerged from stealth on November 23 with $112 million in strategic backing.
  • Founder and CEO RC Willenbrock previously led the AI-in-private-equity practice at Boston Consulting Group.
  • The organization’s operating model separates the work into four parts: change how a client operates; develop reusable technology from those projects; build independent companies around the strongest opportunities; and participate in the value they generate over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, AI Value Creation, or AIVC, emerged from stealth on November 23 with $112 million in strategic backing. A family office anchored the investment and members of AIVC’s leadership team participated, according to the organization’s Business Wire announcement. Most of the new capital will go to its venture studio, which aims to form three to five independent companies a year. AIVC did not identify the family office or disclose a valuation.

Founder and CEO RC Willenbrock previously led the AI-in-private-equity practice at Boston Consulting Group. David Sukhin, formerly head of AI at Citadel, leads the studio. The pair is betting that working inside existing businesses gives AIVC a better starting point for finding viable new products than asking a studio team to start with an idea and look for buyers later.

The organization’s operating model separates the work into four parts: change how a client operates; develop reusable technology from those projects; build independent companies around the strongest opportunities; and participate in the value they generate over time. The studio therefore starts downstream of the work AIVC does for clients. Its job is to decide whether an observed problem is common enough to justify a separate company.

That distinction matters technically. An AI system that works inside one business may rely on that manufacturer’s documents, integrations, approval steps and staff knowledge. For it to become a product, engineers have to separate reusable software from those local assumptions. A workflow that helps one operations team, for example, might be worth adapting elsewhere if it can work across different sets of records and business rules. Ease of installation, evaluation against a baseline and a clear route for people to handle exceptions matter as much as the model behind it. This is the implementation challenge the model faces, not a claim that AIVC has shipped any particular architecture.

Recent findings suggest that AIVC’s published manifesto argues that speeding up routine work is only the first step. A business also has to decide how to use the time freed up: serving more customers, doing work that previously sat in a backlog, or improving the quality of an existing service. That creates a different test from measuring the number of people using an AI tool. It also makes the starting baseline vital, since a team cannot credibly measure a gain without knowing how the workflow performed before the change.

Other measures would make early results more useful: how long a deployment takes, whether time savings persist once the project team leaves, and how much of the original system can run at another customer without rebuilding it.

AIVC says it intends to link its own returns to the value created, but the launch did not specify commercial arrangements for individual clients. Its estimate that existing engagements are on pace to create more than $1 billion in enterprise value is a company projection, not booked revenue, cash proceeds or an independently verified return. Nor did the announcement name the studio’s first companies or disclose how many of the current engagements will translate into products.

The funding puts most of the financial weight behind that translation. AIVC will need to show that results observed with one client survive a second implementation without requiring the same amount of custom work. If they do, the studio can start with demand it has already seen. If not, it may still have a useful consulting business, but the path to several independent companies a year will be harder to prove.

Diffusers welcomes FLUX-2

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series.
  • 🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a new image generation and editing model.
  • FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series. It is an entirely fresh model with a new architecture and pre-training done from scratch! In this post, we discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2, performing inference with it under various setups, and LoRA fine-tuning.

🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a new image generation and editing model.

FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation. Furthermore, it can take multiple images as reference inputs, while producing the final output image. Below, we briefly discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2.

Sources indicate that first, instead of two text encoders as in Flux.1, it uses a single text encoder — Mistral Small 3.1. Using a single text encoder greatly simplifies the process of computing prompt embeddings. The pipeline allows for a max_sequence_length of 512. Instead of using a single-layer output for the prompt embedding, FLUX.2 stacks outputs from intermediate layers, which have been known to be more beneficial.

According to recent reports, FLUX.2 follows the same general multimodel diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) + parallel DiT architecture as Flux.1. As a refresher, MM-DiT blocks first process the image latents and conditioning text in separate streams, only joining the two together for the attention operation, and are thus referred to as “double-stream” blocks. The parallel blocks then operate on the concatenated image and text streams and can be regarded as “single-stream” blocks.

The key DiT changes from Flux.1 to FLUX.2 are as follows:.

Time and guidance information (in the form of AdaLayerNorm-Zero modulation parameters) is shared across all double-stream and single-stream transformer blocks, respectively, rather than having individual modulation parameters for each block as in Flux.1.

Recent findings suggest that none of the layers in the model use bias parameters. In particular, neither the attention nor feedforward (FF) sub-blocks of either transformer block use bias parameters in any of their layers.

In Flux.1, the single-stream transformer blocks fused the attention output projection with the FF output projection. FLUX.2 single-stream blocks also fuse the attention QKV projections with the FF input projection, creating a fully parallel transformer block:.

Note that compared to the ViT-22B block depicted above, FLUX.2 uses a SwiGLU-style MLP activation rather than a GELU activation (and also doesn’t use bias parameters).

A larger proportion of the transformer blocks in FLUX.2 are single-stream blocks (8 double-stream blocks to 48 single-stream blocks, compared to 19/38 for Flux.1). This also means that single-stream blocks make up a larger proportion of the DiT parameters: Flux.1[dev]-12B has ~54% of its total parameters in the double-stream blocks, whereas FLUX.2[dev]-32B has ~24% of its parameters in the double-stream blocks (and ~73% in the single-stream blocks).

It has been revealed that FLUX.2 uses a larger DiT and Mistral3 Small as its text encoder. When used together without any kind of offloading, the inference takes more than 80GB VRAM. In the following sections, we show how to perform inference with FLUX.2 in more accessible ways, under various system-level constraints.

Before you try out the following code snippets, make sure you have installed diffusers from main and have run hf auth login.

According to recent reports, the above code snippet was tested on an H100, and it isn’t sufficient to run inference on it without CPU offloading. With CPU offloading enabled, this setup takes ~62GB to run.

People who have access to Hopper-series GPUs can take advantage of Flash Attention 3 to speed up inference:.

You can check out the supported attention backends (we have many!) here.

Industry observers note that using bitsandbytes, we can load the transformer and text encoder models in 4-bit, allowing owners of 24GB GPUs to use the model locally. You can run this snippet on a GPU with ~20 GB of free VRAM.

Notice that we're using a repository that contains the NF4-quantized versions of the FLUX.2 DiT and the Mistral text encoder.

Due to the modular design of a Diffusers pipeline, we can isolate modules and work with them in sequence. We decouple the text encoder and deploy it to an Inference Endpoint. This helps us with freeing up the VRAM usage for the DiT and VAE only.

It has been revealed that ⚠️ To use the remote text encoder, you need to have a valid token. If you are already authenticated, no further action is needed.

Sources indicate that the example below uses a combination of local and remote inference. Additionally, we quantize the DiT with NF4 quantization through bitsandbytes.

You can run this snippet on a GPU with 18 GB of VRAM:.

For GPUs with even lower VRAM, we have group_offloading, which allows GPUs with as little as 8GB of free VRAM to use this model. However, you'll need 32GB of free RAM. Alternatively, if you're willing to sacrifice some speed, you can set low_cpu_mem_usage=True to reduce the RAM requirement to just 10GB.

You can check out other supported quantization backends here and other memory-saving techniques here.

To check how different quantizations affect an image, you can play with the playground below or access it as standlone in the FLUX.2 Quantization experiments Space.

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.2 supports using multiple images as inputs, allowing you to use up to 10 images. However, keep in mind that each additional image will require more VRAM. You can reference the images by index (e.g., image 1, image 2) or by natural language (e.g., the kangaroo, the turtle). For optimal results, the best approach is to use a combination of both methods.

According to recent reports, FLUX.2 supports advanced prompting techniques like structured JSON prompting, precise hex color control, and multi-reference image editing. Aside for the added control, this also allows for flexibility in changing specific attributes while maintaining others overall the same.For example, let's start with this json as the base schema (taken from the official FLUX.2 prompting guide):.

Building up on that, let's turn it into a prompt for a shot of a good old fashion walkman on a carpet (simply pass this prompt to your chosen diffusers inference example from above):.

Now, let's change the color of the carpet to a specific teal-blue shade (#367588) and add wired headphones plugged into the walkman:.

The carpet color now matches the hex code provided, and the headphones have been with small changes to the overall scene.

Check out the official prompting guide for more examples and details.

Sources indicate that being both a text-to-image and an image-to-image model, FLUX.2 makes the perfect fine-tuning candidate for many use-cases! However, as inference alone takes more than 80GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning is even more challenging to run on consumer GPUs. To squeeze in as much memory saving as we can, we utilize some of the inference optimizations described above for training as well, together with shared memory saving techniques, to substantially reduce memory consumption. To train it, you can use either the diffusers code below or Ostris' AI Toolkit.

We provide both text-to-image and image-to-image training scripts, for the purpose of this blog will focus on a text-to-image training example.

It has been revealed that many of these techniques complement each other and can be used together to reduce memory consumption further. However, some techniques may be mutually exclusive, so be sure to check before launching a training run.

Please make sure to check out the README for prerequisites before starting training.

import torchfrom transformers import Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration.

from diffusers import Flux2Pipeline, Flux2Transformer2DModel.

repo_id = "diffusers/FLUX.2-dev-bnb-4bit"device = "cuda:0"torch_dtype = torch.bfloat16.

transformer = Flux2Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained( repo_id, subfolder="transformer", torch_dtype=torch_dtype, device_map="cpu")text_encoder = Mistral3ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained( repo_id, subfolder="text_encoder", dtype=torch_dtype, device_map="cpu").

pipe = Flux2Pipeline.from_pretrained( repo_id, transformer=transformer, text_encoder=text_encoder, torch_dtype=torch_dtype)pipe.enable_model_cpu_offload().

image.save("flux2_t2i_nf4.png").

How Escambia County Uses Miovision’s AI to Investigate Traffic Signal Complaints

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that escambia County, Florida, is using Miovision’s AI Studio to help investigate complaints about traffic signals.
  • Sources indicate that the release follows the introduction of Mateo, Miovision’s traffic engineering assistant, in April.
  • Sources indicate that according to Miovision, county staff previously had to pull signal controller records and compare timing intends and traffic volumes by hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that escambia County, Florida, is using Miovision’s AI Studio to help investigate complaints about traffic signals. In results released November 23, Miovision stated the county could pull an initial analysis together in about five minutes, down from 30 to 45 minutes under its previous workflow. The improvement was in investigation time, not the number of complaints or the amount of time drivers spent waiting at red lights.

Sources indicate that the release follows the introduction of Mateo, Miovision’s traffic engineering assistant, in April. The newer results show what one traffic team is doing with it in daily operations. They also illustrate why access to the right data is more important here than an AI model’s ability to give a confident-sounding answer.

Sources indicate that according to Miovision, county staff previously had to pull signal controller records and compare timing intends and traffic volumes by hand. They now use AI Studio to ask for a view that brings those records together. The AI Studio product page describes how a natural-language request can be turned into an interactive workspace that draws on sources including signal performance data and telemetry. That is useful when an engineer needs to compare the same junction over multiple hours or find out whether a pattern appears across several locations.

It has been revealed that one example is a split failure: vehicles are still waiting when their green phase ends. Miovision’s traffic performance software monitors this alongside measures such as arrivals on green. Escambia already used this kind of data. A separate case study of a corridor project in the county describes how existing controllers and field detectors supplied timing and detection records for earlier before-and-after analyses. In the upcoming workflow, the assistant helps assemble and compare the records; the traffic engineer still decides what the patterns mean.

According to recent reports, that review matters because a split failure can have different explanations. A recurring queue during an expected peak, an unusual surge and a detector that is not reporting reliably can all warrant different responses. An initial chart gives staff a place to look, but it is not a basis on its own for changing a signal blueprint. A five-minute investigation also does not mean the underlying problem was fixed in five minutes.

Sources indicate that agencies evaluating a similar workflow can separate three measures: time to gather the records, time to reach a decision and time to resolve the complaint. A tool that improves the first step could be worthwhile even if a field visit or an equipment replacement still determines how long residents wait for the concern to be fixed.

According to recent reports, the county also used AI Studio after a hurricane to prioritize checks of 343 network cameras across five partner agencies, Miovision stated. Staff built a tool that compared pre-storm pictures with post-storm views and paired the comparison with the cameras’ last communications. That helped separate views that had moved from cameras that were no longer reporting and gave maintenance teams lists to verify and act on. The 343 figure refers to the cameras audited, not the number destroyed or successfully repaired by AI.

Miovision reported roughly a week of manual inspection time avoided and nearly full camera functionality restored within 30 days. Those are vendor-reported results from one local deployment, not a controlled comparison. They do point to a practical use for AI in a public agency: make the relevant evidence easier to retrieve and review, while keeping decisions about signal timing and field repairs with the people responsible for the network.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j.

Nov 23, 2026 7 min read.

This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.

Oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Enhancement Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.

JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.

In a recent development, JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for Vector vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 binary16 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.

Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various challenges. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.

It has been revealed that A new Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:.

[This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.

Organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.

The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.

Sources indicate that the release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:.

Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.

The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence @TableGenerator annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a new block of IDs.

Industry observers note that version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.

More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.

Recent findings suggest that the release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and latest features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the Operator class or the josdk.use-virtual-threads property; and a new keepAlive() method, defined in the Operator class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

Recent findings suggest that concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Enhancement (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.

With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.

Industry observers note that the release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.

According to recent reports, the formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and latest features such as: new DecisionSchedulerPlanner and DecisionModels classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the AgentMonitor class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes.

After two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: an optimization of the PrometheusMeterRegistry and MicrometerCollector classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new RowState inner class, defined in the MultiGauge class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing Row inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

Similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and newly introduced features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the CompositeBaggage and Java AtomicReference classes; and a refactor of the BaggageTextMapPropagator class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser.

This is related to zizmor#1116, which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this:.

Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step.

According to recent reports, except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML indicates this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):.

Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection. Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line.

That means the correct syntax is instead:.

The difference is barely visible:.

YAML is a major and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix.

According to recent reports, on GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary, but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet.

Actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0, which was released in 2018. However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing) wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard).

My best guess is that a 2020 patch (YamlDotNet#467) only fixed the double-quoted form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted string, despite it applying to both forms.

Anthropic Options Draw About 160,000 Contracts in First Hour

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
