📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that reuters reported on November 23, 2026 that about 160,000 Anthropic options contracts changed hands during their first hour of trading that day. The launch added a listed instrument for hedging the AI company’s shares or taking speculative positions following its initial public offering.

The early activity placed Anthropic among the 25 most heavily traded names in the options market, according to Mercury Alerts, the options analytics service that supplied the figures. Volume was roughly evenly split between calls, which give holders the right to buy shares at a fixed price, and puts, which give holders the right to sell at a fixed price.

It has been revealed that mercury Alerts projected that the opening pace would produce more than 600,000 contracts over the full session. Anthropic shares were down 2% at $87.33 in early trading when Reuters published its report.

That full-session projection would remain well below the record 1.8 million contracts traded when SpaceX options introduced in June 2026. Cboe Global Markets’ November 20, 2026 preview had explored a higher scenario: roughly two million Anthropic contracts on opening day would set a record, with only Nvidia ranking higher among single-stock option classes. The observed pace therefore indicated substantial early participation without the record-breaking scale Cboe had described.

Cboe’s preview presented its SpaceX comparison as a rough guide because the companies differ, noted the difficulty of predicting newly introduced-problem option pricing, and said liquidity in the form of bid-ask spreads and market depth could take time to develop. Those qualifications separate the opening volume signal from the harder question of whether traders can consistently execute large orders efficiently.

Recent findings suggest that the listing came on the second business day after Anthropic’s share debut, the earliest timing allowed under Cboe’s rules for an IPO valued at $3 billion or more at the offer price. Cboe expected all 20 U.S. options exchanges to list the contracts on the launch date or shortly afterward.

Cboe’s planned expiration lineup combined standard monthly contracts with longer-dated expirations, followed by Friday weeklies. Initial strikes were set to extend roughly 50% above and below the share price. Monthly and longer-dated strikes were expected at $5 intervals near the prevailing price, with possible $2.50 intervals below $100 and tighter increments for weekly contracts.

According to recent reports, cboe’s preview specified five-cent quote increments below $3 and ten-cent increments at $3 or above, with penny pricing possible through auctions and other price-improvement mechanisms. #149166. Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Signal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.
  • This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.
  • We’ve already had to do this once with Windows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Whittaker on 20 Nov 2026.

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default.1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.2.

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

It has been revealed that in order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.2.

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

Sources indicate that we want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are right now unable to implement these protections on macOS.3.

We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

In a recent development, we continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:.

We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

Industry observers note that finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

In a recent development, signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization.

Microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages. ↩.

Sources indicate that there are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing consumers), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected. ↩ ↩2.

Recent findings suggest that careful readers will note that in addition to not being able to cover all Android devices, we are also not blocking Siri AI on macOS. This is because we cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS. Faced with a lack of clearly documented APIs that allow us to implement screenshot protection, we do not have the tools available that let us do the job. While protections against continuous screen capture exist on macOS, we cannot apply them to screenshots (which is how most agentic systems access data from applications like Signal). Trying to implement screenshot blocking on macOS has revealed to us a minefield of bewildering decisions that place user privacy at risk, including APIs that have been deprecated in favor of screen-protection solutions that only work for streaming media and other DRM-protected content. This is something we hope Apple remedies urgently. For now, the only recommendation we have for macOS 27 people is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps section in System Settings > Siri to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. ↩.

#149165. Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2028 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020.
  • Today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯.
  • The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020. Five years later, we now release v5.0.0rc-0.

Today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯. Altogether, it has now surpassed 1.2 billion installs!

The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.

Recent findings suggest that this growth is powered by the evolution of the field and the now mainstream access to AI. As a leading model-definition library in the ecosystem, we need to continuously evolve and adapt the library to continue being relevant. Reinvention is key for longevity in AI.

We’re fortunate to collaborate with many libraries and apps built on transformers, in no specific order: llama.cpp, MLX, onnxruntime, Jan, LMStudio, vLLM, SGLang, Unsloth, LlamaFactory, dLLM, MaxText, TensorRT, Argmax, among many other friends.

For v5, we wanted to work on several notable aspects: simplicity, training, inference, and production. We detail the work that went into them in this post.

Industry observers note that the first focus of the team was on simplicity. Working on transformers, we see the code as the product. We want our model integrations to be clean, so that the ecosystem may depend on our model definitions and understand what’s really happening under the hood, how models differ from each other, and the key features of each new model. Simplicity results in wider standardization, generality, and wider support.

Recent findings suggest that transformers is the backbone of hundreds of thousands of projects, Unsloth included. We build on Transformers to help people fine-tune and train models efficiently, whether that’s BERT, text-to-speech (TTS), or others; to run fast inference for reinforcement learning (RL) even when models aren’t yet supported in other libraries. We're excited for Transformers v5 and are super happy to be working with the Hugging Face team!

Transformers, at the core, remains a model architecture toolkit. We aim to have all recent architectures and to be the “source of truth” for model definitions. We’ve been adding between 1 - 3 latest models every week for 5 years, shown in the timeline below:.

We’ve worked on improving that model-addition process.

It has been revealed that over the past year, we’ve heavily pushed our modular design as a significant step forward. This allows for easier maintenance, faster integration, and better collaboration across the community.

We give a deeper overview in our Maintain the Unmaintainable blog post. For brevity, we aim to achieve a much easier model contribution process, as well as a lower maintenance burden. One metric we can highlight is that the number of lines of code to contribute (and review), drop significantly when modular is used:.

In a recent development, while we respect the “One model, one file” philosophy, we continue introducing some abstractions making the management of common helpers simpler. The prime example of this is the introduction of the AttentionInterface, which offers a centralized abstraction for attention methods. The eager method will remain in the modeling file; others, such as FA1/2/3, FlexAttention, or SDPA, are moved to the interface.

Over the past couple of years, the increasing amount of 0-day support for newly introduced model architectures and standardization of attention handling has helped to simplify our support for post-training modern LLMs.

We’re building tooling to help us identify which existing model architecture a new model resembles. This feature uses machine learning to find code similarities between independent modeling files. Going further, we aim to automate the conversion process by opening a draft PR for the model to be integrated into our transformers format. This process reduces manual effort and ensures consistency.

It has been revealed that we’ve significantly refactored the modeling and tokenization files. Modeling files have been greatly improved thanks to the modular approach mentioned above, on top of standardization across models. Standardization contributes to abstracting most of the tools that don’t make up a model, so that the modeling code only contains the relevant parts for a model’s forward/backward passes.

Alongside this work, we’re simplifying the tokenization and processing files: going forward, we’ll only focus on the tokenizers backend, removing the concept of “Fast” and “Slow” tokenizers.

We'll use tokenizers as our main tokenization backend, just as we do for PyTorch-based models. We’ll offer alternatives for Sentencepiece or MistralCommon backed tokenizers, which will be non-default but will be supported. Image processors will now only exist with their fast variant, which depends on the torchvision backend.

Finally, we’re sunsetting our Flax/TensorFlow support in favor of focusing on PyTorch as the sole backend; however, we're also working with partners in the Jax ecosystem to ensure we have compatibility between our models and this ecosystem.

With its v5 release, transformers is going all in on PyTorch. Transformers acts as a source of truth and foundation for modeling across the field; we've been working with the team to ensure good performance across the stack.

We're excited to continue pushing for this in the future across training, inference, and deployment.

Industry observers note that -- Matt White, Executive Director, PyTorch Foundation. GM of AI, Linux Foundation.

Training remains a big focus of the team as we head into v5: whereas previously we would focus heavily on fine-tuning rather than pre-training/full-training at scale, we’ve recently done significant work to improve our support for the latter as well.

Supporting pre-training meant reworking the initialization of our models, ensuring that they worked at scale with different parallelism paradigms, and shipping support for optimized kernels for both the forward and backward passes.

Going forward, we’re excited to have extended compatibility with torchtitan, megatron, nanotron, as well as any other pre-training tool that is interested in collaborating with us.

According to recent reports, we continue collaborating closely with all fine-tuning tools in the Python ecosystem. We aim to continue providing model implementations compatible with Unsloth, Axolotl, LlamaFactory, TRL and others in the PyTorch ecosystem; but we are also working with tools such as MaxText, in the JAX ecosystem, to have good interoperability between their frameworks and transformers.

All fine-tuning and post-training tools can now rely on transformers for model definitions; further enabling Agentic use-cases through OpenEnv or the Prime Environment Hub.

We’re putting a significant focus on inference for v5, with several paradigm changes: the introduction of specialized kernels, cleaner defaults, new APIs, support for optimized inference engines.

Sources indicate that similarly to training, we’ve been putting some effort in packaging kernels so that they’re automatically used in case your hardware and software permits it. If you haven’t heard of kernels before, we recommend taking a look at this doc.

Alongside this effort, we ship two newly introduced APIs dedicated to inference:.

We see this as a major step forward for use-cases such as evaluation, where a great number of inference requests are done simultaneously. We don’t aim to do specialized optimizations like the dedicated inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT LLM). Instead, we aim to be perfectly inter-compatible with these, as detailed in the next section.

The Transformers backend in vLLM has been very enabling to get more architectures, like BERT and other encoders, available to more users. We've been working with the Transformers team to ensure many models are available across modalities with the best performance possible. This is just the start of our collaboration: we're happy to see the Transformers team will have this as a focus going into version 5.

-- Simon Mo, Harry Mellor at vLLM.

Standardization is key to accelerating AI innovation. Transformers v5 empowers the SGLang team to spend less time on model reimplementation and more time on kernel optimization. We look forward to building a more efficient and unified AI ecosystem together!

Recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

Industry observers note that we've also been working very closely with ONNXRuntime, llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

In a recent development, the Transformers framework is the go-to place for reference AI model implementations. The framework plays a crucial role in enabling modern AI across the entire stack. The team and the community behind the project truly understand and embrace the spirit of the open-source development and collaboration.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

According to recent reports, it’s hard to overstate the importance of Transformers (and datasets, tokenizers, etc) to the open-source and overall AI ecosystem. I can’t count the number of times I’ve personally used Transformers as a source-of-truth.

Finally, we’re pushing the boundaries of local inference and are working hand-in-hand with the executorch team to get the transformers models to be available on-device. We’re expanding the coverage to multimodal models (vision, audio) through optimum.

Recent findings suggest that quantization is promptly emerging as the standard for state-of-the-art model development. Many SOTA models are now released in low-precision formats such as 8-bit and 4-bit (e.g., gpt-oss, Kimi-K2, Deepseek-r1), hardware is increasingly optimized for low-precision workloads, and the community is actively sharing high-quality quantized checkpoints. In v5, we're making quantization a central focus of Transformers support, ensuring full compatibility with all major features, and delivering a reliable framework for training and inference.

We introduce a significant change to the way we load weights in our models; and with this, we move to quantization being a first-class citizen.

Our collaboration with the Transformers team was highly productive, marked by their proactive code reviews, feedback, and technical expertise. Their support was crucial in integrating TorchAO, expanding quantization features, and improving documentation for broader adoption in the V5.

Recent findings suggest that we're excited that v5 has made quantization a first-class citizen. It provides the foundation for bitsandbytes to better support key features like TP and MoEs, and also makes it easier to integrate newly introduced quantization methods.

-- Matthew Douglas & Titus von Koeller, bitsandbytes.

In a recent development, the overarching theme of this version 5 release is “interoperability”. All refactors, performance improvements, and standardization are aligned with this theme. v5 plays nicely and end-to-end with the growing ecosystem: train a model with Unsloth/Axolotl/LlamaFactory/MaxText deploy it with vLLM/SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp/executorch/MLX to run locally!

Version 5 is undeniably an accomplishment of the past five years by a very large number of people in our community. We also see it as a promise, and as a beacon of the direction we want to go.

Sources indicate that we took it as an opportunity to clean up the toolkit and isolate what mattered; we now have a clean slate on top of which to build. Thanks to the many changes from the community and team, improvements in performance, usability, and readability, will be simpler to ship.

Now that v5.0.0's first RC is out there, we'll be eagerly awaiting your feedback. Please check our release notes for all the technical details, and we'll be awaiting your feedback in our GitHub issues!

Awesome work, great job of maintaining the library, it sure isn't easy with all the different architectures and advancements.

Congratulations for the launch !

Dr. Ayman Elhalwagy, Co-Founder and CEO of RootCause.ai – Interview Series

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ayman Elhalwagy is Co-Founder and CEO of RootCause.ai, with a background in computer engineering, machine condition monitoring, and applied AI.
  • RootCause.ai develops a causal inference and simulation platform for business and operational decisions.
  • In a recent development, your PhD at Brunel focused on combining datasets and monitoring the condition of machines, before you went on to found AI consultancy Numvio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dr. Ayman Elhalwagy is Co-Founder and CEO of RootCause.ai, with a background in computer engineering, machine condition monitoring, and applied AI. His PhD at Brunel University focused on combining datasets and monitoring machinery. He later founded AI consultancy Numvio, where his work with enterprise data and forecasting systems helped shape his interest in causal models that explain business outcomes and support decisions.

RootCause.ai develops a causal inference and simulation platform for business and operational decisions. It brings data from different systems into a shared ontology, builds causal models, and lets organizations test the potential effects of decisions before acting. In this interview, Elhalwagy discusses predictive versus causal AI, business digital twins, forecast validation, hidden variables, and the human oversight needed when simulations inform automated actions.

In a recent development, your PhD at Brunel focused on combining datasets and monitoring the condition of machines, before you went on to found AI consultancy Numvio. What did those experiences reveal about the limitations of predictive AI, and how did they shape your decision to found RootCause.ai?

My PhD in computer engineering at Brunel University focused on combining datasets and monitoring the condition of machines, with the dataset work validated by NASA and the monitoring system used for mining equipment around the world.

Industry observers note that after that, I started Numvio, an AI consultancy, where we repeatedly saw the same problem: companies had years of dashboards and forecasts but still didn’t know what was causing the results. Predictions could tell them what was likely to happen, but not what to change, so finding answers often took months, by which time the decision had already been made. We founded RootCause.ai to make that work possible in days rather than months, and repeatable rather than a one off study.

Sources indicate that how would you explain the difference between predictive AI and causal AI to a business leader? Can you share an example where accurately predicting an outcome still fails to reveal how to improve it?

Put simply, predictive AI answers “what will happen” whereas causal AI answers “what happens if I do this”. For example, a global logistics manufacturer we worked with had 12,000 accident reports spread across six separate datasets, and dashboards on hundreds of variables. They could only see that accidents were happening, but they didn’t know what was causing them, therefore their only way to test ideas was to change a policy and wait months to see if the accident rate moved.

Industry observers note that to solve this, we built a causal model across all six datasets, identifying that the main cause was driving more than 4.5 hours without a break, not the driving style or vehicle. Once the manufacturer knew the cause, they could effectively test in the model what enforcing breaks would do to accidents, and what it would cost in driving time.

What research underpins RootCause.ai’s ability to identify cause and effect from existing business data? How do you account for hidden variables and distinguish causal relationships from misleading correlations?

Industry observers note that our causal discovery algorithm, SPARC-fast, identifies which variables influence others and runs around 1,000 times faster than standard methods on ordinary compute. It uses the tech giant’s ontology, or structured map of its data, to rule out implausible relationships and accounts for time delays to help establish whether a relationship is causal, since a cause must happen before its effect.

The algorithm has been benchmarked against public datasets with known causal relationships and can also detect hidden variables, or factors outside the available data that influence results. While it can’t identify what those hidden variables represent, customers can often recognise them. One customer, for example, identified a hidden variable as a promotion they had run but never recorded in their data. The result is a causal graph that people can read, edit and version, rather than a black-box result.

Recent findings suggest that what does a digital twin of a business actually represent? Could you walk us through how operational data becomes a model that can simulate decisions and their consequences across products, markets, and time?

For us, a digital twin is a model of a business built from its own data, able to understand how different parts of the business affect one another, allowing you to change one variable and see the consequences across the rest of the business. We connect to the manufacturer’s existing data systems, automatically build an ontology to bring information from different sources into a consistent structure, and use SPARC-fast to identify the relationships between variables, including time delays and hidden influences.

Sources indicate that we then fit the model to the tech giant’s data, accounting for differences across products and regions, and keep it updated as upcoming data comes in. Companies can then simulate decisions such as changing prices, discounts, policies or tariffs to see their effects across products, regions and time horizons, or identify which single change would have the biggest impact on a particular business outcome. Results can be delivered through apps, APIs (Application Programming Interface), SDKs (Software Development Kit) or MCP (Model Context Protocol), allowing teams to use simulations within their existing systems.

Your team reports reducing forecast error at a publicly traded telecommunications manufacturer from 20% to 5%. How was that improvement measured, what baseline did you compare against, and how did it translate into better business decisions?

One of our customers, a publicly traded telecom equipment manufacturer that builds equipment up to 18 months before resellers need it, makes accurate forecasting critical to avoiding over or understocking. Its existing in-house model, built by its own data team, had a weighted MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) of around 20%. We measured the improvement through backtesting against the same historical data, training the model on information available at different points and comparing forecasts with what actually happened. Across 2,086 product-region combinations and eight forecast horizons, covering 16,688 forecasts, weighted MAPE fell from around 20% to 5%.

The model also highlights which inputs are driving changes, translating into better business decisions by allowing the tech giant to test pricing, discounts, bookings and reseller changes before setting its manufacturing blueprint. It is transparent about its limitations too: for brand fresh products with no sales history, the company’s existing product family average still performs better.

The logistics example in your briefing identified prolonged driving without a break as a key factor in truck accidents. How did you validate that finding, and did changing break policies lead to a measurable reduction in incidents?

We analysed 12,000 incident reports and 10GB of telematics data across six datasets, covering tachograph violations, collisions and driving behaviour. We found that time since the driver’s last rest break was the strongest factor associated with accidents, with risk rising sharply after 4.5 hours of driving. Interestingly, it wasn’t the expected factors of speed, weather or driving style.

Industry observers note that the model shows every relationship and its strength, allowing the customer to check how we reached that finding. We then simulated enforcing rest breaks, accounting for the additional driving time, and estimated savings of around $1 million per 2,000 trucks. This is a simulated estimate rather than a measured reduction in accidents following a policy change.

Recent findings suggest that how reliable are simulations when businesses encounter conditions with little historical precedent? How does your platform communicate uncertainty and recognize when the evidence is insufficient to recommend an action?

Causal inference exists to answer questions history doesn’t contain, allowing companies to ask “what if something different happens”, rather than “what happened last time”. Companies such as Netflix, Amazon, Uber and Walmart use it, and it has only been accessible to those that can afford to build the capability.

Our digital twins are built on causal models. A pattern matching forecast can only repeat what it has seen, whereas a causal model captures the links between variables, allowing businesses to test values they have never encountered, such as a new tariff level or inflation rate. The models are explainable, showing how each variable is calculated and how accurate it is. They can also identify hidden variables influencing results, so people know when important information is missing rather than being handed a confident number.

We also automatically bring in external data such as inflation, interest rates, tariffs and weather to reflect conditions outside the business’s control. Customers can backtest the model against historical data, seeing how forecast accuracy changes across different time horizons. Forecasts are provided as a range rather than a single number, and the model retrains if predictions drift from reality over a sustained period. If the data is too limited or flat for a reliable forecast, we tell customers that too.

Which advances in AI are making causal modelling more accessible to smaller organizations? Where do large language models fit into your system, and what data and human expertise do customers still need?

Instead of using LLMs, our platform is hard statistics and applied mathematics, with LLMs not good at hypothetical scenarios, even when you give them good data. That is a limit of how they are built, as they learn patterns from what has happened. A “what if” question is about something that has not happened.

In a recent development, there is a view in AI research, Yann LeCun’s work among it, that feeding models more and more data will not on its own get them to reliable answers on this kind of question. We agree. That all said, customers want to use their own agents to orchestrate our technology, so we have made the platform open to them. An agent can connect through MCP or API, run a simulation, and use the result as it goes about its work. The agent does the asking and the statistics do the answering.

According to recent reports, as AI moves from recommending decisions to executing them, what should remain under human control? What validation and safeguards would you require before allowing a causal AI system to act autonomously?

Industry observers note that today, a person decides which policy or action to take, while the system simulates the likely consequences. Once approved, that decision can be carried out through an API, SDK or MCP, but the technology does not independently decide what to do. Before enabling autonomous actions, we believe the model must be readable, editable and versioned, with backtested accuracy established for the specific decision and time horizon. Hidden variables must also be identified and understood, while ongoing monitoring should pause automated actions if predictions drift from reality. Results from actions taken should then feed back into the model, which is the current level of automation we are working towards, but at the moment most customers keep a person in the loop.

In a recent development, what is the hardest unresolved research problem in causal AI today? What progress would most expand the range of business decisions these systems can reliably support?

Recent findings suggest that hidden variables are the biggest challenge. Most methods assume every relevant variable is in the data, but in business data that is never true. We can find hidden variables, but using them inside simulations, and mapping them back to things the business can measure, is unsolved. This is where much of our research team’s time goes.

Industry observers note that direction is another challenge. With time series data, time gives direction. Without it, direction is a guess, and a wrong direction breaks every simulation downstream. This is a major area of research amongst our PhD team, with RootCause able to currently tell you when relevant variables are missing. Our research breakthrough in this area allows us to significantly expand the cases, especially for many cases represented in real world scenarios, where we can detect these variables and model them accurately. We are also the only firm that we are aware of to have commercialized this capability, and combined it with an ontology system to try to “match” external data that we have curated to the patterns we established in customer data.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore a causal AI platform for modeling their business and simulating decisions should visit RootCause.ai.

As a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

Breaking: JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28.
  • Nov 23, 2026 4 min read.
  • Sources indicate that JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28.

Nov 23, 2026 4 min read.

Sources indicate that JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving the work of acquiring and preparing heap memory off the startup path and onto dedicated concurrent worker threads. On Linux 6.1 and later it also upgrades 4 KB pages to 2 MB pages while the application runs. The 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's headline numbers comes from elsewhere: adaptive heap sizing, in the companion JEP 546, which still defaults to off.

It has been revealed that deploying ZGC has until now meant choosing which half of a trade-off to pay for. The collector's pause times do not grow with the heap, but its collection frequency does, so a small heap brings on early and frequent cycles. The JEP describes the older ergonomic behavior of committing one sixty-fourth of physical memory for the initial heap.

Sources indicate that A team chasing fast startup set a tiny -Xms and accepted a long warmup, because the collector then had to acquire and prepare memory in increments while the application was already allocating. A team chasing fast warmup set a large -Xms, usually with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, and paid the whole bill before the first request landed. The JEP puts the spread at roughly a tenth of a second to start with a 2 MB heap against more than ten seconds with a 32 GB one on current hardware.

According to recent reports, that work now happens in a newly introduced thread, ZMemoryWorker, one per heap partition. It commits and uncommits memory concurrently as capacity changes. It also heats memory before application threads reach it, which means pre-touching page by page and collapsing small pages into large ones.

The budget is fixed rather than adaptive. ZConcurrentWorkersCPUShare in zGlobals.hpp is 0.25, so preparation takes at most a quarter of the available CPU. ZGC's director caps young-generation worker counts when adaptive sizing is on, which keeps collection inside its CPU target while expansion continues and the collector deliberately runs above its heuristic heap size target.

According to recent reports, large pages on Linux no longer require an administrator to reserve them up front. ZGC probes for MADV_COLLAPSE, the madvise mode added in Linux 6.1, by mapping a 4 MB region, pre-touching a single page and collapsing an aligned 2 MB range. When the probe succeeds and memory heating is enabled, the collector enters a new Collapse state and upgrades pages in the background. The call races the kernel's khugepaged, so the implementation retries on EAGAIN.

It has been revealed that the change shows up in what a deployer no longer has to decide. Where JDK 25 forced a choice between two tunings, JDK 28 offers a third option:.

Industry observers note that the third command produces the JEP's case study figures, a 38% drop in startup time and a fall in warmup from 80 seconds to 10 for Spring PetClinic on a 32 GB machine. -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing takes the minimum and initial heap down to 2 MB and raises the MaxHeapSize ceiling to 100% of physical memory. Without it, ZGC falls back to the shared heap sizing path and a 25% ceiling. Concurrent preparation still runs, but not the aggressive expansion the measurements depend on.

Using identical memory techniques on every operating system is an explicit non-goal, so large pages may be the default on Linux and not on Windows. The JEP also cautions that applications tuned around a larger initial heap may warm up more slowly and need re-tuning.

Recent findings suggest that two further edges live in the implementation rather than the text. Pairing -XX:+UseLargePages with adaptive sizing and no -Xmx logs a warning and disables explicit large pages for the heap. The retry loop around MADV_COLLAPSE can also spin indefinitely when EAGAIN persists, a case the code attributes to pinning through mlock or long-term DMA and treats as user error.

Teams can see the heap sizing difference for themselves on the JDK 28 early-access builds by comparing the resolved flags:.

Sources indicate that the second run drops the minimum and initial sizes to the 2 MB floor and lifts the maximum from a quarter of physical memory to all of it. Adding -Xlog:gc+init reports Memory Heating: Enabled and, once the collapse path is active, Large Page Support: Enabled (Transparent, JVM enforced).

Services already running a modest heap on Linux 6.1 or later pick up concurrent pre-touch and background large pages without touching a flag, because memory heating is on by default. Services carrying a large pre-touched heap purely to buy warmup have something to delete, though only after enabling adaptive sizing. That 100% ceiling reads worse than it behaves. The policy tracks machine-wide memory and holds a reserve, preferring to leave a fifth of the machine free, fighting for a tenth and enforcing a twentieth, with those margins widening when usage is unstable or compressed.

Industry observers note that JDK 28 reaches Rampdown Phase One on December 3, 2026, with general availability scheduled for March 9, 2027. The JEP's own future work points at better CPU sharing between concurrent collection and concurrent commit, and at ahead-of-time compilation from JEP 544, already Completed for JDK 28, which frees JIT cycles the memory workers could spend instead.

We Got Claude to Fine-Tune an Open Source LLM

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills.
  • Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks.
  • The model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills. Not just write training scripts, but to actually submit jobs to cloud GPUs, monitor progress, and push finished models to the Hugging Face Hub. This tutorial shows you how it works and how to use it yourself.

Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks. The hf-llm-trainer skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about training: which GPU to pick for your model size, how to configure Hub authentication, when to use LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and how to handle the dozens of other decisions that go into a successful training run.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

The model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

This isn't a toy demo. The skill supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 70B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

Hugging Face skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. With integrations on the way for Cursor, Windsurf, and Continue.

This repo includes gemini-extension.json to integrate with the Gemini CLI.

You have to authenticate to your Hugging Face account with a write-access token so that the job can create a model repo.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use your write token by sending it in either the HF_TOKEN or Authorization: Bearer HTTP Headers.

For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hf-skills https://huggingface.co/mcp?bouquet=skills --header "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN".

According to recent reports, let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to see the full workflow, then explore more advanced capabilities.

Start with a simple and clear instruction to fine tune a specific model.

Recent findings suggest that the coding agent analyzes your request and prepares a training configuration. For a 0.6B model on a demo dataset, it selects t4-small—enough GPU for this model size and the cheapest option available.

Industry observers note that the open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

According to recent reports, this works for vision language models too! You can simply run "Fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on llava-instruct-mix".

Before your coding agent submits anything, you'll see the configuration:.

Sources indicate that this is your chance to adjust anything. Change the output repo name, pick different hardware, or ask Claude to modify training parameters. Once you approve, the agent submits the job.

For example, you can ask the agent to try a test run:.

After submission, you get job details:.

Recent findings suggest that the skill includes Trackio integration, so you can watch training loss decrease in real-time. Jobs run asynchronously so you can close your terminal and come back later. When you want an update:.

Then the agent fetches the logs and summarizes progress.

When training completes, your model is on the Hub:.

That's the full loop. You described what you wanted in plain English, and the agent handled GPU selection, script generation, job submission, authentication, and persistence. The whole thing cost about thirty cents.

It has been revealed that the skill supports three training approaches. Understanding when to use each one helps you get better results.

According to recent reports, SFT is where most projects start. You provide demonstration data—examples of inputs and desired outputs—and training adjusts the model to match those patterns.

It has been revealed that use SFT when you have high-quality examples of the behavior you want. Customer support conversations, code generation pairs, domain-specific Q&A—anything where you can show the model what good looks like.

The agent validates the dataset, selects hardware (a10g-large with LoRA for a 7B model), and configures training with checkpoints and monitoring.

For models larger than 3B parameters, the agent automatically uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce memory requirements. This makes training 7B or 13B models feasible on single GPUs while preserving most of the quality of full fine-tuning.

DPO trains on preference pairs—responses where one is "chosen" and another is "rejected." This aligns model outputs with human preferences, typically after an initial SFT stage.

Recent findings suggest that use DPO when you have preference annotations from human labelers or automated comparisons. DPO optimizes directly for the preferred response without needing a separate reward model.

DPO is sensitive to dataset format. It requires columns named exactly chosen and rejected, or a prompt column with the input. The agent validates this first and highlights you how to map columns if your dataset uses different names.

Industry observers note that you can run DPO using Skills on vision language models too! Try it out with openbmb/RLAIF-V-Dataset. Claude will apply minor modifications but will succeed in training.

GRPO is a reinforcement learning task that is proven to be effective on verifiable tasks like solving math problems, writing code, or any task with a programmatic success criterion.

It has been revealed that the model generates responses, receives rewards based on correctness, and learns from the outcomes. This is more complex than SFT or DPO, but the configuration is similar.

The agent selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions.

Recent findings suggest that for tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train promptly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

It has been revealed that for small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

It has been revealed that for medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable.

When testing a workflow, start small:.

The coding agent configures minimal training—enough to verify your pipeline works without real cost.

Always run a demo before committing to a multi-hour production job. A $0.50 demo that catches a format error saves a $30 failed run.

Dataset format is the most common source of training failures. The agent can validate datasets before you spend GPU time.

The agent runs a quick inspection on CPU (fractions of a penny) and reports:.

If your dataset needs transformation, the agent can show you how:.

The agent provides mapping code and can incorporate it directly into your training script.

According to recent reports, real-time monitoring helps you catch problems early. The skill configures Trackio by default—after submitting a job, you can watch metrics at:.

This reveals training loss, learning rate, and validation metrics. A healthy run shows steadily decreasing loss.

Ask the agent about status anytime:.

If something goes wrong, the agent helps diagnose. Out of memory? the agent suggests reducing batch size or upgrading hardware. Dataset error? The agent identifies the mismatch. Timeout? The agent recommends longer duration or faster training settings.

After training, you might want to run your model locally. The GGUF format works with llama.cpp and dependent tools like LM Studio, Ollama, etc.

The agent submits a conversion job that merges LoRA adapters, converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to Hub.

In a recent development, we've shown that coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI can handle the full lifecycle of model fine-tuning: validating data, selecting hardware, generating scripts, submitting jobs, monitoring progress, and converting outputs. This turns what used to be a specialized skill into something you can do through conversation.

Industry observers note that the skill is open source. You can extend it, customize it for your workflows, or use it as a starting point for other training scenarios.

DeepMath: A lightweight math reasoning Agent with smolagents

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that deepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).
  • We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.
  • 🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that deepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1.

Recent findings suggest that large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

It has been revealed that deepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:.

Accuracy Reward: +1 for correct answers.

Using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

Sources indicate that temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

It has been revealed that dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

It has been revealed that we benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:.

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

We compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

We observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and shows the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

It has been revealed that deepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

Check out the GitHub repo and share your feedback! Contributions welcome. 🚀.

If you use DeepMath in your research, please cite:.

Scope: we focused on a small model and on mathematical reasoning.

Generalization: evaluated on contest-style math; results may not transfer to open-ended mathematical creativity or formal proofs.

Executing generated code is inherently risky. DeepMath uses strict sandboxing and resource limits, but any deployment should carefully manage attack surfaces and enforce rate limits.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Igor Nora builds the Parniera brand identity from silk and sculpted gold, with a bespoke typeface and a silk moth mark in pale yellow.

The idea is a collision the project calls Sculpted Duality. On one side, fine silk in fluid motion, pale yellow, soft and light. On the other, solid sculpted gold forms with architectural weight. The identity holds both at once: garments described as vulnerability and armor, built for a woman who commands the room with quiet power. Nothing shouts. The yellow field does the talking, and the black line work sits on it with total control.

The wordmark is a bespoke typeface drawn for the house. Thin, delicate strokes carry the lightness, while high contrast serifs give the letters their structure. The detail that holds it together is the ligatures: internal connective strokes, clearest in the N, I, E and R, link the characters the way woven silk holds a thread, so the name reads as one continuous piece. A construction frame highlights the letters PA on black, with guide bars and notes on the straight serifs and the joins between letters.

According to recent reports, the moth mark works the same way. It is built from four overlapping geometric forms, a line drawing of the Bombyx mori silk moth, the living link between the Persian name Parnia, a canvas of fine silk, and the sculpted gold the house stands for.

The system stays physical wherever it lands. The moth mark sits alone on a pale yellow tile, then repeats as a woven petal pattern in yellow, gold and tan. The brand book opens in a black ring binder: a yellow page carries the wordmark embossed into the paper, facing a white page headed "Essence of allure." The same yellow carries the shopping bag, the wordmark pressed into the paper along the bottom edge, with black ribbon handles.

It has been revealed that at street level the system scales up without changing its voice. A tall yellow banner hangs on a red brick building beside a panel with the moth mark, and the closing collage pulls the whole world together: moth tile, beaded gown detail, patterned envelope, shopping bag, the wordmark on yellow, and the line "Presence without the noise." It is a quiet luxury, stated once and left alone.

Today, we're announcing swift-huggingface, a latest Swift package that provides a complete client for the Hugging Face Hub.

You can start using it today as a standalone package, and it will soon integrate into swift-transformers as a replacement for its current HubApi implementation.

When we released swift-transformers 1.0 earlier this year, we heard loud and clear from the community:.

swift-huggingface is a ground-up rewrite focused on reliability and developer experience. It provides:.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest improvements is how authentication works. The TokenProvider pattern makes it explicit where credentials come from:.

The auto-detection follows the same conventions as the Python huggingface_hub library:.

This means if you've already logged in with hf auth login, swift-huggingface will automatically find and use that token.

Building an app where users sign in with their Hugging Face account? swift-huggingface includes a complete OAuth 2.0 implementation:.

Recent findings suggest that the OAuth manager handles token storage in Keychain, automatic refresh, and secure sign-out. No more manual token management.

Downloading large models is now straightforward with proper progress tracking and resume support:.

If a download is interrupted, you can resume it:.

For downloading entire model repositories, downloadSnapshot handles everything:.

The snapshot function tracks metadata for each file, so subsequent calls only download files that have changed.

Remember the second problem we mentioned? "No shared cache with the Python ecosystem." That's now solved.

swift-huggingface implements a Python-compatible cache structure that allows seamless sharing between Swift and Python clients:.

The cache location follows the same environment variable conventions as Python:.

You can also use the cache directly:.

To prevent race conditions when multiple processes access the same cache, swift-huggingface uses file locking (flock(2)).

Here's what downloading a model snapshot looked like with the old HubApi:.

And here's the same operation with swift-huggingface:.

The API is similar, but the implementation is completely different — built on URLSession download tasks with proper delegate handling, resume data support, and metadata tracking.

According to recent reports, but wait, there's more! swift-huggingface contains a complete Hub client:.

Industry observers note that and that's not all! swift-huggingface has everything you need to interact with Hugging Face Inference Providers, giving your app instant access to hundreds of machine learning models, powered by world-class inference providers:.

Check the README for a full list of everything that's supported.

We're actively working on two fronts:.

Integration with swift-transformers. We have a pull request in progress to replace HubApi with swift-huggingface. This will bring reliable downloads to everyone using swift-transformers, mlx-swift-lm, and the broader ecosystem. If you maintain a Swift-based library or app and want help adopting swift-huggingface, reach out — we're happy to help.

Faster downloads with Xet. We're adding support for the Xet storage backend, which enables chunk-based deduplication and significantly faster downloads for large models. More on this soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building on our work to get Claude Code to train open source models, we are now getting Codex to go further. We gave Codex access to the Hugging Face Skills repository, which contains skills for Machine Learning and AI tasks such as training or evaluating models. With HF skills, a coding agent can:.

Industry observers note that this tutorial dives even deeper and indicates you how it works and how to use it yourself. So let's get started.

Codex uses AGENTS.md files to accomplish specialized tasks, whilst Claude Code uses 'Skills'. Fortunately, 'HF-skills' is compatible with both approaches and works with major coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI.

With HF-skills, you can tell Codex something like:.

Industry observers note that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

This isn't a toy demo. The extension supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 7B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

In a recent development, we explored this single prompt approach in the Claude Code tutorial. However, we can now go further and get OpenAI Codex to do end-to-end Machine Learning experiments. For example, Codex should be able to monitor progress, evaluate the models, and maintain an up to date training report. This will allow engineers to delegate experiments to Codex and review reports in a more hands-off way. It will also allow Codex to make more decisions on its own based on the training report and evaluation results.

Codex is OpenAI's AI coding agent included in ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Edu, and Enterprise plans. Codex brings AI assistance directly into your development workflow.

See the Codex documentation for installation and setup instructions.

The Hugging Face Skills repository includes an AGENTS.md file that Codex automatically detects and uses.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use relevant MCP servers like Jobs in the Settings page.

Then start Codex and you'll be directed to the Hugging Face MCP authentication page.

Let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to improve code solving abilities, using the open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset and the openai_humaneval benchmark.

The open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

Sources indicate that codex then converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to the Hub. If we trained a LoRA adapter, it will merge the LoRA adapters into the base model.

It has been revealed that codex selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions. You can use the Hardware Guide to see the hardware options and costs, but codex will do it for you and select the best option.

For tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train swiftly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

Industry observers note that for small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

For medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

Recent findings suggest that for large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable for this scale yet. But stay tuned because we are working on it!

What important features should you look for in a home security camera?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when you're shopping for the best home gadgets, a lot of decisions tend to be based purely on budget or personal preferences.
  • With security cameras, though, your decisions can be deadly serious.
  • In a recent development, I've tested or owned a number of security cameras for more than a decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when you're shopping for the best home gadgets, a lot of decisions tend to be based purely on budget or personal preferences. No one needs an RGB lamp, for example, and an accessory that works with Google Home will usually function just as well paired with Amazon Alexa or Apple Home. There's a reason why Apple's latest HomeView and HomePod mini 2 come in multiple colors — form might matter as much as function to some customers.

With security cameras, though, your decisions can be deadly serious. If a camera fails when you need it most, the results could be vandalism, property theft or yes, someone getting hurt or killed. Even your choice of doorbell camera matters, given the number of porch pirates out there.

In a recent development, I've tested or owned a number of security cameras for more than a decade. At this point, I'm very familiar with the requirements for a great one. Just be warned that you may not be able to check off every item on your wishlist, especially if your goal is a security system that can operate 24/7, even when power or Wi-Fi goes out.

When it comes to a camera's sensor, resolution isn't as crucial as you might think. 4K is nice to have — but more important than that is the device's night vision and field of view. The wider the view, the more a camera can potentially capture, with 180 degrees being ideal. As for night vision, you don't necessarily need color, but a sensor should be sensitive and sharp enough to clearly discern faces when little to no ambient lighting is available. I wouldn't buy a camera with less than 2K/1080p resolution and recommend searching online for real-world sample images.

In a recent development, outdoor cameras should be fully water- and dust-resistant, with a rating of IP68 or better. Ensure the device's temperature limits are suitable to the climate you live in. Both wired and battery-powered cameras are potentially viable outside, but be aware that without a compatible solar panel, you're going to have to recharge batteries every six to 12 months at best. Actual runtime depends on factors like motion activity, signal strength and how often you check live feeds. You should be able to go at least a month between charges.

AI-based recognition of people, packages, animals and/or vehicles is sometimes crucial to avoiding a flood of generic motion alerts. That technology is often tied to both internet access and a subscription, though, so you might want to focus on models that handle recognition on-device at no extra charge. As subscription features go, cloud recording is more valuable. While local recording to an SD card is cheaper, it won't help you much if a thief steals or destroys your equipment.

It has been revealed that third-party platform support may also be vital. If you've already got one of Amazon's Echo Show or Fire TV devices in your home, for example, it only makes sense to pick up cameras with Alexa integration. You'll be able to check activity without pulling out your phone and set up camera-linked automations — for instance, triggering lights when motion is detected and you're away from home. Apple and Google offer similar hardware and software options. Note, however, that Apple Home can only be controlled using first-party hardware. That might make it a no-go if anyone in your home relies on an Android phone.

Sources indicate that if you're away often enough that someone might break in when power or internet access is down, search for battery-equipped cameras with cellular and SD card backup. This combination is going to be expensive, even before you factor in a monthly data strategy, but it's the only bulletproof solution. Alternately, you might invest in a Wi-Fi router with cellular backup and a whole-home battery solution, but the battery component alone will probably cost you thousands of dollars.

According to recent reports, the one remaining question is whether it's worth paying for professional monitoring. That's more subjective. Based on my own experience, the cost probably isn't worth it. All monitoring crews can do is call emergency services for you, and you might as well call the police yourself if you've received an intruder notification. There might be some value if you're regularly out of town for days or weeks at a time, as you're probably preoccupied, and you can't just dial 911 (or your regional equivalent) to reach the police in your hometown.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

It has been revealed that this feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:.

Recent findings suggest that this auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

You can also point to a local directory of GGUF files:.

Industry observers note that on the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:.

All loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:.

Sources indicate that the built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.
