📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs.
  • If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these new multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Sources indicate that traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Industry observers note that similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

According to recent reports, multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):.

According to recent reports, VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:.

It has been revealed that some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

The model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

According to recent reports, with a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):.

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:.

Sources indicate that as expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

You might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

Sources indicate that for retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:.

Under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:.

It has been revealed that these methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

It has been revealed that multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:.

According to recent reports, the reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:.

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:.

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:.

According to recent reports, since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():.

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:.

The "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:.

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:.

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:.

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

You may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:.

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts.
  • Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard wrote in contemplating the nature of creativity. “You open your safe and find ashes.”.

Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning.

According to recent reports, C.S. Lewis (November 29, 1898–November 22, 1963) offers a wonderfully counterintuitive perspective on our notions of generosity and our ideas about what it means to be interesting in his memoir Surprised by Joy (public library).

With an eye to the ideal structure of the creative life, he writes:.

It is a life almost entirely selfish. Selfish, not self-centred: for in such a life my mind would be directed towards a thousand things, not one of which is myself. The distinction is not unimportant. One of the happiest men and most pleasing companions I have ever known was intensely selfish. On the other hand I have known people capable of real sacrifice whose lives were nevertheless a misery to themselves and to others, because self-concern and self-pity filled all their thoughts. Either condition will destroy the soul in the end. But till the end, give me the man who takes the best of everything (even at my expense) and then talks of other things, rather than the man who serves me and talks of himself, and whose very kindnesses are a continual reproach, a continual demand for pity, gratitude, and admiration.

This is also why, Lewis intimates, the “thrill” of our greatest creative breakthroughs — those revelations that give us back to ourselves, out of which we give our best work to the world — is rooted in “self-forgetfulness”:.

Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else — whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard — does the “thrill” arise.

Industry observers note that shut your mouth; open your eyes and ears. Take in what is there.

Recent findings suggest that couple with John Steinbeck on the art of receiving, then revisit C.S. Lewis on what we long for in our existential longing.

— Published November 5, 2026 — https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/05/interesting/ —.

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

According to recent reports, granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

It has been revealed that granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

It has been revealed that figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

In a recent development, figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

The LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically crucial—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing concerns when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model says, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

We employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

To complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

Industry observers note that after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

Sources indicate that after SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

In a recent development, figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

In this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient patch therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

Industry observers note that to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

It has been revealed that in this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Recent findings suggest that granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

In a recent development, figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Recent findings suggest that figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

According to recent reports, we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

In a recent development, granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that "Block the AI bots" is one line in most robots.txt files, and it hides a real distinction. OpenAI documents separate crawlers: GPTBot for model training, OAI-SearchBot for the ChatGPT search index, ChatGPT-User for fetches when a user asks about a page. Blocking GPTBot does not remove you from ChatGPT search. Blocking OAI-SearchBot does. Anthropic splits them the same way (ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, Claude-User). Perplexity has PerplexityBot for search and Perplexity-User for user fetches, and claims the second generally ignores robots.txt (docs). OpenAI's list is here.

Sources indicate that ai-crawler-access applies the robots.txt rules per crawler (named group beats *, longest rule wins, Allow wins a tie, wildcards) and labels each one as search, user-fetch or training. It can also send one request per bot user-agent string and tell you if your CDN answers 403 to a bot that robots.txt allows. Here is what it printed for our own home page:.

partial means the path is open and some other paths (an API route, in our case) are closed.

We ran schema-check on our own home page before publishing. It reads the raw HTML, the way a crawler that does not run JavaScript sees it, and printed six findings: no WebSite entity, no description on the Organization, and no availability on four of our Offer entries. All six are real. We have not fixed them yet.

In a recent development, the Anthropic provider was tested live. Gemini, OpenAI and Perplexity are written from the vendors' docs and tested on recorded fixtures only. 28 offline tests cover the robots.txt matcher, llms.txt rules, JSON-LD parsing and the logic of the gap and brand audits.

Recent findings suggest that illyism/seo-skills is the broader repo: 30 skills across technical SEO, content, links and copy, with far more traction. We read it before writing ours and did not copy from it. Three of its AI-search skills (aiseotracker, ai-seo-report, content-coverage) use the AI SEO Tracker service, and seo-roast checks robots.txt and fetches a page as four AI user-agents with curl. Ours are runnable scripts for per-crawler verdicts, llms.txt and JSON-LD. If you need on-page SEO or link building, use his.

The skills check one site at a time and leave the writing of the fixes to you. CitedBy crawls the whole site up to your blueprint's page limit and gives the exact fix per page. The first check is free: citedby.eu.

If one of the checks is wrong on your site, open an issue with the URL. We treat a check that is false on more than one page in ten as not measured.

Breaking: System Design, Plainly — Season 2, Part 4: Sagas & the Outbox Pattern

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that part 3 gave you the protocol that makes several machines agree on one outcome — and demonstrated why it blocks.
  • It has been revealed that book a trip.
  • The benchmark hook for this part is the compensation economics, and it runs in the opposite direction from the intuition that "failure handling is an edge case." With five steps each failing 1% of the time, 4.9% of sagas run a compensation — roughly one saga in twenty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that part 3 gave you the protocol that makes several machines agree on one outcome — and demonstrated why it blocks. This part is the escape hatch: give up the single agreement, commit step by step, and keep an undo action ready for every step. That is the saga, and the transactional outbox is the small, boring mechanism that makes sagas actually work in production.

It has been revealed that book a trip. One service reserves the seat, a second takes the payment, a third books the room, a fourth sends the confirmation email. The room booking fails after the payment has landed. The customer has now paid for a trip that does not exist. There is no single database transaction spanning four services, so there is no rollback. What you do instead is run the steps in reverse: refund the payment, release the seat, cancel the booking — each undo a compensating transaction, written in advance, one per step.

The benchmark hook for this part is the compensation economics, and it runs in the opposite direction from the intuition that "failure handling is an edge case." With five steps each failing 1% of the time, 4.9% of sagas run a compensation — roughly one saga in twenty. At one million multi-step jobs a day with ten steps each and a 1-in-1,000 step failure rate, that is ~10,000 sagas a day needing their undo path. And the second-order failure is the one that actually hurts: if a compensation itself fails 1% of the time, ~1 saga in 1,040 ends unresolved — sitting in a queue for a human, about 960 a day at that volume. (Part 3 quoted ~1 in 2,040; that assumed a 0.5% compensation-failure rate. The unresolved rate is exquisitely sensitive to that one number, which is exactly the point: your saga is only as reliable as its worst compensation.).

Recent findings suggest that you are assembling flat-pack furniture with a friend, but you live in different houses and can only text. You agree on an order: you build the frame, your friend attaches the legs, you add the shelves, your friend tightens everything.

Halfway through, your friend texts: "the legs don't fit." In a single-database world you would both rewind time and pretend nothing happened. In the real world, the frame is already built — you cannot un-build it by wishing. So each of you agreed, before starting, on the undo for your own step: your friend unscrews the legs, you disassemble the frame, and you both end up back where you started, one undo at a time, in reverse order.

Recent findings suggest that that is a saga. Three rules make it work: every step commits immediately (no locks held across services); every step has a named compensation written before the saga starts, not improvised after a failure; and every compensation is idempotent — running it twice has the same effect as running it once — because the network will redeliver, the orchestrator will restart, and your refund will be attempted twice.

According to recent reports, A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each atomic inside one service's own database. After each step commits, the saga records its progress in a durable log — the saga log — and triggers the next step. If a step fails, the saga walks backward, running each completed step's compensation in reverse order. The saga never blocks: a failed step is undone, locks were already released when each local transaction committed, and no participant waits on any other participant's recovery.

There are two ways to drive it:.

The choice is usually decided by one question: when a saga fails at 3 a.m., who gets paged, and can they see what happened? Production teams that have run both tend to pick orchestration for that reason. One practitioner report — 12 microservices, 8,000 distributed transactions a second — is blunt about the history: they abandoned 2PC after it caused three outages in two months, moved to orchestration-based sagas, and now run at 99.7% saga completion, a 0.3% compensation rate, 1.2 s average duration, 4.8 s p99, and a 0.002% failed-compensation rate. Those are real fleet numbers, not a benchmark — and note what they imply: at 8,200 sagas a second, a 0.3% compensation rate is still ~25 compensations a second, every second, all day. Compensation is a hot path, not an exception handler.

The curve is the argument for writing compensations first and testing them like forward steps. Every step you add is another chance to pay the undo tax: at 1% per-step failure, a 10-step saga compensates almost twice as often as a 5-step one (9.6% vs 4.9%). The practical consequences follow directly: keep sagas short, make the expensive steps late (so fewer steps need undoing when they fail), and put the step with no good compensation — "email the customer and apologize" — as far from the start as you can, because its undo is a human.

A saga's failure mode is not the failed step. It is the failed compensation. A step that fails cleanly is routine; a compensation that fails leaves the system in a state no protocol can resolve, and the saga lands in a dead-letter queue for a human.

Industry observers note that two things matter here. First, the unresolved rate is dominated by the late steps: a failure at step 5 undoes four steps, so it has four chances for a compensation to fail, while a failure at step 2 has only one. Second, the compensation-failure rate is the only number in the whole design that you fully control — and the cheapest way to move it is idempotency plus retry. A compensation that fails because the service was briefly down is not a human problem; it is a retry problem. Retry it with backoff, forever, and the only compensations that reach a human are the ones that fail deterministically: the refund API rejecting the charge, the inventory record already deleted, the seat already resold. That is why the field figure (0.002%) is two orders of magnitude below the toy 1% assumption: in production, most compensation failures are transient, and retries absorb them.

The non-obvious corollary: a compensation must be written for the world as it is when it runs, not as it was when the step ran. "Void the authorization" is correct on the day of the purchase and wrong the next day, when the card network requires a refund instead. "Increment the inventory count" is wrong if another reservation took the same units in the meantime — the compensation must release that specific reservation. These are semantic compensations, and they are where most saga bugs live: not in the happy path, and not in the retry logic, but in an undo that no longer matches the state it is undoing.

In a recent development, sagas have a second, quieter failure hiding inside every step: the step itself usually needs to do two things at once — enhancement its own database and tell the next service. Write the row, then publish the event, and a crash between the two loses the event: the order exists but nobody ever hears about it. Publish first, then write, and a crash leaves a ghost event for an order that never existed. Two independent writes with no shared transaction cannot both be guaranteed, and the gap between them is a loss window you can measure:.

In a recent development, the fix is to stop having two writes. The transactional outbox pattern, catalogued by Chris Richardson, folds the event into the step's own local transaction: the service inserts the business row and an outbox row in the same database transaction, and a separate relay publishes the outbox rows to the broker afterward. Either both rows exist or neither does — the database you already trust becomes the single source of truth, and everything after the commit is a retry loop.

According to recent reports, the guarantee that buys is at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. The relay can publish an event, crash before recording its progress, and publish the same event again after restarting. There is no version of this pattern that delivers exactly once — KIP-939, which would let Kafka participate in two-phase commit, is still under development as of October 2026 — so the consumer side must do the second half of the job: deduplicate on the event ID (generated in application code, so it survives relay restarts) and make every handler idempotent. The outbox plus an idempotent consumer is the whole pattern; either half alone is a bug.

Getting rows out of the outbox table has two standard implementations, and the choice is a latency-versus-operations trade:.

Either way, the outbox table needs housekeeping: published rows must be deleted or archived, or the table grows without bound. Debezium's Outbox Event Router treats the table as insert-only and filters out deletes automatically; a polling relay has to do its own cleanup.

Part 3 ended with the comparison table. Here is the same trade with the outbox folded in, because the outbox is what makes the saga column livable:.

It has been revealed that the decision ladder from Part 3 still holds, with one rung added: if the data can live in one database, keep it there. If it is one logical database spread over nodes, use a distributed SQL database and let it run the commit protocol. If it is two different systems run by one team at low volume, XA/2PC is fine. If it is independent services, use a saga — and the moment a step has to notify another service, write the event into the outbox in the same transaction, or the saga's first failure will be a lost event nobody can explain.

The missing compensation is the failure that ships. Every step has a forward action that gets written, tested, and demoed. The compensation gets written last, tested never, and discovered missing the first time the step fails in production — which, at 4.9% of sagas, is the first week. The operational rule is to test compensations the way you test forward steps: run the saga, kill a step on purpose, and assert the system returns to the state it started in. Chaos testing for sagas is not a nice-to-have; it is the only way the undo path ever gets exercised before a customer does it for you.

The non-idempotent compensation is the failure that double-charges. At-least-once delivery means every compensation will eventually run twice. A refund that is not idempotent refunds twice; an inventory release that is not idempotent releases stock that was never reserved. The signal is a reconciliation report that never quite balances, and the fix is to key every compensation on the same event ID the forward step used, so the second run is a no-op. Idempotency is not a property of the saga framework. It is a property of each compensation, written by hand, one at a time.

It has been revealed that the unreadable in-between state is the failure your readers hit. A saga's intermediate states are visible: the payment is taken, the room is not yet booked, and a reader querying in that window sees a trip that is half-built. If your UI, your reports, or your downstream services assume a saga is either done or not started, they will show a customer a charge with no booking — and the customer will call support before the compensation runs. The fix is to design the read path for in-between states: mark the order PENDING, hide it from the customer-facing list until the saga completes, and treat "saga in progress" as a first-class status, not an error.

In a recent development, the unmonitored outbox is the failure that fills a disk. CDC's replication slot and the polling relay's backlog are both silent until they are not: slot lag grows, the outbox table grows, and the first symptom is either a full disk or events arriving hours late. Alert on outbox age — any row older than a minute is a stuck relay — and on slot lag, the same way Part 3 said to alert on in-doubt transactions. The outbox is infrastructure now; monitor it like infrastructure.

Latest Update: BIAN. Quando usar o Business Capability Model e o Service Landscape

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that pintura em guache de inspiração nabista.
  • Sources indicate that parte 3 de 9 da série BIAN e arquitetura bancária.
  • Na revisão do banco, alguém põe dois desenhos na tela.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that pintura em guache de inspiração nabista. Uma pessoa observa a cidade diante de um mapa, um binóculo e uma bússola. A escolha do instrumento representa a escala adequada para discutir capacidade de negócio ou responsabilidade de um domínio de serviço.

Sources indicate that parte 3 de 9 da série BIAN e arquitetura bancária. Nesta série, vamos seguir jornadas bancárias para entender onde cada responsabilidade começa, termina e passa para outra equipe.

Na revisão do banco, alguém põe dois desenhos na tela. Um mostra que o tratamento de exceções precisa ganhar capacidade. O outro distribui o trabalho entre domínios de serviço. A diretora pergunta qual caixa receberia investimento, e a equipe de engenharia quer saber quem publica a decisão de elegibilidade. Eu preciso responder às duas perguntas sem obrigar os desenhos a terem as mesmas caixas.

According to recent reports, nesta parte da série de BIAN e arquitetura bancária, vou usar um banco hipotético para comparar o Business Capability Model com o Service Landscape. Quero mostrar como eu localizo uma lacuna no negócio, encontro as responsabilidades que participam dela e preservo essa relação ao medir e testar o piloto. O caso segue a abertura de contas elegíveis em um dia útil, com dados inventados e nomes de funções locais que ajudam a distinguir o banco da referência publicada pelo BIAN.

It has been revealed that O Business Capability Model organiza o que o negócio precisa ser capaz de fazer. O Service Landscape organiza os domínios de serviço do BIAN como funções operacionais delimitadas, com responsabilidades que podem ser atribuídas e combinadas. O próprio BIAN publica uma análise de alinhamento entre os dois modelos. Notas do BIAN 12.0 sobre o alinhamento dos modelos.

Imagem sépia de inspiração pictorialista. Cada lente de um binóculo mostra um lugar diferente, com uma bússola sobre a mesa. As lentes representam as duas formas de ler o mesmo problema de arquitetura, enquanto a bússola ancora a decisão que as conecta.

Na abertura de contas, avalie capacidades como verificar identidade, analisar elegibilidade e ativar a conta. O mapa de capacidades ajuda a associar cada uma ao resultado e a identificar onde há lacuna de desempenho ou controle. Se o atraso estiver nos encaminhamentos para revisão manual, a liderança pode priorizar a capacidade de tratar exceções.

Depois, investigue as funções que colaboram nessa parte da jornada. Uma função registra o resultado da verificação. Outra decide a elegibilidade. Outra mantém o estado da conta. Use o Service Landscape para avaliar essas fronteiras e discutir os domínios de serviço aplicáveis. Uma capacidade pode depender de vários domínios, e a mesma função pode contribuir para várias capacidades.

Recent findings suggest that figura 1. Fluxograma de uso do BIAN. A partir do mesmo objetivo, observe como a lacuna orienta a prioridade da capacidade e os domínios delimitam responsabilidades na realização.

Na revisão, eu levaria um pequeno mapeamento entre capacidade, item da jornada, domínio, responsável e evidência. Isso mostra à diretoria por que a mudança merece investimento e dá à equipe uma forma de avaliar o desenho sem exigir uma correspondência artificial entre mapas, serviços e aplicações.

Service Landscape e Business Capability Model, BIAN.

Eu começaria a revisão de investimento com uma amostra fictícia de duzentas aberturas. Parte delas leva menos de um dia útil, porque a evidência é completa e o banco já utiliza a integração ao longo do expediente. Outras são encaminhadas a uma fila que pede confirmação adicional. Ao olhar os horários, a diretoria percebe que o maior atraso está entre o pedido de análise e a decisão. A baixa capacidade de absorver casos no horário de pico vira uma hipótese que a equipe consegue testar.

O mapa de capacidades me ajuda a fazer uma pergunta de gestão. A organização consegue decidir a elegibilidade de forma consistente, com volume e prazo compatíveis com a jornada? Para responder, eu registraria indicadores de desempenho, competências, processos, dados e dependências. O comitê pode financiar uma rotina de triagem ou melhorar a qualidade das evidências. As duas alternativas passam pela mesma capacidade, mas alteram partes diferentes da execução.

Em seguida, consultaria o Service Landscape para conversar sobre a função que controla cada operação. No exemplo, quem coleta a evidência deve conseguir explicar sua origem. Quem decide a elegibilidade registra o resultado e o motivo. Quem inicia a conta precisa receber o conjunto de precondições acordadas. Quem mantém a situação da oferta confirma que os termos continuam válidos. Esses limites apoiam a descoberta de quais interações precisam de revisão.

Figura 2. Diagrama de sequência da revisão. Observe a passagem dos casos de atraso ao diagnóstico operacional e aos contratos que Engenharia precisa rever.

Pintura surrealista de precisão ilusionista. Uma ponte sai de um armário de objetos e leva a miniaturas cobertas por redomas, perto de um relógio mole. O caminho materializa a passagem da capacidade desejada para o desenho de responsabilidades que a entrega usa.

Eu montaria uma planilha simples em que cada linha registra capacidade, etapa da jornada, domínio de referência, função local, responsável e evidência. Uma linha poderia apontar de “decidir elegibilidade” para a etapa de análise e para a equipe que publica a decisão. A evidência seria um conjunto de casos sintéticos em que a política e o motivo permanecem recuperáveis. Outra linha poderia ligar a mesma capacidade à origem da evidência de identidade, com responsável, janela de validade e tratamento de indisponibilidade.

Ao mapear o banco, encontraria casos em que o mesmo sistema executa várias funções. Um fornecedor pode entregar verificação e decisão preliminar num produto só. Eu manteria as responsabilidades distinguíveis mesmo que a integração seja única e revisaria qual parte continua sob registro e controle do banco. Também encontraria funções distribuídas entre aplicações, como uma verificação que depende de documento enviado no canal e comprovação em um serviço externo. O mapa ajuda a perguntar quem coordena o resultado entre essas partes.

It has been revealed that figura 3. Diagrama de estados da decisão de investimento. Observe como a lacuna priorizada precisa gerar fronteiras avaliadas antes de um piloto obter aceite.

In a recent development, se a conclusão do piloto mostrar que a fila melhorou, eu ainda perguntaria se essa mudança reduziu o tempo total. Uma decisão mais rápida pode transferir carga para a oferta ou para a ativação. Observe também quais exceções continuam abertas depois do próximo turno. Compare dados do mesmo tipo de conta e da mesma definição de elegibilidade para entender o efeito.

A seguir, voltaria ao mapa de capacidades e registraria qual capacidade melhorou, qual ficou limitada e como a evidência foi obtida. No desenho de serviço, atualizaria só as responsabilidades e contratos afetados. O objetivo é permitir que a diretoria explique a prioridade e que a equipe demonstre a mudança na rotina. BIAN, catálogo Service Landscape.

Quando a diretoria pede onde investir, eu gostaria de mostrar por que a espera que ela vê tem uma causa que ainda pode ser testada. Na abertura, o banco recebe a solicitação, reúne evidências, avalia elegibilidade, executa a ativação e comunica o resultado. Cada trecho usa capacidades que podem aparecer em outras jornadas. Verificar identidade pode servir a uma nova conta, à recuperação de acesso e a um pedido de produto feito em agência. O mapa de capacidades permite discutir o que a organização consegue fazer com qualidade, volume e estabilidade em mais de um contexto. Se a solução técnica muda, a pergunta sobre a capacidade continua reconhecível.

Eu pediria três medidas antes de propor investimento. A primeira acompanha a duração da espera, desde que o caso fica disponível para análise até receber a decisão aplicável. A segunda identifica retrabalho por motivo, como evidência ausente ou referência que uma equipe precisa recuperar. A terceira mostra quantas decisões podem ser reconstruídas quando alguém compara a versão da política com as provas disponíveis. Juntas elas permitem descobrir se a fila cresceu por falta de capacidade, por entrada mal preparada ou por obrigação de controle adicional. A decisão orçamentária pode financiar treinamento, ajuste de integração ou melhoria de evidência dependendo da hipótese sustentada.

No exemplo hipotético, a fila manual envelhece depois do almoço. Eu levo uma amostra de quarenta pedidos do mesmo produto que entraram no mesmo período. Em quinze, uma revisão pede novamente um documento que já chegou ao canal. Em dez, a autorização da oferta venceu antes de a análise terminar. Os demais demoram porque a equipe disponível só consegue assumir parte do pico. Começo a discutir o tratamento de exceções e, em paralelo, olho para a qualidade da evidência e a relação com a validade da oferta. Se eu concentrar todo o investimento em um novo motor de decisão, o banco pode continuar perdendo tempo ao buscar dados ou reaplicar uma condição de negócio.

No mapa eu marcaria a lacuna com seu recorte e uma data. Ela aparece para determinado tipo de conta, em um intervalo de chegada e numa política conhecida. Outro produto pode usar a mesma capacidade de revisão e ter uma distribuição diferente. Se a liderança propuser ampliar o investimento com um único padrão de fila, eu perguntaria em que medida os dados das duas jornadas são comparáveis. Se houver dependência comum de uma origem externa, a priorização conjunta pode trazer mais benefício que duas iniciativas isoladas. Se houver diferentes condições de exame, a melhoria da capacidade pode precisar de caminhos próprios. O mapa me dá um ponto para conversar sobre essas escolhas sem precisar decidir a interface naquele momento.

Industry observers note that quando a pergunta passa a ser quem publica a decisão, eu desço de escala. Procuro o domínio de referência cujo propósito se aproxima da função que analiso e comparo seus limites com o que o banco faz. O Service Landscape organiza domínios de serviço para que a equipe possa localizar e combinar responsabilidades. Eu verificaria a versão consultada e os artefatos que sustentam o mapeamento, como os cenários, as operações e os registros de controle disponíveis. As notas do BIAN 12.0 registram o trabalho do grupo que esclareceu a ligação entre capacidades e domínios. Na aplicação local, eu uso essa relação como referência para levantar a responsabilidade e ainda preciso confirmá-la com quem opera a jornada.

Um contrato local pode associar uma capacidade a várias funções. Para decidir elegibilidade, eu preciso da coleta de documentos, de uma fonte que confirme o resultado de identidade, da interpretação da política e de uma forma de comunicar o encaminhamento. Cada função pode estar mais próxima de um domínio de referência distinto. Também encontro o movimento inverso. A mesma função de manter a evidência de identidade ajuda a abrir uma conta e a alterar um produto existente. Na revisão, eu escrevo que tipo de contribuição cada função dá à capacidade. Uma condição de entrada, uma decisão de negócio e uma confirmação de efeito têm relações diferentes, mesmo quando compartilham um sistema.

In a recent development, eu faria um desenho para o caso em que uma oferta expira durante a análise. Uma função sabe quando a oferta perde validade. Outra já recebeu um pedido com evidência válida e precisa decidir o que fazer depois do corte. O núcleo talvez só possa iniciar abertura quando recebe ambas as condições. Se o banco coloca a lógica inteira no canal porque é onde a interface aparece, torna mais difícil reproduzir a regra em outros canais. No desenho, eu identifico quem produz o fato da oferta, quem define o efeito da expiração, quem executa a abertura e quem comunica o estado à cliente. A tabela de responsabilidades permite que o time altere uma interação e saiba quais consumidores precisam continuar observando o mesmo efeito.

In a recent development, também faria o exercício com um produto de fornecedor que implementa duas funções no mesmo contrato. O banco recebe a verificação de identidade e uma recomendação no mesmo retorno. Eu separaria a proveniência da verificação da autoridade que aprova o resultado final. A integração pode ser única e a divisão de decisão continuar explícita. Depois volto ao mapa de capacidades para ver se a contratação melhora o tempo perdido que motivou o trabalho. Se ainda for necessário buscar evidência em outro sistema para explicar a decisão, a equipe pode pedir mudança contratual ou incluir o caminho de recuperação no piloto. A fronteira ajuda a expor esse trabalho antes da compra.

No exemplo técnico vou simular um comitê que quer contar atrasos de uma coorte. O banco validou, num pequeno exercício, as lacunas associadas a cada pedido atrasado. Eu registro a relação da ocorrência com a capacidade e separo as funções que contribuem para realizá-la. Assim uma solicitação com duas lacunas pode aparecer nas duas linhas relevantes. Para saber quantas pessoas tiveram atraso, uso a população de pedidos e conto cada identidade uma vez. Para planejar uma mudança, recupero as funções que precisam colaborar no piloto. A mesma base responde a essas perguntas com granularidades diferentes.

A solicitação S2 tem dois motivos associados à revisão e só conta uma vez nessa capacidade. Ela também aparece em outra porque a oferta expirou. Quando leio o resultado, evito somar os números das linhas para apresentar volume de pessoas. A coorte sintética tem dois pedidos vencidos e os dois podem exigir tarefas em mais de uma capacidade. Os pedidos cujo prazo ainda corre ficam fora dessa contagem. Em uma base de operação eu usaria instantes consistentes, políticas de calendário versionadas e uma maneira de recuperar quais fatos estavam conhecidos no momento da conferência. Se a classificação de uma lacuna muda durante o trabalho, preservo a razão e a revisão que sustentam a comparação.

According to recent reports, no exemplo, o ranking deveria orientar outra pergunta. A repetição dos dois motivos em Tratamento de exceções revela que eu posso ensaiar uma transferência de evidência já vinculada ao pedido antes de aumentar a equipe. A tabela de realização mostra quem precisa testar o novo caminho, mas o efeito real ainda depende de medir idade da fila e tempo completo da abertura. O tipo da coluna «papel» é uma escolha do banco hipotético. No registro de arquitetura, eu acrescentaria a versão do domínio de referência, a obrigação do contrato local e a evidência selecionada. Assim, a equipe consegue rever um mapeamento errado sem reclassificar retroativamente a população que motivou o investimento.

Em um desenho inicial eu poderia associar «acompanhar solicitação» a uma única função do banco. No primeiro teste, o canal recebe o aceite da abertura, mostra a solicitação em processamento e busca o estado oficial depois. Ao mesmo tempo, o atendimento consulta um histórico e tenta explicar a condição que ficou pendente. Se os dois consumidores precisam de informações diferentes, eu preservo uma origem responsável pelo fato e especifico o que cada leitura pode inferir. A organização pode implementar as leituras no mesmo serviço, ou em superfícies distintas, sem mudar a relação da capacidade com a experiência. O problema aparece quando uma equipe cria estados definitivos a partir de dados que só serviam como previsão.

Eu daria consequência explícita ao mapeamento escolhido. Se uma área é responsável pela regra de elegibilidade do produto, ela precisa dizer quem publica a decisão hoje e como outra equipe chega à revisão da política. Se uma função fornece uma condição de entrada, eu escrevo o que acontece quando ela não está disponível. A transferência de uma interface pode mudar o prazo que o produtor é capaz de cumprir. Uma mudança de domínio de referência entre versões do catálogo pode pedir nova leitura do material. Nenhuma delas substitui a evidência local. Eu manteria uma ficha que liga a referência consultada, o responsável local e um caso que prova a obrigação entre produtor e consumidor. Dessa forma, uma pessoa consegue perguntar se aquele alinhamento vale para a versão em operação.

Recent findings suggest that mais tarde, a liderança pode perguntar por que um investimento compartilhado não melhorou o tempo total. Imagino que a equipe automatize a coleta de identidade para abertura e troca de produto. A primeira tem uma fila grande antes de receber essa evidência. A segunda já resolve a coleta cedo e costuma parar na confirmação de termos. No mapa, o investimento contribuiu para uma capacidade usada pelas duas jornadas. Na medição, o efeito relevante foi concentrado na primeira. Eu manteria essa atribuição e abriria uma investigação específica para a segunda. Se a equipe apresenta só quantas operações foram atendidas pelo novo serviço, ela pode mostrar adoção sem explicar por que o resultado do negócio mudou pouco.

In a recent development, eu também compararia o custo de implementar uma fronteira nova com o custo de tornar a arquitetura vigente explícita. Às vezes a responsabilidade já tem um produtor claro e falta que consumidores preservem seu identificador e revisem estados intermediários. O primeiro investimento pode ser um contrato, um teste e uma intervenção na forma de reutilizar dados. Em outros casos, duas aplicações realmente tomam a mesma decisão com versões diferentes da política. Antes de migração plena, eu designaria a autoridade e testaria uma situação de coexistência. A aplicação antiga pode manter leitura de pedidos históricos enquanto o novo produtor responde pelas decisões que começam depois da data combinada. Esse recorte permite financiar a fronteira que resolve a falha observada e preservar o caminho para investigar o passado.

Ao registrar o que sobrou, eu diferencio dependência necessária, melhoria possível e decisão ainda em aberto. A primeira limita o teste. A segunda pode entrar em outra etapa se mostrar valor. A terceira precisa de alguém que possa escolher e de um prazo para obter a evidência. Na revisão, isso evita reabrir toda a arquitetura quando uma função muda de tecnologia. O mapa da jornada identifica onde recomeçar a conversa, e a trilha de decisão conserva a hipótese que orientou a ordem do trabalho.

Sources indicate that eu destacaria no mapa de capacidades o motivo da mudança, o impacto que espero e o limite da amostra. Na vista de realização, mostraria os eventos que a equipe precisa produzir e consumir. Começo com uma solicitação do pico que chega com evidência completa, mas precisa de consulta a uma pessoa analista. Registro quando a evidência fica utilizável, quando a autoridade decide e quando a oferta ainda permite seguir. Se a equipe reduz quinze minutos na consulta e o resultado perde validade antes da ativação, o próximo teste precisa tratar a condição incontornável. As duas vistas permitem descobrir qual melhora é necessária sem confundir tempo de atividade com mudança de prazo fim a fim.

Sources indicate that eu também pediria que uma pessoa explique como investiga o caso depois de trocar o fornecedor. Se o mapa de capacidades estável aponta para a decisão da mesma jornada, o local e as condições de recuperar a prova podem mudar. A documentação de serviço registra a revisão do contrato, o nome da função que assumiu a origem e a forma de reproduzir a mensagem anterior para pedidos existentes. O indicador continua verificando se o banco atende ao compromisso. A equipe corrige o que de fato mudou na realização. Numa empresa que reorganiza serviços com frequência, essa separação ajuda a preservar a relação entre a pergunta executiva e o sistema em operação.

Em outro ensaio hipotético, a conta de pessoa jurídica compartilha a função de identidade, mas precisa tratar responsáveis distintos. A capacidade de validar a solicitação mantém o nome funcional e ganha um recorte novo de complexidade. No Service Landscape, eu verificaria como os papéis e as relações relevantes aparecem nos domínios de referência, antes de combinar o desenho local de prova para cada representante. Se o caminho depende de mais de uma revisão, os eventos registram qual resultado satisfaz qual condição. A revisão conjunta ajuda a decidir se reutilizar uma função é suficiente, ou se a capacidade precisa de investimento adicional para o produto novo.

Quando volto aos dois desenhos da abertura, entrego à diretora a lacuna com evidência, população e próximo teste. Com Engenharia, aponto a responsabilidade que precisa publicar a decisão e as interações que conservam a explicação do resultado. Depois peço a Operações que execute o mesmo caso nos dois recortes. Se o mapa que justificou o investimento e o contrato que chegou ao plantão levam à mesma prova, posso avaliar a expansão com conhecimento do que mudou. Se uma pessoa ainda precisa perguntar qual equipe produz o fato ou por que determinado caso ficou fora do teste, o vínculo entre os mapas merece mais trabalho. É na volta ao pedido que eu descubro se as duas escalas ajudaram a decidir.

Discircle builds the Lemonade Global Ventures brand identity on a gold lemon globe, Zero Sugar discipline, and a black and acid yellow system.

Sources indicate that the whole system starts with one image: a lemon cast in gold, its pitted peel catching the light on pure black. Discircle, a studio from Curitiba, built the identity for Lemonade Global Ventures, an investment fund founded by entrepreneurs, backing profitable businesses with proven cash generation. The mark fuses the lemon with a globe: a calculated elliptical profile, its longitudinal lines reading as citrus segments and as earth meridians at the same time. Gold carries the value, black the weight, acid yellow the shouting. The studio calls the approach Zero Sugar, paired with Squeeze: growth demands sour decisions, an appetite for risk, and no easy formulas.

The type does the talking in a tight grotesque with close tracking. Headlines run large and blunt: HOW TO MATURE on the book cover, Investment Perspective across the report, Squeeze the Extraordinary beside the steel squeezer. Small caps do the quiet work underneath: MADE WITH BRAZILIAN LEMONS, POTENTIAL, CONCENTRATED, GROWTH REPORT. The LGV monogram sits beside the line drawn lemon globe.

The grid stays strict. Report A runs on three columns, Diagnosis, Strategy, Execution, each with the same measure, and the same three moves return as L1, L2, L3: structural diagnosis and expansion vectors, organization and leverage, consolidation and scale. Each stage gets a white oval and a pill label at the bottom, AGO, SET, OUT. Type sits on generous black space, so a few lines read louder than a full page.

The finishes stay physical. The gold lemon is a solid object, peel texture and all. The same mark turns into a gold lapel pin, its meridian lines cut into polished metal, on a black suit lapel. Report A pairs an acid yellow front and a grey board back, the letters L, G and V large at the corners, with inside pages showing the paper grain. The squeezer in the closing frame is a real steel object, ribbed and reflective.

It has been revealed that the system stretches without thinning. Brazil becomes a map of gold lemons under the line Tropical Capital. The Lemonade Makers wall lists fifteen names, from Martin Luther King Jr. to Oscar Wilde, separated by small yellow lemons, with the line Lemonade Makers squeeze the real greatness running underneath. The book How to Mature carries the same headline and mark, and the report keeps the same discipline.
