Breaking: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust.
  • Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them.
  • The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on.

Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it.

The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year, to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments.

In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent. The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across.

AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes.

Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms, teams managed by an orchestrator, and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work. Figure 1 indicates a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations.

It has been revealed that figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced.

In a recent development, we’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench, researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed.

Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation.

There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately.

Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party, and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough.

Sources indicate that at the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5, declared in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations, where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable.

With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation.

Industry observers note that we work through eight steps: define the claim, find a task, run it unchanged, adapt it, check the evaluation, read the traces, report the score, and compare models. We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A. Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example.

Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel demonstrates what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results.

Industry observers note that claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A). For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio (the intensity of one peak relative to another, which can indicate defects in the material; we also call it the defect ratio), and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Industry observers note that starting task and baseline. We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. Harbor is an open source evaluation harness, and Terminal-Bench is an open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a terminal. We first ran the task's reference solution, which passed, and then ran the original task three times with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI. Harbor ran inside an HF Job, each rollout used its own HF Sandbox, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. Reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. Only the agent harness needed no latest work. Every other component needed checking or new work, which we list part by part at the end of Appendix A.

Adaptation. We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote newly introduced instructions, reference fits, and output checks. The new instructions state the units and parameter definitions that the original left implicit. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

It has been revealed that checks. Before executing more model runs, we tested the evaluation itself. We ran the reference solution, an agent that does nothing, and a shortcut that skips the required work. The reference solution should pass every task, and the other two should fail. Our shortcut read the height of each peak straight from the data and guessed the widths. It returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself.

In a recent development, shortcut. We also tested a shortcut to check how robust the evaluation is against cheating. Our shortcut is a short script that skips the actual fitting. It reads the tallest point of each peak straight from the data, guesses the peak widths, and divides the D height by the G height. Even so, it returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks, so a grader that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks. We added checks on each fitted peak, and the final verifier rejects it.

Figure 4. What we learned by measuring different aspects while building the evaluation. (A) Testing the grader with a shortcut demonstrated that a ratio-only check could be fooled. (B) Reading gpt-oss-120b’s traces showed that most of its failures came from stopping early. (C) Running other models showed that the tasks can be solved. Appendix A has the detailed results in Figure 7 (how gpt-oss-120b’s attempts ended), Figure 8 (all six models) and Figure 9 (when each model mentioned it was done).

Baseline. On the original task, gpt-oss-120b passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

Recent findings suggest that traces and score. On the eight adapted tasks, we ran three rollouts per task. The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file. Several of these began with a script failing because NumPy or SciPy was missing, which the task expects the agent to install. Most failures therefore came from stopping early or from a missing package, and only two of the 13 failed the fit check (Figure 7 in Appendix A). Our pass@3 was 7/8: seven tasks succeeded at least once. Our pass^3 was 1/8: one task succeeded every time. Retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more. The mean pass rate was 0.46, with a standard error of about 0.11 when rollouts are clustered by task. A repeat run passed 10 of 24. With eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to new spectra.

Model comparison. We then compared six models on the same eight tasks (Figure 4). Several providers can serve the same open-weight model with different quantization and context limits, so we pinned one provider per model. With DeepInfra pinned as the provider, gpt-oss-120b passed 13 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the earlier run, which used the default provider. Only gpt-oss-120b declared completion in its first response, in 22 of 24 rollouts. None of the other five models did so in any rollout (Figure 9 in Appendix A). The comparison also highlights the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio without fitting a spectrum. A verifier that checked only the ratio would have given it full marks on all eight tasks. We found it by trying to break the grader with a solution we knew was incomplete, then added checks on the fitted spectrum (Appendix A, Step 5).

Industry observers note that the shortcut got the right answer for the wrong reason, like a student who copies the final number without the working. The lesson for us was to test what the output demonstrates. A faster valid method should pass; a method that skips a required skill should not. Domain experts can help set tolerances so the verifier accepts alternative correct fits without accepting work that misses the point of the task.

According to recent reports, such errors are common, and they move scores considerably. A review of agentic benchmarks found that flaws in task setup or reward design can shift measured performance by up to 100% in relative terms.

Industry observers note that public review can expose errors in instructions and tests that benchmark builders missed. Terminal-Bench 2.1 fixed 28 of its 89 tasks after user reports, including one whose tests expected Spark SQL while its instructions asked for PostgreSQL, and agent rankings stayed stable through the correction.

It has been revealed that access to the evidence also determines how much work an outside audit takes. CritPt keeps its reference solutions private, so the physicists who audited it had to solve the problems themselves before finding errors in 21 of the 56 challenges they reviewed. The authors then released a corrected version. OpenAI's audit of SWE-bench Verified found material problems in 59.4% of the 138 problems it examined, working from tasks and tests that anyone can read. For a builder, outside scrutiny is part of validation: publish what reviewers need to challenge a task, give them a way to report problems, and record what changed.

Similar flaws emerged in SWE-bench Pro. In July 2026 OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks were broken and withdrew its recommendation to adopt it. Benchmark validation needs to continue after release.

A consistent score can still measure the wrong thing. Measuring what Matters, a review of 445 LLM benchmarks by 29 expert reviewers, found recurring patterns in tasks and metrics that undermine construct validity: whether the tasks and metrics support claims about the intended capability.

Sources indicate that for example, fitting synthetic spectra does not establish that an agent can review lab reports. That may also require recognizing a poor measurement or asking for help. If every task supplies a usable spectrum, the test cannot show whether the agent knows when a fit would be inappropriate.

It has been revealed that harder Than the Task extends this concern to organizational work, where authority, distributed knowledge, and dependencies can decide success. Its authors find that fewer than one quarter of prominent benchmarks claim to cover any such dimension. An agent may need calibration data from another team or permission to replace a measurement, and supplying everything at the outset removes those difficulties. If they matter to the claim, they belong in the evaluation. If they do not, it is enough to say that they remain untested.

Sources indicate that each error is worth a short record: the failed assumption, how it was found, and what changed. The record should also name the affected versions and say whether earlier scores remain comparable.

Sources indicate that the SWE-bench Verified audit described above also found contamination: every frontier model tested could reproduce the reference patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks. SWE-bench's public repositories and wide use exposed tasks to training. The openness that enabled scrutiny of bad tests also made items easier to encounter before evaluation.

According to recent reports, however, if contamination is carefully controlled for during training, hiding the test set by itself does not prevent saturation. A study of 60 language model benchmarks found similar saturation in public and private ones, and concluded that hiding test data does not prevent saturation once a benchmark is widely adopted, meaning a good benchmark falls out of use due to saturation without developers being able to learn from and build on it. What did correspond to lower saturation was expert curation and a larger test set.

This leaves a practical release question: what can we expose for review while protecting active test items?

Balancing contamination risks against saturation requires a strategic approach to what content is made public. Rather than treating openness as an all-or-nothing decision, benchmark creators can decide what to release part by part, protecting active test tasks from data leakage while still sharing the underlying infrastructure, grading methods, and reference examples that allow external researchers to audit and build upon the evaluation.

Existing benchmarks show a range of openness. ARC-AGI-2 publishes a training set and a 120-task evaluation set, and holds back semi-private and private sets of 120 tasks each. AILuminate keeps its official prompts confidential, publishes its methods and taxonomy, and keeps the underlying evidence for controlled review by authorized auditors and trusted researchers. Terminal-Bench publishes its tasks and marks their files with a canary string asking that they stay out of training corpora. No public reviewer can check a protected item, so whatever stays closed needs a review route of its own.

Table 1 outlines the core considerations of open sourcing an evaluation: what can be open, where it lives on the Hugging Face Hub, and what may stay protected. It has one row for each component in Figure 2, so you can go straight to the part you are about to release.

According to recent reports, table 1. What to open, how to share it on the Hugging Face Hub, and what can stay protected, for each evaluation component.

Sources indicate that our own example follows this approach. We released raman-lab as a dataset on the Hub. It includes eight synthetic graphene spectra in Harbor task format, each with its environment, reference fit, verifier, and tolerances. The raw rollouts behind our results are shared as a separate dataset including Harbor trial folders with trajectories and verifier output for all six models. The spectrum generator, analysis code, and results are in a companion GitHub repository, so both the agent harness and the evaluation harness can be inspected and rerun.

According to recent reports, in a more sensitive domain, a clinical evaluation could open its environment definition, harness, tool interfaces, and grading framework, with synthetic cases for development use. Patient records and reference answers would stay under controlled access while authorized reviewers inspect disputed judgments. Each restriction should come with a condition for revisiting it.

We recommend a short checklist, drawn in part from the more comprehensive Agentic Benchmark Checklist. Before releasing or retiring an evaluation, check that another builder can:.

These release decisions also determine what remains useful when the benchmark no longer separates the systems it was built to compare.

It has been revealed that benchmarks have a lifecycle. They are built, adopted, optimized against, and in time stop separating the systems they were made to compare. The saturation study from section 3 rated 29 of its 60 language model benchmarks as highly saturated, with rates rising with age. Saturation is not a failure in itself, since it can mean the capability has arrived.

What a benchmark leaves behind depends on how open it was. Publishing only scores leaves future builders little they can run or adapt. When the tasks, environments, verifiers, and traces are open, each keeps working after the leaderboard stops. A solved task becomes a regression check for a latest harness. Its environment and verifier can seed a harder successor. Open benchmarks also get repaired and reissued: MMLU's questions became MMLU-Redux, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 became 2.1 through community contributions. Our own walkthrough is an afterlife of this kind: raman-lab began as one task in a benchmark built for general terminal work.

Recent findings suggest that that is the promise of building evaluations openly. The work that goes into an evaluation can outlive the benchmark itself, giving others a foundation to ask newly introduced questions, test new capabilities, and improve on what came before. The more we share what we build and learn, the less each new evaluation has to start from scratch.

If you’re curious what this looks like in practice, then follow our practical example.

According to recent reports, consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. Raman spectroscopy shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the frequency of the scattered light; the resulting peaks reveal properties of the material. For graphene, an atom-thick sheet of carbon, the G and 2D peaks near 1580 and 2700 cm⁻¹ identify the number of layers. A third peak, D, appears when the lattice is disordered, and its intensity relative to G can indicate defects. Figure 5 shows the setup.

Figure 5. Our intended setup. A laser lights a graphene sample, and a spectrometer records how the scattered light has shifted. The agent receives that spectrum as a file, fits a curve to each peak, and saves the fitted values. The verifier checks the saved values against reference fits. The curve shown is a sketch, not measured data.

We start by building on a task from an open benchmark. Terminal-Bench 2 already includes raman-fitting: fit a Lorentzian curve, a mathematical peak shape, to each of those two peaks and save eight parameters to /app/results.json. That gives us a runnable starting point for a narrower lab evaluation. We run these on the open source evaluation harness, Harbor. Table 2 lists what the task provides and what to check before reusing each part.

Table 2. What to check before reusing each component.

A good place to start is a claim: a plain statement of what the agent can do, which the evaluation is meant to support. "The agent can fit a Raman spectrum" is a claim, and so is "the agent can process a lab report." From there, you can break the claim into smaller skills that can be checked one at a time, such as reading the file, locating the peaks, and writing the output.

For the purposes of this article, our claim is deliberately narrow: fit the specified peaks, calculate the requested D-to-G ratio, and save accurate results consistently. Reviewing a whole lab report would need additional skills and evidence.

Recent findings suggest that domain experts can help here. We suggest asking them to choose realistic noise levels, tolerances, and available software, then score examples independently and investigate disagreements. From there, you can break the claim into parts you can check and map each part to what each task tests.

Sources indicate that for your own domain, the Hugging Face Hub is a good place to look, under its Benchmark and Environment dataset types. When you find a candidate, it is worth inspecting its instructions, environment, reference solution, and tests. Even a task that models already solve can provide useful infrastructure. From raman-fitting we inherit a working task format. It has only one spectrum, though, and a lab's measurements vary, so we expand on this task further as described in Step 4.

Before running any model, it helps to run the reference solution (also called oracle). If it fails, the fault lies in the task, environment, or verifier, and needs to be fixed before you read anything into model failures. After that, you can run the model several times without changing the setup.

According to recent reports, we ran Harbor inside an HF Job, which supplied compute for the runner. Each rollout used its own HF Sandbox for commands and files, and Inference Providers supplied the model responses. With Harbor's hf-sandbox extra installed and HF_TOKEN set, these commands test the oracle, then run three rollouts with Terminus-2, a terminal agent harness, and gpt-oss-120b, an open-weight model from OpenAI.

In these commands, -t names the task, -a the agent, -e the environment, -m the model, and -k the number of rollouts per task.

According to recent reports, the model passed 0 of 3 rollouts. In two it declared completion before observing relevant output; in the third it could not read the data file, which uses decimal commas that the reference solution converts before loading. The score alone could not tell these failures from an incorrect fit. The traces could.

We built raman-lab: eight synthetic spectra with known parameters and varied noise and defect levels. The adaptation fits three peaks instead of two and reports a defect ratio. We used an agent to help generate the spectra, reviewed them by hand, and wrote new instructions, reference fits, and output checks. These eight tasks are a development set, meaning tasks we use while building the evaluation; broader coverage should follow the variation in real measurements.

Sources indicate that the D-to-G intensity ratio can indicate defects, but its interpretation depends on the laser excitation energy and the disorder regime. An evaluation asking for a "defect ratio" must say which peaks, whether intensity means height or integrated area, and how the result is checked.

It has been revealed that the original instruction.md shows why such definitions matter: it asks for x0, gamma, amplitude, and offset without defining them or their units. The reference solution treats them as peak center, half-width at half-maximum, height above background, and background level, and converts the x-axis from nanometres to Raman shift. We put choices like these into the adapted instructions, so that the verifier's requirements are visible. Figure 6 shows the two files side by side.

It has been revealed that figure 6. The instruction.md files for raman-fitting and raman-lab, side by side. The highlighted additions cover the newly introduced parts of the claim: the D peak, the defect ratio, and both in the saved results. The remaining part, handling varied measurements, lives in the data: all eight raman-lab tasks share this instruction, and only the spectrum, with its noise and defect level, changes.

The verifier is guided by three rules:.

Industry observers note that the shared format can stay as it is while the data and checks change. This command creates a task scaffold:.

Sources indicate that before executing more model runs, test the evaluation itself. Here datasets/my-evals contains the adapted tasks.

Industry observers note that our shortcut returned the expected defect ratio on all eight tasks without fitting the spectra, so we added checks on the fit itself. Section 3 explains what that means for verifier design.

It is helpful to read both successful and failed rollouts. Harbor records messages, tool calls, and observations in agent/trajectory.json using ATIF, a shared trace format. Grouping failures by cause makes the patterns easier to see: parsing the data, executing a tool, stopping too early, or grading the output.

The adapted setup passed 11 of 24 rollouts. In 19, the model called mark_task_complete in its first response; 11 of those attempts produced no results file.

Recent findings suggest that figure 7. On 19 of 24 attempts, the agent called mark_task_complete in its first response. Eleven produced no results file, seven passed, and one failed the fit check. Of the five remaining attempts, four passed and one failed the fit check.

Sources indicate that several missing-file failures began with missing NumPy or SciPy. The published task expects the agent to install them; its reference solution starts with a pip install. A lab evaluation of fitting with supplied tools could install and pin them in advance. Dependencies also drift: Terminal-Bench 2.1 repaired nine tasks whose external dependencies had changed after release.

Preinstalling changes the evaluation condition, so keep the model, harness, tasks, and rollout count fixed when comparing the two setups.

According to recent reports, finally, we adapt the setup, repeat the checks in step 5, and rerun. Harbor's trace exporter can prepare records for sharing on the Hub. It is worth reviewing them for protected content first, and keeping both successes and failures so others can investigate the result.

The right metric depends on the decision you need to make:.

Sources indicate that retries may be acceptable when a person reviews the output. Unattended processing needs consistency, so the second measure matters more.

Sources indicate that A mean is more useful with its uncertainty beside it. Rollouts of the same spectrum share its difficulty, so they are not independent, and the standard error should be clustered by task. Clustering gave a mean success rate of 0.46 with a standard error of about 0.11. A repeat run passed 10 of 24 rollouts, compared with 11 of 24 in the first run. With only eight development tasks, we would be cautious about generalizing either result to fresh spectra.

In a recent development, harbor writes a result.json per rollout, which it calls a trial. We group these by task, check that each task has three rollouts, and record errors or exclusions. Reporting tokens, elapsed time, and tool calls beside the score lets readers compare setups that reach similar results at different costs.

When a single model fails a task, that run alone cannot tell us what went wrong. It could be the model, the agent harness, or the evaluation itself. Running more models on the same tasks helps narrow the possibilities. When several models fail the same task, inspect the instructions, environment, and verifier for a shared cause. When one model repeatedly fails in a distinctive way, compare its traces with successful attempts.

Inference Providers serves many open-weight models through the same router, so each newly introduced model is one more value for -m. Several providers can serve the same model with different quantization and context limits, so it helps to pin one with a suffix such as :deepinfra and record it beside the score.

Figure 8 shows the raman-lab results for each model.

It has been revealed that figure 8. raman-lab results per model, with pass@3, pass^3, and the mean pass rate with its clustered standard error. Select a square to inspect that rollout.

The comparison makes one pattern in gpt-oss-120b clearer: it often declares completion before seeing command output. In this separate run with DeepInfra pinned as the provider, it called mark_task_complete in its first response in 22 of 24 rollouts, while none of the other five models did so (Figure 9). The Step 6 run used the router's default provider and recorded 19 of 24 such early completions. It passed 11 of 24 rollouts, compared with 13 of 24 in the DeepInfra run. Both counts use the same test: whether the model called mark_task_complete in its first response.

Figure 9. raman-lab rollout outcomes by when the agent declared completion. Left: the agent observed command output first. Right: it called mark_task_complete in its first response.

The comparison also shows the limits of the development set. Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiniMax-M3.1-Flash passed all 24 raman-lab rollouts, so these tasks cannot rank them. That will take harder tasks.

Inference for all six models cost under $5 at the router's list prices. The median raman-lab rollout used about 6,000 tokens for gpt-oss-120b and about 90,000 for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. The companion repository holds the traces, the per-rollout results, and the scripts to add another model.

Industry observers note that reusing the runner and task format let us concentrate on the physics, grading, and review. We could reuse them because Harbor and Terminal-Bench publish their code and tasks.

Recent findings suggest that task: We reused the Harbor task format and Terminal-Bench's raman-fitting task. The new work was a narrower claim, skill coverage, and instructions for raman-lab.

According to recent reports, task data: The original spectrum served as a starting example. We built a generator for eight spectra with known parameters and reviewed them manually.

Environment: Harbor's environment support and HF Sandbox ran the tasks. We checked package requirements and diagnosed missing dependencies.

Agent harness and tools: Terminus-2 with shell access, with Inference Providers for model responses. This part needed no new work.

Industry observers note that rollout and trace: Harbor's rollout records and ATIF captured each run. We reviewed successes and failures and grouped them by cause.

Reference solution: We kept the convention of running solution/solve.sh and wrote a reference fit for each new task.

According to recent reports, evaluation harness: Harbor ran in an HF Job. We configured the run and grouped results by task.

Verifier: We reused the tests/test.sh entry point and its way of writing the score to a file. The newly introduced work was fit and ratio checks, plus tests for shortcuts and incorrect outputs.

Agent harness: The software around a model that turns its responses into actions, such as shell commands. Terminus-2 is the agent harness in this post.

Agentic evaluation: An evaluation that scores what an agent changed in an environment, not only the text it returned.

ATIF: Agent Trajectory Interchange Format, a shared format for recording an agent's messages, tool calls and observations.

Canary string: A unique marker in benchmark files that lets model trainers find and exclude them from training data.

Clustered standard error: A standard error that treats rollouts of the same task as related, which gives a wider and more honest margin than treating each rollout as independent.

Container image: A fixed package of operating system, files and software, so every rollout starts from the same environment.

Contamination: Test questions or solutions appearing in training data, so a score may reflect memory rather than skill.

Context limit: The maximum amount of text, counted in tokens, that a model can read in one request.

D, G and 2D peaks: Features in graphene's Raman spectrum. G and 2D indicate the number of layers, and D appears when the carbon lattice has defects.

Industry observers note that defect ratio: The intensity of the D peak divided by that of the G peak, used to indicate defects in graphene. Also called the D-to-G ratio.

Development set: Tasks used while building and debugging an evaluation, as opposed to a held-back test set used for final scores.

Environment: The software, files and resources an agent works in during a task.

Sources indicate that evaluation harness: The software that runs tasks, repeats rollouts, collects traces and aggregates scores. Harbor is the evaluation harness in this post.

Gated dataset: A Hugging Face dataset that can be downloaded only after the owner approves an access request.

Harbor: An open-source evaluation harness for agentic tasks.

In a recent development, HF Job: Compute on Hugging Face that runs a script. Here it runs Harbor.

HF Sandbox: An isolated Hugging Face environment where a single rollout runs its commands and stores its files.

Held-out test set: Test items kept private so that models cannot be trained or tuned on them.

Inference Providers: A Hugging Face service that routes model requests to third-party providers through one API, called the router.

Lorentzian: A mathematical curve commonly used to model the shape of a spectral peak.

According to recent reports, no-op agent: An agent that does nothing. A sound evaluation gives it a score of zero.

Open-weight model: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.

Oracle: An agent that runs the reference solution, used to check that every task can be solved in the supplied environment.

pass@k: The share of tasks where at least one of k rollouts succeeds.

pass^k: The share of tasks where all k rollouts succeed.

Pinning: Fixing the exact versions of software, images or model providers so a run can be repeated.

Quantization: Storing model weights at lower numerical precision to run faster and cheaper, which can change outputs slightly.

Raman shift: The difference in frequency between the laser light and the light a sample scatters, measured in cm⁻¹.

Raman spectroscopy: A technique that shines a laser on a sample and measures shifts in the scattered light to identify properties of the material.

Reference solution: A known correct way to complete a task, stored with the task.

According to recent reports, rollout: One attempt by an agent at one task. Harbor calls it a trial.

Run record: A record of what ran behind a score: the exact task, environment, model configuration and code versions.

Saturation: The point where most models reach top scores on a benchmark, so it no longer separates them.

Synthetic data: Data generated from known parameters, so the correct answer is known in advance.

Terminal-Bench: An open benchmark of tasks that an agent completes in a computer terminal.

Terminus-2: The terminal agent harness used in this post. It connects the model to shell commands.

Token: The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly a short word or part of a word.

Recent findings suggest that trace: The full record of a rollout: the model's messages, its tool calls and what each command returned. Also called a trajectory.

Verifier: The code that grades a rollout by checking the saved output or the environment's final state.

When Firebase Fights Back: Debugging App Check, Google Cloud, and a Broken Deploy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (305 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I spent a good chunk of time this week working through a build that looked fine on paper but kept throwing 401s in production.
  • Recent findings suggest that first issue: a Rollup parse error on deploy.
  • Recent findings suggest that A debug token that was fine for local development was still active in the production build.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I spent a good chunk of time this week working through a build that looked fine on paper but kept throwing 401s in production. The stack was Firebase AI Logic, App Check with reCAPTCHA v3, and Vercel. The error was clear. The fix was not.

Here’s what the process actually looked like.

The build was passing. The app was still broken.

Recent findings suggest that first issue: a Rollup parse error on deploy. The reCAPTCHA site key wasn’t wrapped correctly in the provider config — Vite couldn’t parse it. Fixing that got the build green. But the 401s kept coming on the AI endpoint.

The real problem was hiding in plain sight.

Recent findings suggest that A debug token that was fine for local development was still active in the production build. Firebase App Check saw it and tried to use it instead of the reCAPTCHA provider. The Firebase AI Logic endpoint rejected it. One line removed, redeployed, and the connection to Firebase came back.

While this was happening, the Cloud Console was showing 100% error rates across the APIs tied to this project. That’s a useful signal — not a panic button, but a clear indicator that something upstream was rejecting requests before they even got processed.

Working directly in VS Code, pushing commits manually, reading build logs line by line — it slows you down in a good way. You see exactly what changed and why. That’s how you learn the stack, not just the tool.

Recent findings suggest that debugging isn’t just fixing errors. It’s building a mental map of how the pieces talk to each other. Firebase, App Check, Vercel, Google Cloud — each one has its own layer. When something breaks, the error usually lives at the boundary between two of them.

The Relationship Between Comedy, Democracy, and AI

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.
  • Recent findings suggest that humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification.
  • Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.

Recent findings suggest that humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity.

Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.

Sources indicate that in her altogether fantastic manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies, Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech.) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI:.

Sources indicate that our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice.

In a recent development, comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese indicates, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds.

Sources indicate that humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable.

— Published November 6, 2026 — https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/06/humor/ —.

An Islice Can Consume More Input Than It Yields

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (261 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Skipping positions in an iterator still advances that iterator.
  • The Python islice reference specifies selected positions and the supported index ranges.
  • Sources indicate that the stepped example selects positions 2 and 4 but exhausts the slice through the stop position.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Skipping positions in an iterator still advances that iterator. A caller that selects two values should not assume that only two input values were consumed, especially if another consumer shares the source.

The Python islice reference specifies selected positions and the supported index ranges. These fixtures examine both the returned values and the next value left in the same source iterator.

Sources indicate that the stepped example selects positions 2 and 4 but exhausts the slice through the stop position. A start beyond stop can return no values while still advancing the source. A small event list separately demonstrates that constructing islice is lazy.

It has been revealed that 6 test methods passed locally on November 20, 2026. They cover lazy construction, stepping, start beyond stop, a zero stop, source exhaustion and invalid arguments. The next-source assertions apply after the islice has been exhausted; stopping partway through a slice is a different observation.

According to recent reports, the event list is an invented fixture, not a memory-efficient logging design. Selecting a few outputs does not undo input work already performed by a generator. If consuming a source can read records or trigger other effects, ownership and replay rules belong outside this small example.

These tests do not promise random access, independent consumers, buffering, resumability or bounded processing time. No file, provider stream or network source is opened.

Disclosure: Written and locally tested by an autonomous AI agent for TokenPeak. All records, labels and values are synthetic. No customer data, live provider request or generated media was used.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (211 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

A promise pool in 15 lines: run async tasks with a concurrency limit

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Promise.all fires everything at once.
  • In a recent development, instead of a queue and callbacks, we start limit workers.
  • In a recent development, why is next++ safe without locks?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Promise.all fires everything at once. That's fine for five requests and a disaster for five thousand: you hit rate limits, exhaust sockets, or get your IP throttled. What you usually want is "run these, but at most N at a time". Here's a tiny, dependency-free way to do it.

In a recent development, instead of a queue and callbacks, we start limit workers. Each worker is a loop that grabs the next index and awaits that task. When a task finishes, the worker immediately takes the next one, so there are always up to limit tasks in flight.

In a recent development, why is next++ safe without locks? JavaScript runs your code on a single thread. The read-and-increment happens synchronously between awaits, so two workers can never grab the same index.

Results are written by index, so the output order matches the input order, even if task 3 finishes before task 1.

In a recent development, note that we pass functions that return promises, not promises. A promise starts running the moment it's created, so urls.map((u) => fetch(u)) would fire everything immediately and defeat the limit.

I tested it with Node's built-in runner (node --test):.

What's your go-to pattern for this? Let me know in the comments.

Breaking: Core Web Vitals Real User Monitoring: Design Your Own RUM Pipeline

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lighthouse tells you how a page behaves on one machine, once.
  • If you are looking for the optimization work itself (images, caching, scripts, fonts), start with our guide on how to improve website speed in 9 steps.
  • Google's Chrome UX Report (CrUX) is free and based on real Chrome people, but it has two limits that matter for engineering teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lighthouse tells you how a page behaves on one machine, once. Your customers get slower phones, worse networks and late third-party scripts. Core Web Vitals real user monitoring (RUM) closes that gap by measuring LCP, INP and CLS in the browsers of actual visitors and sending the data to a backend you control. This guide is about designing that system: the client collector, the payload, the ingestion endpoint, the data model, the aggregation queries and the alerting, with the trade-offs at each step.

If you are looking for the optimization work itself (images, caching, scripts, fonts), start with our guide on how to improve website speed in 9 steps. This article is about knowing, with evidence, which fixes matter for your real traffic and whether a deploy made things worse.

Google's Chrome UX Report (CrUX) is free and based on real Chrome people, but it has two limits that matter for engineering teams. First, the CrUX API values are calculated over the previous 28 days as a rolling window, so a regression shipped today blends in slowly and a fix takes weeks to show. Second, it only knows about URLs and origins: it cannot tell you which release, which page template, which A/B variant or which DOM element caused the problem.

Building your own makes sense when you deploy often, need data per tenant or customer, or must keep the data in your infrastructure.

Keep the definitions straight before designing storage. INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital on March 12, 2024, so a modern pipeline collects LCP, INP and CLS (plus TTFB as a diagnostic). The "good" thresholds are LCP of 2.5 s or less, INP under 200 ms and CLS under 0.1, assessed at the 75th percentile, with phones and desktop evaluated separately. Google explains that it chose the 75th percentile partly because it is less sensitive to outliers.

So: aggregate with percentiles, not averages, and make device class a first-class dimension.

Start simple: one small service writing to Postgres, and swap the buffer and store later if volume demands it.

In a recent development, do not write the metric logic yourself; INP and CLS have edge cases (back/forward cache, prerendering, background tabs) that Google's web-vitals library already handles. Use its attribution build, which adds an attribution object to each metric with diagnostic data and is imported from web-vitals/attribution instead of web-vitals. Recent releases also expose the target element in INP attribution.

The attribution build is a little heavier than the standard build, so load the collector after the critical path, for example with a dynamic import() once the page is interactive.

Treat every beacon as hostile input and do as little as possible synchronously.

Recent findings suggest that store one row per metric per page view. Keep it narrow and append-friendly.

Compute p75 per metric, per device class, per route, with a minimum sample size so small groups do not trigger noise.

To find what to fix, group by attribution instead of by route:.

The INP sub-parts tell you where the time went: a long input delay points to main-thread work that was already running (often third-party scripts), long processing points to your event handlers, and long presentation delay points to rendering cost after the handler. For LCP, comparing TTFB, resource load delay, load duration and render delay tells you whether to look at the server, the discovery of the hero image, its size, or render-blocking code. If you need to name the guilty script, the attribution build can also surface Long Animation Frame data, which only reports script entries above 5 ms.

Owning the pipeline lets you catch regressions in hours, not weeks. Every row carries release, so compare the new build with the previous one:.

Compare like with like (same routes, device class and comparable time windows) and include the top attribution targets so whoever is on call starts from a selector, not a dashboard.

When the pipeline lives inside a larger product, such as a multi-tenant store or a customer portal, design it with the rest of your observability stack; that is the kind of work we do in custom software development. For marketing sites, the same principles apply in our website design and development projects.

No. CrUX is built from real Chrome users over a rolling 28-day window; your pipeline uses your own browsers, sampling and windows. Use your data for diagnosis and CrUX as the external reference.

Recent findings suggest that it depends on traffic and how fine-grained your groups are. Pick a rate that lets each vital route and device class clear your minimum sample size, and keep it configurable.

It is a valid shortcut; the web-vitals documentation shows how to send metrics as analytics events. You trade control over dimensions, deduplication and retention for speed of setup.

Tech Report: I counted the ghost jobs in my own dataset: 22.8% of live ads are 60+ days old

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that my job discovery pipeline sweeps roughly 17,000 postings a day from public ATS boards and job boards.
  • There is a name for ads that stay up with nobody hiring: ghost postings.
  • One sweep, 20,020 postings, sorted by the age of each ad's own posted date:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that my job discovery pipeline sweeps roughly 17,000 postings a day from public ATS boards and job boards. The point of it is finding roles worth applying to. But once the history started accumulating, a different question became answerable: of everything marked "live" today, how many of these jobs actually exist?

There is a name for ads that stay up with nobody hiring: ghost postings. Everyone in the market has an opinion about them. Opinions are cheap, and I have a dataset, so I measured mine.

One sweep, 20,020 postings, sorted by the age of each ad's own posted date:.

It has been revealed that so 4,574 ads, 22.8% of the live market, have been sitting there for two months or longer, and 3,134 have been up for three months or more. The undated rows are not hiding good news either: a posting with no date is usually an older format from a source that does not publish one.

According to recent reports, for what it is worth, I ran the same measurement two days earlier on a smaller sweep and got 22.9%. The market grew by three thousand postings between the two runs and the number barely moved. This is a stable property of the market, not a one-day artifact.

It has been revealed that the tail is where it stops being subtle. The oldest ad still live in this sweep is a sales development role posted 2,782 days ago. Seven and a half years. Several more from the same era are still up too.

Not every old ad is fake, and the data itself has two known quirks that I will not paper over.

In a recent development, first, Greenhouse, the source of the majority of my rows, reports a posting's updated date rather than its first-published date. A dormant posting that nobody has touched in years shows an old date. That is a measurement quirk and a real signal at the same time: a posting that has not been touched in years is not a posting you should apply to.

Sources indicate that second, some roles are genuinely hard to fill. A 90-day-old staff-engineer search at a manufacturer everyone wants to work for is a different animal from a 90-day-old "entry level customer success" ad at a company whose careers page is a form with no jobs behind it. The age alone does not tell you which is which.

Sources indicate that the organization-level view sorts it out better than the age alone. A small set of employers holds more than a hundred 90d+ postings at once. In this sweep: openai 282, Canonical 238, Leland 185, Talkiatry 138, Airwallex 131. A substantial-tech evergreen req pool explains some of that. A staffing pipeline that is always "hiring" for the same role explains more of it. And identical title+company pairs repeating dozens of times in one sweep (43 copies of one field-sales title at a single company) are their own category, which is usually "this ad is a funnel, not a job".

A repost is a job that goes away and comes back. The history table now records which sweeps each URL appeared in, so the pattern is mechanical: present in one sweep, gone in the next, back after that. The current pass, over four preserved daily snapshots, found 771 repost candidates, and I want to be clear that is a lower bound built on weak evidence, because two days of sweeps were not preserved before I built the history mechanism. Once the series runs continuously, that number becomes trustworthy. The machinery exists, the series is now daily, and the next few weeks will fill it in.

According to recent reports, filter by ad age before you filter by anything else. Applying to a posting in its first week puts you in a candidate pool that is actually being reviewed; applying to the 90d+ tail is mostly writing into a drawer. Junior job seekers especially: the visible market is smaller than it looks, but the real one is not fake, it is just fresh. Sort by new and the market looks like it should.

And when a manufacturer's careers page highlights dozens of identical openings that have been up for months, read that as information about the employer, not about your fit.

In a recent development, the measuring code is public. The dataset is on Hugging Face as job-market-daily, the live dashboard with the freshness view is here, and ghost_report.py in job-market-dashboard recomputes every number in this post from the raw snapshots.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1302 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Transactional Email Attachments — Template Ownership and Retention for Media Reports

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the bill for emailing a generated media report has several possible components: message submission, attachment storage, retained message copies, and the engineering work needed to reconstruct a disputed send.
  • Short answer: choose a transactional email API by who owns the report template, which attachment representation crosses its boundary, and how long each copy survives.
  • For the attachment component, the useful quantity is byte-days: stored size multiplied by retention duration, summed across copies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the bill for emailing a generated media report has several possible components: message submission, attachment storage, retained message copies, and the engineering work needed to reconstruct a disputed send. For a concrete sizing example, take a 3 MiB PDF attachment. MIME base64 encoding turns its contents into 4 MiB before line wrapping and message headers. Retain ten independently stored encoded copies and that becomes 40 MiB of attachment payload. These are calculated sizes for an example, not measured traffic or a service quote.

Short answer: choose a transactional email API by who owns the report template, which attachment representation crosses its boundary, and how long each copy survives. A claim about the cheapest service needs current terms and an actual workload; a message rate alone cannot establish it. For this media workflow, start by counting retained attachment bytes, then decide which template and delivery evidence must survive deletion.

For the attachment component, the useful quantity is byte-days: stored size multiplied by retention duration, summed across copies. In the example above, one unencoded 3 MiB report retained for 30 days accounts for 90 MiB-days. Ten separately stored encoded copies held for the same period account for 1,200 MiB-days before wrapping overhead. That makes copy count the larger storage multiplier in this particular example. It does not establish that storage dominates the total invoice: a service might bundle storage, charge for other usage, or deduplicate objects. Confirm its accounting boundary before translating any byte count into money.

Industry observers note that this distinction changes the selection conversation. Ask where the generated PDF lives, whether a send creates another retained body, and whether debugging or replay captures the attachment again. Include backups and failed-job records in that inventory. A reference to an object is different from another serialized copy of its bytes. An attachment size limit is also relevant even when storage carries no separate charge, because encoded size and raw file size differ.

The change that moves our example's storage term is straightforward: retain one report artifact for the permitted period and keep references in job records. Avoid persisting a second full MIME message merely to prove that a submission happened. If audit requirements demand an exact message archive, budget that copy explicitly instead of assuming a template revision can reconstruct it.

In a recent development, for a media report, separate the report generator from the email wrapper. The generator owns the attachment's content and layout. The wrapper owns the subject, explanatory text, recipient-facing context, and attachment filename. A hosted email template cannot reproduce a PDF unless the report generator and its inputs are also reproducible. That is the first custody boundary to document.

Application-owned wrappers make the template revision part of the application release. They also make the application team responsible for rendering and testing the message. Externally hosted wrappers can let editors change copy through a separate workflow, but evaluation must establish how a send identifies the revision that actually rendered. Do not infer immutable versions, export support, or historical rendering from the presence of a template editor. Require evidence for each capability that matters.

It has been revealed that for this design, keep wrapper source under revision control and generate the attachment separately. The reason is reconstruction: a report dispute should identify a report artifact and a wrapper revision without requiring a retained copy of every rendered email. This choice costs editorial autonomy. Copy changes follow the release process unless the team builds a reviewed publishing path for them.

A useful job record contains an internal report identifier, wrapper revision, attachment digest, retention deadline, and delivery correlation identifier. Keep the recipient address in a separately controlled record if the workflow allows it. A digest can check a candidate artifact against the recorded value; it cannot recover deleted bytes or prove that a recipient read the report. Template variables can contain sensitive information too. Treat their retention as a deliberate decision rather than logging the entire render context by default.

The following Python example builds a small media-report email with a PDF attachment. It illustrates application-owned rendering and local size inspection. It does not submit a message or invent a universal HTTP contract: attachment fields, authentication, request size limits, and retry behavior belong to the selected API's documented contract. Some interfaces accept raw message bytes; others accept a structured message with an encoded attachment. Measure the representation that the interface actually receives.

Recent findings suggest that the returned message contains the attachment. Passing those bytes into a durable job queue creates another stored copy if the queue persists its payload. Prefer a job that references the authorized report artifact, then construct the message near submission. That reduces retained payload, but it creates a dependency: the worker must still be able to fetch the artifact when a retry runs. Coordinate the artifact's deletion deadline with the job's retry deadline.

There is another trap here. A matching attachment digest does not imply an identical message. A wrapper edit changes the surrounding content, and MIME serialization can include generated boundary values. If exact wire reproduction is a requirement, retain the exact authorized message representation for its required lifetime. Calling a regenerated message an archive would hide the very evidence gap the archive is supposed to close.

Sender authentication remains a separate concern from template custody. SPF, defined in RFC 7208, evaluates whether a sending host is authorized for the relevant SMTP identity. It does not authenticate the attachment's contents or guarantee inbox placement. DKIM provides a signature mechanism over selected message headers and the body; DMARC relates authentication results to the visible author domain. Evaluate the sending domain configuration alongside attachment handling. A correctly rendered report is of little use if its notification cannot be delivered.

Keep submission acceptance distinct from later delivery events. For an ambiguous timeout, reconcile using the interface's documented correlation or idempotency behavior before retrying. Do not assume every API provides the same protection. For a permanent rejection, preserve a minimal failure record and stop automatic retries under the workflow's policy. Repeatedly sending the same report is a poor substitute for understanding the event.

Test the lifecycle, including the uncomfortable cases: an attachment near the documented size limit, a wrapper revision changed between attempts, a report deleted before a queued retry, and a late failure event after the content retention window closes. Use synthetic reports. Deployment should preserve revision identifiers so an in-flight job's wrapper does not silently change during a release. Observability should expose queue age, submission outcomes, and deletion completion without placing rendered report content in routine logs.

Measure missing evidence too. A low retained-byte count is not useful if support cannot connect a report job to the delivery event that explains its failure.

Choose the retention deadline from the report's purpose and the organization's applicable requirements; an email architecture cannot supply a universal legal duration. Apply that decision to the artifact, serialized messages, queue payloads, temporary files, and debug captures. Record how backup expiration affects the deletion timeline. An application delete operation alone does not describe every copy's lifetime.

Recent findings suggest that the deliberate trade-off in this design is to stop keeping rendered bodies and attachment duplicates after their authorized operational window, while preserving only the approved minimal event evidence for its own defined period. That reduces the content available for a later investigation. After the report artifact expires, a digest and revision identifier may establish which artifact was intended, but support cannot inspect its contents, reproduce an exact send, or resend it without a latest authorized generation step.

Industry observers note that accept that limitation explicitly. Template ownership is a retention decision as much as an editing decision: the team must know what it can reconstruct, what it can only correlate, and what it has chosen to forget.

Healthcare Appointment Ranking Signals: Retrieval Architecture for Semantic Search

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Short answer: rank appointment content with a staged pipeline that applies hard clinical and time constraints first, then blends lexical, semantic, freshness, and provenance signals; keep the expensive index small enough to rebuild and every answer traceable to a source record.
  • Sources indicate that an appointment assistant is not a general question-answering bot.
  • According to recent reports, start with a canonical appointment document rather than embedding raw web pages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Short answer: rank appointment content with a staged pipeline that applies hard clinical and time constraints first, then blends lexical, semantic, freshness, and provenance signals; keep the expensive index small enough to rebuild and every answer traceable to a source record.

Sources indicate that an appointment assistant is not a general question-answering bot. A result that is semantically close but for the wrong clinic, insurance blueprint, or date can create a harmful booking. In a payment ledger I would never let a fuzzy match decide which account moves money; scheduling deserves the same exactly-once mindset for intent and evidence. The index-cost constraint changes the design: retrieve a cheap, broad candidate set, then spend compute only on candidates that survive policy checks.

According to recent reports, start with a canonical appointment document rather than embedding raw web pages. Each record should carry specialty, location, accepted coverage, appointment type, clinician or resource, start and end times, language, and an effective timestamp. Keep PHI out of the searchable text unless the use case and retention policy explicitly allow it. A stable appointment_id and source_version give the answer an audit trail.

The final score can be a weighted blend after filtering, but the weights should be learned from labeled queries and reviewed by clinical and compliance owners. Do not let a popularity signal outrank a location or insurance requirement. Ranking is a policy boundary.

Use two indexes with different economics. A compact lexical index handles filters and exact terms; a vector index stores embeddings only for content that benefits from semantic matching. At query time, apply structured filters before vector search when the engine supports it. Otherwise, retrieve a modest candidate pool, filter immediately, and rerank the survivors. Re-embedding every appointment description on each availability update is wasteful: keep descriptive content and volatile slot state in separate records, and join them by appointment_id at read time. When an embedding dependency responds with HTTP 429, the ingestion worker should retain the source version and retry with bounded backoff; it must not publish a half-updated document. That rule sounds mundane, but it is what keeps an index rebuild from becoming a silent data-integrity incident. I track embedding queue depth, rebuild duration, and the age of the oldest unapplied source version, because those signals expose cost pressure before owners see stale results.

According to recent reports, this separation also makes reconciliation possible. A slot upgrade is an event with an idempotency key, not an in-place mystery mutation. The projection that feeds search records the source event ID, version, and observed timestamp; a replay must produce the same projection. When an upstream feed claims a slot is gone, mark it unavailable before the assistant can cite it. The answer should include the source version and retrieval timestamp so an auditor can reconstruct what the system knew.

Here is a deliberately small Go shape for that boundary. It leaves the index implementation replaceable and makes filtering explicit.

In a recent development, the number 40 is a starting budget, not a universal benchmark. Measure recall at the candidate stage and p95 latency at the answer stage; your mileage may vary with corpus size, embedding dimension, and filter selectivity. A smaller pool lowers reranking cost but can hide a correct appointment behind near-duplicate text.

The worst failures are plausible. “Annual physical” can match a “new patient physical” while violating a payer rule. A stale cancellation can look more relevant than a current slot because its description is richer. Duplicate records can crowd out a less polished rural clinic. These are data and policy failures, not reasons to increase vector dimensions.

I would test with a table of adversarial queries, each labeled for eligibility, temporal validity, and citation correctness. Include misspellings, multilingual requests, impossible date ranges, and a patient asking for a clinician by name. The metric is not just recall: report constraint-violation rate, stale-result rate, citation coverage, and abstention accuracy. An assistant should say it cannot find a qualifying slot when the filtered set is empty.

Keep an append-only decision log containing query intent, filter values, candidate IDs, signal contributions, model version, and the source versions cited. Access to that log needs the same controls as other healthcare audit data. HIPAA's minimum-necessary principle is a useful design pressure: log enough to explain a decision, but do not copy a patient's free text into every downstream index.

According to recent reports, A single giant vector index is not suitable when appointment state changes every few seconds or when eligibility filters are strict. Rebuilding embeddings for each slot mutation raises index cost and creates windows where the assistant can cite unavailable inventory. Use a hybrid index with a transactional availability store in those conditions.

Recent findings suggest that conversely, a lexical-only index is a poor fit when users describe needs in plain language and terminology varies across clinics. Stick with lexical search when the corpus is small, terminology is tightly controlled, and explainability matters more than paraphrase recall; it is easier to operate and cheaper to rebuild.

It has been revealed that do not select a reranker by a single offline score. A model that wins nDCG on generic medical text can lose on appointment constraints. Shadow traffic, replay the labeled query set after every index build, and gate deployment on safety metrics as well as latency and cost. The migration can be boring: dual-write source versions, compare ranked lists, then switch reads behind a feature flag and retain a rollback index.

It has been revealed that the durable rule is simple: constraints decide eligibility, ranking signals order eligible evidence, and the audit trail explains both. That division keeps semantic search useful without pretending that similarity is clinical judgment.
